translations.text: Clement [The story of Clement, who was a follower of Simon Peter.]
I, Clement, was from Rome, the city of the Romans. In the first years of my youth, I found that I could live in chastity and purity.
For from my childhood my thoughts suppressed the desire within me through toil and distress. There was in me a thought [?], but where it began I do not know.
It continually set the thought of death before me: What then? When I die, will I no longer exist, just as I did not exist before?
And who will ever remember me, since this endless time brings everything belonging to everyone into oblivion and causes it to be forgotten?

Will I be as though I had never existed? For I have seen those who existed become as though they had never existed, neither knowing nor being known, as though I had never existed and never would exist. And did this world come into being at some time?
And before it came into being, what was there? Or has it existed from eternity, at all times and forever? And if it did come into being,
will it also be dissolved? And after its dissolution, what will there be? Perhaps only silence and oblivion. Or perhaps what will happen cannot be known.
So I continually pondered these things and others like them, though I do not know where these thoughts came from. Painful distress was with me, and thus I wasted away
and grew weak from great exhaustion. What was harder still was that whenever I wanted to drive this worry away from me, as something harmful and useless, this
torment would stir within me again with greater force. Because of this I was in great distress and sorrow. Yet this very thought within me became a good cause leading to eternal life,

as I eventually learned and understood through experience, and I thanked and praised God, the Lord of all. For through this thought, which had troubled me from long before, toward searching out and discovering these matters
I was compelled to advance. Then I pronounced woe on those whom previously, in my ignorance, I had been inclined to call blessed.
So from the time I was a child, I was occupied with these and similar thoughts
throughout my growing years. And in order to learn something true, I devoted myself constantly to the teaching of the philosophers.
Among them I found nothing but the construction and elaboration of doctrines, their refutation and destruction of one another’s teachings, many disputes and quarrels, and skillful arguments,
tricks for trapping people, and arrangements of words. Sometimes they would take the position that the soul does not die. When [?] does not die, I rejoiced.
But whenever they maintained that it was mortal, I was distressed. I was especially saddened and troubled because I could not establish either position firmly in my mind.
Nevertheless, I perceived that judgments about these subjects depended on those who investigated and taught them: they seemed false or true
rather than appearing as they really were. So when I eventually realized that understanding the subjects under investigation did not depend on the subjects themselves,
but on the investigators themselves, who prevailed in shaping people’s judgments, I became still more tightly bound, as though by chains, to these
matters, and I sighed from the depths of my soul. For I could not establish anything firmly in my mind, and driving away my worry and anxious reflection about these things was not something
I could do. For I wanted very much to do so, as I said before. Yet whenever I repeatedly ordered myself to be silent, somehow, secretly, as though
through the hidden eye of the heart, reflection on these and similar things would enter me. And again, when I found myself in doubt, I would say to myself:
Why am I laboring in vain? The matter is clear: if, when I die, I no longer exist, I ought not to be distressed now, while I do exist. For this reason I should put the matter aside.
As for that time when I do not exist, I will not be distressed either. But if I do exist, something unnecessary is now being added to me: this distress I feel.
Then, immediately afterward, another thought came into my mind. For I was saying, “What if those things there distress me more than the things that distress me now? [?]”
“There I have something harsh to endure, because I have not conducted myself justly and righteously, and I am handed over, as the sayings of certain philosophers declare,
“to Pyriphlegethon and Tartarus, like Sisyphus or Tityus or Ixion or Tantalus, and I remain in Sheol forever under punishment.”
Then again I would argue against these thoughts and say, “But these things do not exist.” Then again I would say, “But what if they do exist?” And because
the matter was unknown and hidden, I would say again, “This is better, and there is no danger in it: that I should righteously
“conduct myself throughout my life.” Then again I would consider how I could overcome the body's desires for the sake of justice, when punishment and hope were unknown. Nor, indeed, did I
fully know what righteousness was that pleased God. Nor was I convinced that the soul was immortal, nor could I establish which teaching was true.

Nor could I silence the turmoil of these thoughts and anxieties. What, then, should I do but go to Egypt, become acquainted with the prophets and those who knew the mysteries of the hidden caves there, and seek out a magician?

Once I found him, I would persuade him with a large sum of money to perform the calling up of a soul, which is called necromancy—divination through the dead—as though I were asking about some particular matter.
But my actual question would concern this: learning whether the soul was immortal.
My knowledge that the soul was immortal would not come from its answering, speaking, and hearing, but solely from its appearing to me, so that, once I had seen it with my own eyes,
this would be enough to bring me relief, simply because it appeared to me and existed. From then on, uncertain words that reached my hearing could no longer undo what I had seen with my own eyes.
I also told this thought to a philosopher with whom I was acquainted and consulted him about it. He spoke to me and advised me
not to dare do this, for many reasons. “For,” he said, “if the soul does not obey the magician, as you say, then you, as someone who has acted contrary to those who detest this practice,
“will have become liable during your lifetime to punishment without pardon. And I think that even your righteousness will no longer accompany

“and go along with you—the righteousness for whose sake you are even daring to attempt this. For they say that God is hostile toward those who disturb and trouble souls after the body's dissolution and death.” But I,

when I heard these things, became reluctant to press these matters. Yet I did not cease from these anxieties and others like them. Rather, because the force of my resolve had been frustrated, I was greatly distressed.
But so that I do not recount these same things to you at length,

while I was occupied with thoughts and matters like these, a report quietly began to spread during the reign of Tiberius Caesar, starting at the turn of Nisan, and kept growing. Like a good angel of God, it ran throughout the whole

world, for God's will could not allow it to remain silent. So it continually increased and grew, and it was being said that a man in Judea, beginning at the turn of Nisan, was proclaiming to the Jews the kingdom of God,

which had existed from eternity, saying that everyone who first set his life in order through good conduct would enjoy it. And so that this man who did these things might be believed, as one who was full of divinity,
he performed many wonders, great signs, and mighty deeds by a command alone, as someone whose authority came from God himself.
For he made the deaf hear and the blind see, strengthened the paralyzed and the lame, and drove away every disease. The dead who were brought to him rose.

And lepers were healed and cleansed merely by seeing him from a distance. There was nothing he could not do. Indeed, as time went on, the news spread widely through the many people who came, and it was confirmed. It was no longer merely a report,
but the reality of the matter itself. Thus gatherings were also held in various places to discuss and consider who this person who had appeared really was
and what he wished to say. For in the very summer of that year, a certain man openly stood in a public place before all the people
and cried out, saying, “People of Rome, listen! The Son of God has come to Judea and has promised eternal life to all who desire it,
if they first conduct their lives according to the will of the one who sent him. For this reason, change your ways
from evil to virtue and from temporary things to eternal things. Acknowledge the one God who is in heaven, in whose world you live unjustly before his righteous gaze.
But if you change and conduct your lives according to his will, you will pass into another world and live forever,
and you will enjoy his hidden blessings, which cannot be expressed.” Now this man was a Hebrew

from that land, and his name was Barnabas. He said of himself that he was one of his disciples. He was staying here in a certain place and readily recounted his master's deeds to those who wished to hear.
I too came with them and stood beside the crowd gathered around him. I listened to his words and recognized their truth, for he was not speaking with elaborate rhetorical skill.
Instead, simply and without elaborate artifice, he gave a convincing account of what he had heard and seen the Son of God who had appeared do and say. And witnesses
in great numbers to these miracles and to the words he spoke, he brought forward and pointed out even from among the crowd standing there.
But because the crowd gladly accepted these things, which were spoken without cleverness or artifice, certain philosophers,
who had been trained in secular learning, wanted to ridicule and mock him. They jeered at him and insulted him with boundless arrogance, using the art of reasoning like a mighty weapon

in debate. But he brushed aside their insolence and did not pursue the cleverness and cunning of their questions. Instead, fearlessly and without being intimidated, he did not depart from what he was saying.
On one occasion someone asked him why a gnat, although it is small, has six legs as well as wings,
while an elephant, the largest of the animals, has no wings and only four legs. After this question, however, he resumed the discourse that had been interrupted.
As though answering the question, he gave a reply and returned to the discourse he had intended from the beginning. He always used this same opening to his discourse whenever they interrupted
his speech: “We have a command from the one who sent us to tell you only his words, his deeds, and his miraculous acts. Instead of verbal
demonstrations, we offer you many witnesses from among yourselves who are standing here, people whom I remember by sight as living portraits.
It is now in your power either to listen or to refuse to be persuaded. But I will not stop telling you what benefits you,
because it would be a loss to me if I remained silent, and harm to you if you were not persuaded. But proofs too

I could have offered concerning your empty questions, if you had been asking out of love for the truth. But as for the difference between the created beings—the gnat and the elephant—being explained to you who do not know the God who is over all—

You—for this is not the time now.” When he said this, they all, as though on cue, broke into uproarious laughter to silence him and overwhelm him with objections, as though he were a Greek and a barbarian [?].
But when I saw these things, I was seized with zeal, I do not know how, and with righteous anger, and I could no longer endure remaining silent
and putting up with it. Instead, I cried out publicly and said, “Justly and rightly God has determined that his will should not be understood by you, because he knew you beforehand,
that you are unworthy of these things which have been made evident until now, through which he has equipped you with knowledge and discerning understanding. For now the heralds of his will
have been sent, not professing skill in grammar, but revealing and making known his will in simple, clear words, without artifice, so that everyone who
hears what is being said, without pretense and without envy [?]. Whoever does not wish to reveal it to everyone [?]. You, then, have approached, and besides this, without

knowing these things, you turn your own benefit into harm to your souls by mocking the truth. Among the barbarians it is practiced and acknowledged, to your condemnation. Even now, when it has come to you, you do not
want to receive it, because of your shamelessness and because of the simplicity of its words, lest you be exposed as lovers of empty, meaningless words rather than lovers of truth
and lovers of wisdom. How long, then, will you keep learning to speak, when you do not even know how to speak? For you have many speeches that are not worth a single
word. What indeed will this assembly of you Greeks say when it becomes entirely one soul, if there is a judgment, as this man said? ‘Why, God, did you not reveal your will to us?’
No! Look, you are constantly hearing—if he considers you worthy even of an answer—such things as these: ‘I know, before the foundations of the world, all the choices that each individual will make.

As each was worthy, I secretly made things known beforehand and made myself known. I wished to make known and explain to those who take refuge in me that this is indeed so: for this reason, from the beginning,

from the earliest generations, I did not allow my will to be proclaimed openly before everyone. But now, at the end of the world, I have sent heralds of my will, who, as you see, are even being mocked,
insulted, and reviled by those who do not wish to receive any help at all. They are harshly questioned because of my love [?]. Oh, what great injustice, that even

to the point of being killed the heralds are brought! These things happen to them at the hands of the very people who are being called to salvation and life. This injustice and lawlessness that takes place
against my heralds would have happened against them all from the beginning, if those who were worthy had been individually called to salvation from the beginning. For this very thing
that they now do unjustly is an arrogant attack on my righteous providence [?]. It was therefore right that, from the beginning, before everyone, the word that deserves honor
should not be exposed by me to insult without benefit. Rather, I wished it to remain in silence, as something honored. I did not keep it silent from those who were worthy of it long ago,
for they received it and shared in it, but from these people and others like them, who are plainly unworthy, who hate even me and do not wish to love themselves.’
And now, stop laughing at this man, and question me in accordance with his promise. Or let anyone among you who wishes answer the question I put to you.
Do not bark like filthy dogs, or with disorderly shouting close and block the hearing of those who wish to live. You wicked people, you haters of God, who destroy the life-giving knowledge
of your minds through unbelief! How can you receive forgiveness when you insult those who promise to tell you about the knowledge of God?
And in doing this, you insult that man whose goodwill toward you it would have been right and proper for you to welcome, even if he had spoken no truth at all.”
While I was saying these things, and other things that followed from them and were like them, a great commotion arose in the crowd.
Some of them supported me, as though they pitied that foreigner. Others, who were foolish and senseless, gnashed their teeth fiercely at me.
Since evening had now fallen, I took Barnabas firmly by the hand, against his will, brought him to my lodging, and made him stay there,
so that no one would lay hands on him. He stayed with me for a few days and let me hear a few words from the teaching of truth—only a little, as was possible in a few days. And he said,
“I am hurrying to Judea because of the customary duties of my teaching ministry.” He now wanted to be with his own people, and this distressed me greatly. For I said to him,
“Just tell me the words of that Son of Man who appeared, and I will adorn them with my own words and proclaim the will of God.
Then, within a few days, I will travel with you to wherever you are going. For I very much want to come to the land of Judea, and perhaps I will even live with you for the rest of my life.”
When he heard this, he answered me, “If you want to see our affairs and learn something that will help you,
travel there with me immediately. Otherwise, the directions to our dwelling and everything you want
I will tell you today, so that whenever you are free to come, you will find me.
For tomorrow I am traveling to my own people.” When I saw that no one could hold him back, I went with him as far as the harbor,
and learned from him the directions to the dwelling of those he had mentioned.
I said to him, “If I were not trying to collect some money owed to me, I would travel with you immediately, right now. But I will catch up with you soon.”
After saying this to him and entrusting him to the officers of the ship, I returned from it in great distress, remembering him as a good friend and a pleasant companion.
I stayed a few days, but because I was in a hurry, I could not collect the whole debt. I gave up the remainder because it was delaying me.
I quickly set out for Judea, and in fifteen days I reached Caesarea of Straton. When I had stepped ashore and gone up into the town, while I was looking for somewhere to stay, I learned
that a man named Peter, the chosen disciple of that Son of Man who had appeared in Judea and performed signs and wonders, would on the following day, with Simon the Samaritan from Gitta,
hold a debate. When I heard this, I asked them to show me where this man was staying. When they had shown me and I had found the doorway,

I approached the threshold, spoke, and explained who I was and where I had come from. Immediately Barnabas came forward. As soon as he saw me, he embraced me with great joy and tears, and took me by the hand.
He brought me in to where Peter was, saying to me, “This is Peter, whom I promised you, a man great in the wisdom of God. I have been speaking to him about you continually,
so that you may know at once that I have truthfully told him about all your good qualities. I have also made your good intentions known to him, so that he too longs to see you.
So I am presenting you to him with my own hands as a great gift.” After saying this, he brought me up to him and said, “This is Clement, Peter.”
He, being good and full of kindness, sprang up as soon as he heard my name, kissed me, and had me sit down. Immediately he said to me, “You did well to receive Barnabas, the herald of truth,
into your lodging with a generous spirit, in honor of him who is the God of truth, without being ashamed or afraid of those undisciplined crowds. And blessed
you will be. For just as you received the messenger of truth into your dwelling with great honor, so Truth himself will make you, who are a stranger to his city, a citizen of his city.”
And then you will rejoice greatly that, because of the small kindness you have now lent, since you have desired good words, you will become an heir to those eternal good things that cannot
be taken away and never come to an end. And now do not be reluctant to tell me about your customary practices, for Barnabas has truthfully told us everything about you,
speaking well of you before me every day. But to speak briefly to you as to a dear friend about the matter before me: if nothing prevents you, join us and travel with us,
sharing in and receiving the words of truth that I am going to present in every city, all the way to Rome itself. And you, too, say whatever you wish.
I then told him about my desires from the very first day, and how I had worn myself out investigating doubtful questions, and everything that I previously wrote down from the beginning,
so that I will not write the same things over again. I told him that I was ready to travel with them.
“You do not know how gladly I desire this very thing. But first I want to be fully instructed about the truth, so that I may know whether the soul is mortal or immortal,
and whether it lasts forever, and whether it must be judged for what it has done here; and what justice and righteousness are that please God;
and whether the world came into being, and from what it came into being, and whether it will be dissolved, and whether it would have been better for it to have come into being in this way,
or not to have existed at all.” And, without listing them one by one, I said that I wanted to learn these things and similar questions connected with them.
Peter answered me on these matters and said briefly, “Clement,
I will give you knowledge of things as they are. But now listen to what belongs in its proper place. The will of God existed,
though it was not revealed, for many reasons: first, because of evil influence, bitter upbringing, hateful habits, bad associations, and misguided preconceptions.
And because of these there are greed, love of empty praise, and countless other evils like these, resembling a great cloud of smoke.

It fills this world as though it were a house in which people live, and it clouds and disturbs the sight of the people inside it. It does not allow them to turn and look upward, to know God their Creator, or to discern and do what pleases him.
For this reason, those who love the truth must cry out and call from within their hearts, and with a truth-loving mind call for help, so that someone who is outside the smoke-filled house [?]
may approach and open the door. Then the sunlight from outside will be able to enter and spread through the house, while the smoke from the fire inside
will go out and disperse. Now, the helper I spoke of—I meant the Prophet, for he alone can enlighten human souls,
so that with their own eyes they may see the path of salvation and eternal life. For it is not possible otherwise,

as you yourself know. You said a little while ago that all arguments are overturned by counterarguments, and that, according to the ability of the person examining them, the very same arguments seem true
or false. Consequently, the matters themselves are no longer seen as they actually are, but receive their assessment from those who examine them:
whether they exist or do not exist, whether they are true or false. For this reason, the true Prophet is needed in every matter concerning reverence for God, so that he may tell us everything

as it really is, and what we ought to believe about everything. Therefore, we must first investigate and examine the Prophet himself through a thorough inquiry into his prophecy. Once we have found him to be true, we should then believe him about everything,
and no longer question him about each individual thing he says. Instead, we should accept these things as true, with the conviction of faith, holding firmly to them through careful examination.
For through one initial demonstration and diligent inquiry from every side, everything can be correctly grasped in the mind. For this reason, before everything else, it is necessary
that we should seek the true prophet himself, because without him no truth can be revealed to human beings. He reassured me by explaining to me who he is and how he can be found.
And he truly enabled me to find him, and showed me clearly, through what I heard, the truth of the teaching about the prophet, more clearly than the things visible before my eyes.
So I was astonished and amazed that no one understands these things, which everyone needs. And at his command I undertook to write down the discourse about
the prophet and send it to you from Caesarea of Straton. For he said that you had instructed him to write down all his discourses and deeds each year and send them to you.

But on the very first day, at the beginning, he spoke to me about the prophet of truth, reassuring and satisfying me about everything. Then he said, “Look, then, and consider the debate I conduct against our opponents.

Even if I should prove deficient, I no longer fear that you might doubt the truth handed down to you because I seemed to have been defeated, rather than the teaching handed down to us through the prophet of truth.

That is, those who have understanding and love the true teaching can recognize from the words themselves which belong to the craft of persuasion, to rhetorical techniques, and to questions meant for amusement,
and which are good and straightforward, persuading solely by their own truth.” When he had said these things to me, I answered him and said,
“I thank God at once, for he has granted me satisfaction just as I wished to hear. But as far as I am concerned, be entirely free of anxiety about all this.
For I will never doubt in this way. Even if you yourself should ever wish to turn me away from the teaching about prophecy,
you would not be able to do so. For I know everything that I have received. And do not think that I am making grand promises to you
when I say that I will never doubt. For neither I nor any other human being who has heard the teaching about the prophet
can ever doubt, once he has first heard about the truth and knows what the certainty of prophecy is. Therefore take courage and be confident in this teaching,
which accords with God's will. For I have overcome every technique and craft of evil.
For nothing can prevail against prophecy: neither techniques, nor the devices of wisdom, nor ingenious arguments, nor any other abundance of anything—provided that the person who hears from the
true prophet truly loves the truth and is not, under the pretext of seeking the truth, pursuing and seeking something else.
And now, my lord Peter, do not be troubled, as though you had given a gift to someone who does not appreciate it and who cannot stray from the truth

given to him. Yet I know that it is possible for someone, however much he wishes, either to receive quickly or not to receive even after a long delay. Therefore I know that I must not despise the proof given to me because it was given quickly. It is beyond comparison, and it alone is the truth.”
11. When I had said these things, Peter said to me, “I thank God both for your salvation and life

and for my own joy and relief. For I was truly reassured when I learned that you understood the greatness of our prophecy. Therefore, as you said, even if I myself should ever wish—may it never happen—
to turn you to some other teaching, I would not be able to turn you away. Begin, then, tomorrow to follow me in the debate against our opponents. Tomorrow's debate is against Simon the magician.”

When he had said these things, he took food by himself and instructed me to take some too. He blessed the food and was distressed after he had eaten his fill, and reassured me with an explanation about this.

Afterward he said, “May God grant that you become like me in everything, be baptized, and share the same food with me.” Having said these things, he instructed me to sleep, for the body's own nature was demanding sleep.

The next day, early in the morning, Zacchaeus came in to us, greeted us, and said to Peter, “Simon is requesting a postponement from now until the eleventh of this month, which is seven days from now. For he says that then he”

I can carefully devote myself to the discussion for a while and come, as I said [?]. But allowing more time also helps, so that there may be many listeners and they may be stirred to judge the things being said. That is,
he said, “If you agree, when we gather, let us have the subjects we are going to examine prepared beforehand through many questions. Let us now tell one another which subject or subjects we intend

to investigate when the appointed time approaches, so that each of us may know beforehand, quietly reflect by himself, study them, and know what he is uncertain about concerning each subject, or whether he is uncertain about anything at all.
And if he is uncertain when he comes to the investigation and they begin the discussion, perhaps he will then receive an answer from his opponent. But if, from every side,

he questions the matter and knows that there is nothing he does not know, and that none of his arguments can be defeated, he demonstrates this in the examination itself, and he has already defeated the person who begins to investigate with him. I grant you this,” he said.

“But I advise, if you too agree, that before anything else the question should be asked: What is the first, irreproachable cause of everything that has come into being, if indeed it came into being? And what is it [?]?
And again, whether what came into being received its existence from one, from two, or from many; and whether it was taken from nothing or from something already existing and came to have this form.
And whether there is some power that raises things upward or brings them downward, something greater or lesser, which has moved from eternity or has never moved.
Or whether these things have existed as they are from eternity, at all times, and forever;
or whether they come into being without anything making them, and are dissolved without anything dissolving them.
If, then, we begin the investigation here, I think it will be possible to discover the nature of the things under examination, which are tested by persistent questioning.
And when this has been discovered, it will then readily give us a way into the matters that follow from these. This, then, is my advice.
It has now been made clear to you. But if you have some other preference to propose, do not hesitate to tell me.”
Peter answered these things and said, “Tell Simon that we will do as you wish, provided you understand that our arguments are always
ready and prepared through God’s providence.” When Zacchaeus heard this, he went out to deliver the reply to Simon. When he had gone out, Peter noticed that I was distressed
because of the postponement of the investigation, and said to me, “My dear Clement, anyone who has accepted and affirmed that the world is governed by God’s good providence
is not distressed by events, however they turn out. For he is convinced that, because God is just and knows these things better, he directs the outcome of all events toward what is beneficial,

especially for those who take refuge in him. Therefore, anyone who knows that this is so knows how, through sound judgment, to drive away from himself whatever distressing thing he encounters. For the good God, Clement,

cannot bring anything to its conclusion without knowledge. Therefore, do not let Simon’s present delay distress you either. For perhaps, through God’s providence, as I said, it has happened for your benefit,
so that, during the delay of these seven days, without disturbance, I might, from beginning to end and according to the tradition of the true Prophet,

entrust and hand over to you the things appropriate to teaching about the fear of God. For he alone knows how the things that have happened happened, and how the things to come will happen, and the things
that were spoken plainly but written obscurely and are read in the assembly, which cannot be understood without the tradition, because of the sins with which people
grow up, as I said before. Therefore, when these things are explained by me according to the will of the lawgiver, you will understand them all correctly.”
By saying these things he reassured me with these brief statements, covering the period from the beginning of creation until that day in Caesarea of Straton.
[Of Straton] [?] I met him, and he said to me, “I have handed these things on to you briefly, according to Simon’s understanding,
so that you might know the principle concerning everything. At another time, however, as suitable opportunities arise, the things that were stated briefly
I will discuss fully in a lengthy discourse, as I promised you from the beginning.
Therefore, since today alone remains for us out of those days that have passed,
I want to explain to you again those same things whose main points were previously stated to you briefly, so that you may be better able to retain them in your memory.” And when he had said
these things, he spoke to me again as follows: “Do you remember, my dear Clement, my account of that world which has no limit?” And when I said to him, “There is not even one thing
that I can fail to remember, Peter,” Peter was pleased with this and answered me: “I am glad that you said this and did not give a hasty answer.
For these primary and lofty matters ought to be honored in silence. But so that your private assurance may be believed, tell me what you remember about that discourse on prophecy,
and it is fitting that you should freely repeat many times what the decree is [?], so that, when I know how attentive your memory is, I too may immediately speak about those things
that I wish, with great joy, readily and easily, to entrust and relate to you.”

15. When I realized that he greatly rejoiced in the recollection of those who listened, I answered as follows: “I remember not only the decree but also the foreordination, and I have continually considered, each in its proper place, the knowledge of everything you entrusted to me.
For the things that were said became as though they belonged to my own soul, since you offered me a sweet drink when I was very thirsty. Therefore, so that you may not suppose of me
that, because I remember them, I am troubling you about how those things were spoken to me privately by you just now,
rather, whenever I heard something from you and moved on, I placed each one of these things in its proper place in my mind, so that, from the very order
of their arrangement, I could know precisely the things that were said. For an orderly arrangement also greatly helps memory.
For the mind seeks whatever is missing, and when it finds it, it keeps it. Or, if it does not remember it, it is not ashamed before the one who teaches it.
Or, if it does not remember it, it is not ashamed to ask and receive from the one who teaches it, to help its memory. But so that I may not delay my reply
to you with lengthy words, hear from me immediately, in brief, about that decree concerning which you questioned me. It is as follows:
He existed from eternity, and he exists in every age, and he exists forever—the one from whom came the first will, which encompassed time, the existence from eternity [?].
From that first will, then, came another will, and then the world; from the world came time, and from it the multitude of humanity; and from that multitude, the choosing of friends,
for whose perfection the peaceful kingdom of God is sought. You promised to tell me the rest of these things in their sequence at another time.
After these things, then, you said that the establishment of time brought existence into being. And you spoke about God’s foreordination: before all his angels, he first declared his will,

and made it an unalterable law for the rest. He decreed two kingdoms—I mean the present one and the one to come—and determined the time of each, commanding them to remain until the day of judgment appointed by him,

on which all generations and races will be judged. Thus the wicked, who are accursed because of their sins, will be thrown into everlasting fire for punishment. But those who conducted their lives according to the will of God, the maker of everything,
will themselves be blessed because of their good deeds and will shine like light. They will enter the eternal world and remain without decay, sharing in and receiving the hidden blessings of God.”

As I was saying these things, Peter truly rejoiced as over his own son. But he became anxious that perhaps I had not remembered the rest, and he was troubled on account of those who were nearby. He said, “You have sufficiently

explained it, and you have given an account of these things even more clearly than I did myself.” I answered him again: “It was skill with words that gave us these things—the skill that entertains many people with
empty words and knows how to mislead them easily. For there are some who choose elegant words that deceive the ear, and are unwilling to live by clear and simple words. For the elegance
of speech can help when truth is set before it. But if it is valued more highly than truth, it does harm. Yet how can you suppose, my lord Peter,
that I rejoice along with the rest of those others? Rather, I rejoice especially at this statement of yours, which embraces everything you said: that God is one and the world is his work,

and that, because he is just toward everything, he repays each person according to their deeds, whenever that may be. After this you went on to say, ‘For the proof of these things, then, my dear Clement, great quantities of words

are unnecessary, so that those who wish to live, once the true prophet has become known to them, no longer need the emptiness of many words.’ Therefore, when the teaching about the prophet was revealed to me,
I relied entirely on the proof and made my mind firm. When I understood, then, that this truly is reverence for God, I immediately answered, ‘You have spoken well, Peter. And for

this reason, entrust to me from now on, as to a faithful confidant, the things that belong to reverence for God, as the prophet of truth himself has approved. You have convinced me to believe in him alone. But the proof

by analogy, which catches unbelievers as though with a snare—keep that for those to whom you have not yet decided to reveal the prophecy that does not err.’ When I said these things to you, you promised me both
that you would tell the account clearly, simply, and without error, and also that you would give me, in due time, the proof concerning each individual matter. That is, you briefly related to me
these things from the beginning of the world to the present day, and how each of them happened. If you wish, I can tell you how I remember these things.

When I had said these things, Peter answered, “I rejoice greatly at your attentiveness, since no word escapes you. For this is a sign of someone who bears and produces fruit for the life of salvation.
For someone who has learned to do good deeds, because he wishes to remember them, knows how to do what he has learned. But someone from whom the words capable of saving him from evil are stolen,
even if he wishes to be saved and live, cannot do so, because from the beginning he has not remembered what he ought to do. Therefore, listen again now to how the world was created,
as the prophet of truth entrusted it to us, so that, when we know who it was that graciously brought this world into existence when it did not exist, we too may strive to love God himself,

who can do everything, and receive what, in his greatness, greatly helps us. Love for him consists in our living according to his will, which has been established as a law for everything that comes into being [?].
But now listen to a brief account, according to the prophet’s tradition, of the main points of what you heard before, so that, as I said earlier, they may remain in your memory.

In the beginning, when God made heaven and earth like a single house, the shadow cast by the bodies of the world darkened what was within them. This shadow, through the light that shone at God’s command,

was swallowed up as though it were nothing. Then the darkness was reckoned as night, and the light was called day. In the midst of the waters that were within, he stretched out the firmament, fixing the waters in place.
He made it like a barrier and named it heaven, honoring it with the earlier name. Thus this entire outstretched expanse, which formed the house [?], he immediately divided into two regions.
The reason for its division was this: that the region above should become a dwelling place for angels.
And what was below was to be given to human beings. Then those waters that remained below, at the will of the one who commanded, settled and gathered in the hollows of the earth.
Thus dry land appeared, and the gathering of the waters was called seas. The earth that had appeared brought forth plants and springs, and the courses of rivers upon the mountains
she displayed within their boundaries, so that the human beings who were to come might find a suitable dwelling, and so that each of them could do there whatever he wished to do.
I mean either good or evil. After these things, he adorned the heavens with stars, and he made the sun and the moon to give light, one at night and the other by day,
while also indicating things that exist and things to come, things belonging to time and things belonging to eternity.

For this reason they also served as signs, for times and seasons. They are visible to everyone, but are understood by those who study them diligently. Then he commanded living creatures to come forth from the earth and the waters, and he made Paradise, which he named the place of delight.
After these things he made the human being, for whose sake he had prepared all these things beforehand, whose image is older, and on whose account
everything received grace, so that the things made and set apart for his service and his dwelling might exist. Then, when everything in heaven had been completed,

and on earth and in the waters, and human beings had multiplied, the eighth generation came. Righteous men who had been living like angels, because of the beauty of women, abandoned their former way of life and engaged in indiscriminate intercourse.

They were trained to do everything without understanding. These are the very beings whose existence was handed down in tradition, and they undertook to commit even greater evil. They were also the ones who enticed all
human beings, partly through fear and partly through persuasion, to sin against the Maker of all. From them, in the ninth generation, were born the giants who have been famous from ancient times.
It was not that they had serpents’ feet, as the Greek tales say, but that they were enormous.
In the size of their bodies they resembled great mountains. Their bones lie here and there as a sign because of unbelief, in those regions that I told you about on another occasion.
Against them God’s righteous providence brought the flood, and the world was being cleansed by the flood. Everything became like that primordial deep, and the dross of the wicked perished.

But the one righteous man found at that time, whose name was Noah, was saved in the ark with his three sons and their wives. After the waters had receded, together with the animals that had entered with him

and with seeds, he came out and lived in [?]. In the twelfth generation, through the blessing with which God blessed them, they began to multiply. They received the first commandment, not to taste blood, for this too had been a reason for the flood.
In the thirteenth generation [twelfth], the middle one of Noah’s sons was the first to dishonor his father.
His descendants were cursed to slavery. His elder brother received by lot the portion in the middle of the earth,
in which is the land of Judah. The third, however, received the eastern portion, in which is the land of the Jews. The third, however, received the eastern portion.
The western portion fell to him by lot. In the fourteenth generation, a man from that cursed line was the first to seek a pretext for sorcery.
He offered demons the honor of blood. In the fifteenth generation, human beings first worshiped fire and made idols. Until then, one language was shared by all: Hebrew, beloved by God.

In the sixteenth generation, they departed from the east and came to the places allotted to their ancestors, and they named those places after themselves. In the seventeenth generation, Nimrod was the first to reign in Babylon.
He built a city, and from there he moved to Persia and taught its people to worship fire.
In the eighteenth generation, cities were built with walls. They organized armies and [?], established the judgments and laws they wished, and built temples.
They worshiped their rulers as gods. In the nineteenth generation, the descendants of the one who had been cursed after the flood abandoned the boundaries of their land, for by lot
They took the western region and drove those whose allotted region was the central one eastward as far as Persia. They themselves settled in the places of those who had been driven out.
Now in the twentieth generation, because of participation in wickedness,
the son was the first to die a natural death, before his father. In the twenty-first generation there was a certain wise man,
from the family of those who had been driven out, descended from Noah’s firstborn. His name was Abraham, and from him our people, the Hebrews, who are also called
Jews, multiplied. Now this man, when the whole world was in error and was about to perish because of its wickedness—not by water but by fire—
and when that plague had begun at Sodom and was about to spread over the whole world, through his knowledge of God and his love for him, by which he especially pleased him, saved the whole world
from perishing. At first, however, he was in error along with everyone else, practicing the art of the Chaldeans. From the ordering of the stars he came to know the one who had ordered them.
And through the providence of God, whom he had come to know, an angel approached him
and testified to him about his election. As for the land that was owed to his family, he promised him not to give it as a gift, but to repay and restore it.
Now while Abraham was troubled and wished to know things as they really are, the true prophet appeared to him—the one who alone knows the will of each individual human being.
In one day he revealed everything to him and also gave him certainty about God and the coming into being of the world,
its dissolution, the soul that does not die, the conduct that pleases God, and also that the dead rise and judgment takes place, and that those who are found virtuous forever
receive hidden blessings, while those who are wicked undergo the punishment of eternal fire. In short, he revealed everything to him and returned [?] to his own inaccessible place.
So Abraham, while he was still without knowledge of the divine majesty, as the truthful account
says, and as the true prophet testifies, and also as the proof of these things was given to you by me on another occasion, had
two sons. One of them was later called Ishmael, and the other Eliezer. From them the peoples of the Arabs and Persians multiplied, and some of them
also intermingled with the Brahmans, who were their neighbors. Some descendants of the one who lived in Arabia also spread into Egypt, which was nearby.
For this reason some Indians and Egyptians are circumcised and observe other purifications with particular care [?].

Although the passage of time changed the goodness of their purity into wickedness for some of them, this same man, who had two sons during the time of his ignorance, when he came to know the truth, asked God, because he was righteous,
that he might have a son by Sarah, who had been his lawful wife since his youth and who was barren.
And she was given the son whom he called Isaac. Isaac fathered Jacob, Jacob fathered twelve, and the twelve fathered seventy-two.

When a famine occurred, their entire household came to Egypt. Over four hundred years they multiplied through the [?] and promise of God, and the Egyptians cruelly oppressed them. While they were being oppressed,

Moses, the true prophet, came to them. He punished the oppressive Egyptians, who would not let the Hebrew people leave and go to the land of their ancestors, and struck them with ten plagues from heaven.

Thus he brought the people whom God loved out of Egypt. Because of this, some of the surviving Egyptians, together with their king, whom they followed in wrongdoing, set out and overtook the Hebrews. They trapped them in one place at an inlet of the sea,
and wanted to destroy them all with swords. But because they were intending to attack them, the prophet divided the sea through his prayer to God, and into two

He divided it into sections so that it would part, and in this way the people crossed. The entire company of Egyptians boldly went in after them and died. For as the last of the Hebrews was coming up,

the last of the Egyptians went down. Thus the sea, which had been held in place by the command of the one who divided it, flowed back to its original state, and the Egyptians who pursued them received their punishment in it.

So Moses, at the command of God, who knows everything, brought the many tens of thousands of Hebrews into the wilderness. He abandoned the short road leading from Egypt to Judea and led them through the long wilderness.
There, as they traveled for forty years, those evils that diminish through long habit [?] the light of time [?]
had accumulated among them. Another period of time, together with the giving of the law, would enter and mingle with them and be able to [?] them. Finally [?], they came to Mount Sinai.

Through heavenly voices they heard the law of God in all ten commandments. The first of these was that, in keeping the law, they should not make themselves any other image to worship. Moses then went up to the mountain.
For forty days, those crowds who had seen Egypt punished with ten blows, and who had crossed on foot through the divided sea,
and had received heavenly manna instead of bread, and had drunk water from the rock that followed them—water whose taste was changed by God's power according to their wishes—
and who also traveled beneath [?] of fire and a pillar of cloud, which shaded them by day because of the sun [?], while at night a pillar of fire gave them light because of the darkness—when
Moses delayed, they made an image of gold [?] resembling the idol in Egypt called Apis, and worshiped it. Even after all those demonstrations, they could not drive their evil habit from their hearts
or put it far away. For this reason, when Moses came down from the mountain, at God's command he abandoned, as I said before, the short road leading from Egypt to Judea.
He brought them through that long wilderness, as I said before, over a period of forty years.

The evils that had accumulated among them through their many habits during their long time in Egypt required another period of time to enter and mingle with the giving of the law and be able to change them. For this reason Moses too, when he came down from Mount Sinai

and saw that transgression, understood, like a good and faithful steward, that it was impossible for that entire people easily to rid themselves of the passion [?] for the sins of idol worship, which had been among them for a very long time
and had grown through their evil upbringing among the Egyptians, and to bring it to an end. For this reason he allowed them to offer sacrifices, but told them to do this in the name of God,
so that even half of this passion might be cut off and brought to an end. The correction of the other half would take place at another time through another person, with due care.
[?] For he said, “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me. Listen to him in everything. Whoever does not obey him shall surely die.”
It is clear that he gave himself to [?]. Along with these things, he also designated a place for them, in which alone they were permitted to offer sacrifices. This entire arrangement was devised
for them so that, when the proper time came, they could hear through him that God desires mercy and not sacrifices. Then the prophet who told them these things would be sent.
Those who believe in him would, through God's wisdom, be led to a fortified place in the land for the preservation of their lives, and would be kept safe from the war that afterward

would come upon those who refused to obey, bringing destruction upon them because of their division. This war, however, did not happen abruptly and unexpectedly. Rather, even before the coming of that prophet
who was to come to abolish sacrifices, that war came upon them many times through God's providence. They were taken captive and handed over to another people.
Because they no longer had the place in which the lawgiver had permitted them to sacrifice, they kept the law without sacrifices and were restored and delivered. And this very thing
They had many occasions to realize that when they kept the law without sacrifices, they were delivered; but whenever they returned to their own land and offered sacrifices, they went out
and were expelled from it, so that they would stop and no longer offer sacrifices. They were slow to recognize this, and it was known to only a very few. Even the knowledge of those few was obscured

by those crowds who entertained contrary thoughts and were unable to examine all this. For understanding without someone explaining things to them does not belong to the crowds; understanding in the mind belongs to the few.
So Moses himself, after arranging and ordering these things, appointed for them as commander a man named Joshua, to lead them to the land of their ancestors through the life-giving words of God. Then

he went up, and Moses died before them all—a death such that, to this day, no one has been able to find his grave. The crowds, however, entered the land of their ancestors, and through God's providence,
at their mere appearance they terrified those wicked nations and put them to flight. They took possession of the land of their ancestors, tribe by tribe, by lot, and until the time of the judges,
they had no kings and remained in good order in their own places. But when they appointed men over themselves who were tyrants rather than kings, then that

place which had previously been designated for them as a house of prayer they abolished, [?]. And under the power of the monarchy, as though this were something they could not do of their own free will,
they were driven by force. Thus, by those wicked kings who ruled over them from time to time, they were led into greater wickedness.
From then on, therefore, since this deficiency needed correction, the appropriate time had arrived, in which the prophet previously proclaimed by Moses was to be revealed.
At his coming, because of God's mercy, he first admonished them to cease and refrain from offering sacrifices. And so
that they would not think themselves deprived of the forgiveness of sins obtained through sacrifices, and this become an obstacle preventing their obedience,
baptism in water for the forgiveness of sins was appointed and made known to them—the baptism which truly does grant forgiveness of sins.
And for those who become perfect, [?] children of eternity who do not die, oil to preserve them, so that, when it pleased God, in his indescribable wrath,
they would be saved from the war that was to come for the destruction of those who had not obeyed. Thus, the very thing they had been unwilling to do of their own free will, this very thing, when
they had left their own land and no longer had that place which had been uprooted from them, they would accept having to observe, even against their will, as it pleased God.
When these things had thus been ordained, the good prophet himself appeared and performed signs. Yet even so, the ancient people did not believe,
although they had already been prepared to believe. For there are some people more wretched than everyone else, who are unwilling to believe either the good or the wicked
on account of excellence. Besides not believing, they do not hesitate to insult them on whatever pretexts they can find, and they call these people sorcerers
and demons. Wickedness can gain such complete victory over the wicked that, had God's wisdom not helped those who love the truth,
perhaps even they would have gone astray. But to us he revealed what was ours. When he came, he first chose us twelve to be apostles,

and then seventy-two chosen disciples, so that, even in this way, through the correspondence, the crowds might recognize that he was the prophet whose coming Moses had previously proclaimed. But perhaps arranging a number is easy for anyone.

The signs and wonders he performed at his coming, however, no one can perform. For Moses performed signs in Egypt, and the prophet who arose like him performed signs among the people themselves, drove away every disease,

and proclaimed eternal life. Yet, through their wicked folly, the wicked brought upon him the punishment of the cross. Even this, by his own power, he changed into something good and beneficial. For together with this suffering of his,

The whole world suffered. For even the sun grew dark, the stars were thrown into confusion, the sea was disturbed, the mountains broke apart, the tombs were opened, and the front of the temple doorway was split, as though
it were mourning over the destruction that was to come upon the place. Because of these things, therefore, all the people were shaken and were compelled to inquire into these events,
and to come forward. Yet there were some whose minds were not stirred to inquire into this, even though the whole world was shaken. Because
it was therefore right [?] those who were not persuaded, that people from the nations should be called to complete the number that had been shown to Abraham, this upheaval occurred
and threw all the people into confusion. That hostile power which opposed those free people was continually darkened, and it prepared them for the burning that comes from the Majesty.

This was so that those who wished to approach the message of salvation might be stronger than the power that had been hindering them, and might readily, by their own choice, receive the victory that comes through salvation. Now, while he was suffering, there was darkness from the sixth hour until the ninth.

But when the sun appeared and those things returned to their former condition, those same wicked people returned to their own ways. For some of them said of the one who had suffered and who could not be found, although he had been under guard,
that he was a sorcerer. They were not afraid to dare to lie. Yet the justice of truth had prevailed. For their lie against us, told because we were few, did not succeed for them.

For we continued to become far more numerous than they, as though through God's zeal, so that even their priests now feared that, through God's providence and to their own shame, all the people would come to our faith.
And they repeatedly sent to ask us to speak with them about Jesus: whether he was the prophet foretold by Moses, who is the Messiah from of old.
For this alone is the point of disagreement between us who believe in Jesus and those who do not believe
among our own people. But although they asked us many times, we were watching for a suitable time.

One week of years had passed since the suffering of Jesus. The church in Jerusalem, which had been established by our Lord, had grown large and was being governed rightly and in good order by James, who had been appointed bishop by our Lord himself.
So, during the days of Passover, we twelve apostles gathered in Jerusalem with a large congregation,
to assemble with our brothers for the festival. Each of us asked James to tell us the main points of what had happened in the world, and he gave us a brief account.
Caiaphas the high priest sent priests to us apostles, asking us to come to him so that either we might persuade him that Jesus is the Messiah from of old,
or he might persuade us that he is not, so that all the people might thus come to whichever faith it was.
He asked us many times to do this. But we deliberated at considerable length, and we were seeking and watching for a suitable time.
And I, Clement, answered him: “I think that this inquiry into whether he is the Messiah is very helpful to the discussion of reverence for God.
For, as you said, even the high priest, along with all the others, repeatedly sent requests, wishing either to learn or to teach the things concerning him.”
Peter answered me: “You have spoken rightly, my dear Clement, and have understood correctly. For just as it is impossible to see without an eye,
or to hear without the faculty of hearing, or to receive smells without nostrils, or to speak without a tongue, or to touch without hands,
so it is impossible to know what pleases God without the true prophet. For in this way reverence for God belongs to the prophet alone, because of his foreknowledge.”
After this I answered him and said, “As for his being the true prophet—”
For you have taught me, and I know. But I want to know what Christ is and why he is called this, so that my knowledge about him may not be vague.
Then Peter began to speak as follows: “God [?], who made the world and is Lord of everything, appointed rulers over everything,
even over plants, stones, springs, rivers, and all created things. For there are many of them that he named according to their likeness.
So then, look [?]: the ruler of angels is an angel; of spirits, a spirit; of stars, a star; of birds, a bird; of animals, an animal; of creeping things, a creeping thing; and of fish, a fish.
And the ruler of human beings is a human being: he is Christ. In religious usage, however, he is called Christ in a special sense. For the name of all rulers
is a common one: the name ‘king.’ But the particular name among the Parthians is ‘Arsaces,’ and among the Romans, ‘Caesar.’ Likewise, among the Jews it is ‘Christ.’
The reason he is called Christ is this: because he was the Son of God and became a human being.
And because he was the first ruler, his Father anointed him from the beginning with oil that comes from the tree of life. Thus, with this oil, he too, in the same way, according to the prior
[?] of his Father, anointed the righteous who resembled him when they came there. Since they had traveled along a difficult road, he anointed them with that oil to give them rest from their toil.
And so they shine like light, receive the Holy Spirit, and become immortal in eternal life. As for the nature of the tree of life,
I know that I told you about it on another occasion. But now I also want to tell you about its likeness.

In this present world, Aaron, the first high priest, was anointed with specially prepared anointing oil, which was a likeness of the true oil. He was given authority over the people, and for this reason, like a king, he received firstfruits.
He also received the poll tax as tribute and issued commands.
As a judge of things here, he was entrusted with distinguishing between what was clean and what was unclean. He was also a prophet to Moses,
as to someone greater than himself, to assist him, not by his own choice. That is, everyone who was anointed with that prepared oil,
by sharing in that which possesses authority, also became worthy of kingship, prophecy, or the high priesthood.
However, this gift, which came through the oil, was temporary. Understand, then, how powerful that precious and pure oil is,

which was to be given by God, since even this oil, which came from it, could bestow the gift of temporary leadership. For what is there in this present world greater than the hope of prophecy, the high priesthood, or kingship?”
And I, Clement, answered him: “I remember that you told me, Peter, about that first human being who came into existence, that he was a prophet.
But you did not tell me that he was anointed. If, then, no one is a prophet without anointing, how was that first human being a prophet when he had not been anointed?”
Peter laughed and answered me: “If that first human being prophesied, it is clear that he was also anointed.
Therefore, although that high priest of the Law was silent about his anointing, the matter is clear to us when we recall it ourselves [?]. For just as, if he had shown that he was anointed,
we would have known from his anointing that the one who was anointed was a prophet, even if this had not been written,
so, because he showed that he was a prophet, it is clear to us that he was also anointed. For without anointing he would not have been a prophet.

Rather, this is what you ought to have said: ‘If that anointing preparation was made by Aaron through the craft of perfumers, how was that first human being anointed with a craftsman’s oil, when crafts did not yet exist?’”

35 And I answered him, saying, “Do not be angry with me, Peter. I am not speaking about that oil compounded in time, but about that pure and simple oil which has been with God from eternity, in whose likeness you say this compounded oil was made.”
36 Peter became angry, as I thought, and said, “What do you suppose, Clement—

that everyone can know everything before its time? Now, so that we do not abandon the subject before us, at another time, when your understanding has advanced further, I will explain this too clearly to you. But with this compounded oil

that high priest was anointed and entrusted with prophecy. He kindled the burnt offering, raised the fire on high, and displayed it to the whole world. Thus, after Aaron, this high priest sprang up from the waters and appeared. I am not speaking about Moses,
but about the one who, after baptism, was named the Son, the Messiah, and was also called Jesus. He extinguished that burnt offering which was continually burning because of sins.
For when this one was revealed, the anointing of the high priesthood, prophecy, and kingship ceased. His manifest coming, then, was foretold by Moses the prophet, who brought God’s law
to the attention of humankind. Another before him also foretold it, as I told you on another occasion: he too announced beforehand that this one would come in his first, humble coming.
But at his second coming, this will be proved to be so. For he fulfilled the first when he came, taught judgment, was judged, and was killed. But at that second coming of his,
he comes to judge and condemn the wicked and give joy to the righteous. His second coming is made credible by his first coming. For the prophets who spoke about his first coming
also spoke about his second. Both of them, Jacob and Moses, are prophets. The greatness of this prophecy, then, is this: it was not foretold, as would have been fitting and natural, that those
who were to come would love him, so that no one should suppose that this was a conjecture rather than prophecy. What I mean is this: when the Messiah came,

it would have been natural and fitting for the Jews to believe in him, since they had been instructed to await this very one for salvation, as their fathers, who knew everything well, had handed down to them; and not
for those among the nations who were in error, who had never even heard his name or of his coming. Yet this prophet revealed and announced beforehand that the unbelievable would happen,
and said that he would become the hope of the nations—that the nations would hope in him, and not the Jews who had received and heard these things. And this is just what happened.

For when he came, those who were awaiting him on the basis of their tradition did not recognize him. But those who had heard absolutely nothing beforehand recognized him when he came, and after his departure they await him. Thus everything in that prophecy, which had seemed unbelievable, was fulfilled exactly.
And he became the hope of the nations. The Jews, then, were mistaken about the first coming of our Lord, and their dispute with us
concerns Jesus alone. For they too know that the Messiah is to come, since they await him. But that he has already come

in humility, and is the one called Jesus, they did not recognize. This very fact confirms and establishes all the more that he is the one, insofar as they do not all believe in him. Our dispute with them, then, is this:

whether this is the one who is to come, who has in fact already come, or whether it is someone else who has not yet come. This, then, is the one prophet, as I explained to you on another occasion in the discussion about prophecy.

But God reserved this one for the end of the world. For the evils of humankind could not be purged and washed away through anyone else, nor could creation be saved and live. I am speaking about conduct

arising from the freedom of a mind that governs itself. While these things are preserved, [?] he will reign with the righteous whom he finds, and with those who, because they pleased him, were taken away to remain in hiding, when the heavenly Jerusalem has received the righteous.

It is far brighter than the light of the sun. Then justice will be brought down upon the heads of those who practiced wickedness, as they deserve, since they themselves considered of little account those lives
which had been given to them, and turned to wickedness. They did not spare this opportunity for wrongdoing [?] the practice of justice. But the rest of what happens there cannot be spoken of.

Neither to angels nor to human beings, but only that they should know that God sits before the good for their benefit, and that forever, without end, it will be well with those who have kept his law and practiced it.
When he said these things, I said to him, “If those righteous people whom Christ’s kingdom reaches receive it and enjoy it, then those who died earlier have missed out on his kingdom.”
Peter answered and said, “You want me to reveal something of those hidden things, Clement. Yet I am not reluctant to reveal as much as I am permitted.”
For he said, “Christ has existed from the beginning, throughout all generations. He was secretly present with those who wished to live in the fear of God.”
They awaited him as though he were far away, because this is an advantage for those in whose time he appears:

They do not have to wait until their bodies have decomposed and then rise, but can remain as they are, if they are found righteous. For all those who pleased him, whenever they lived, follow the example of that first man.
Because he pleased him, he was taken away. Like him, they are in paradise and are being kept for the kingdom of the Good One. But those who have not completed the measure of their righteousness,

since some remnant of evil remained in their bodies, have their bodies decomposed, while their souls are kept in honor in a distinguished place. Thus, at the resurrection of the dead, their souls put on their bodies, which have been purified through decomposition.

Because of their past good deeds, they inherit eternal life. For this reason, blessed are those who encounter and receive Christ’s kingdom: they also escape the punishment of Sheol, are delivered, and remain without decay.
In this way they also escape the terror of the judgment, as they longed to do. Furthermore, they are the first to see the Father, and they are ranked among the first who stand before God.
Because the inquiry about Christ was no small matter, those Jews who did not believe gnashed their teeth fiercely at us, as they wondered whether [?]

he really was the one against whom they had previously sinned and transgressed. Their fear grew and increased still further because, at the very moment when he was nailed to the cross, everything suffered along with him.

Furthermore, although his body was being guarded, it could not be found, and many people were continually coming to believe the message about him. Those who did not believe were therefore compelled, together with Caiaphas, their priest,

to undertake an inquiry about the one who had suffered. For this reason, as I said earlier, he sent to us many times, and they asked us to come so that they might learn or teach whether Jesus was the Christ.
We decided to go up to the temple and testify to them about Christ before all the people, and at the same time to rebuke many of them for their great wrongdoing.

For the people had become divided into many schools of thought, beginning in the days of John the Baptist. When Christ was about to be revealed in connection with the slaughter of sacrifices, and to reveal and make known baptism, that
opposing devil knew the time before [?] and created divisions and factions, so that, if the former sin received repentance and correction, a second transgression might be able to obstruct salvation.
The first of their groups, then, are those called Sadducees, who began in the days of John to separate themselves from the world as righteous people and to deny the resurrection
of the dead. They introduced a seemingly persuasive teaching to support their unbelief, saying, “It is not right for us to worship and fear God for a reward for goodness.”
Dositheus began with this view, as I said, and after Dositheus came Simon, who also began divisions, wishing to act in the same way as he had. Then there are others who are called Samaritans.
They too deny the resurrection of the dead. Instead of Jerusalem, the holy city, they worship Mount Gerizim, and they await the coming of one who is truly a prophet,

to set in order and correct the things that are unknown, as Moses foretold. Through the cunning of Dositheus they fell into divisions, and in this way they were prevented from turning back through Jesus.
The scribes and Pharisees who were baptized by John were persuaded to conceal the word of truth that they had received through Moses, which is like the key to the kingdom of heaven.

But those pure disciples of John separated themselves greatly from the people, and they said that their teacher was, as it were, in hiding. Thus, because of all these divisions among the people concerning [?], faith in Christ’s baptism had been disturbed.

Since, therefore, the high priest, together with the rest of the priests, had often asked us either to learn or to teach the things concerning Jesus, we went up to the temple with our entire congregation, by the decision of the whole church.

We stood on the steps with our entire congregation of believers. With everyone [?] in deep silence, the high priest first began to reassure the people, as though he wished to conduct the inquiry humbly, out of love for the truth.
He chose them as witnesses and judges of the inquiry that was about to take place. Indeed, he was very eager to praise those who seemed to be conducting their discussion for the forgiveness of sins.
He criticized the baptism given through our Jesus. Matthew rebuked him for this, saying that it is not only from the kingdom of heaven that someone is excluded
who has not been baptized, but that he is also in danger at the resurrection of the dead, even if he is good in his conduct and righteous in his thinking,
since he is left out of eternal life. He said these things calmly, testified to the things that followed from them, and then fell silent.
After this, the Sadducees, who do not believe in the resurrection of the dead, became angry when they heard it. One of them cried out from the middle of the crowd and said, “It is an error to suppose
that the dead will ever rise.” My brother Andrew spoke against him and showed that it is not an error to believe that the dead rise, because the one who had been
proclaimed beforehand by Moses as the prophet who was to come—that is, Jesus—had already demonstrated in his own case that the dead rise. But if it is not believed that this is the prophet whom Moses

proclaimed beforehand as the one who was to come, we must first learn everything clearly from his teaching. He said these things, testified to the things that followed from them, and then fell silent.
A certain Samaritan, whose thoughts and plans were opposed to the people and to God, said that the dead do not rise and that Mount Gerizim, rather than the holy place
in Jerusalem, is the place of worship. Speaking against Jesus as an enemy, he said that Jesus was not the prophet whom Moses had proclaimed beforehand as the one who was to come.
James and John, the sons of Zebedee, spoke wisely against this man and another who supported him. For they had received a command that they were not
to enter their city. A way was devised for them neither to speak with those with whom they had been forbidden to speak, nor, on the other hand, to remain silent and seem to have been defeated,

and so damage the sound faith of many. Thus they wisely spoke to them through a kind of silence. For it was desirable that they should believe that the dead rise and that the holy place in Jerusalem should be honored. Now

James rebuked them for thinking wrongly in not believing that the dead rise. His brother showed that they were going astray in something still more serious: they praised Mount Gerizim and dishonored the holy place in Jerusalem.
After these things, he immediately added that if they had known Jesus through his teaching, they would consequently also have believed in the resurrection of the dead,
and they would have found the place of Jerusalem. For this reason he said, “Before everything else, we must know whether this man, who performed signs and wonders like
Moses, is the prophet whom Moses proclaimed beforehand as the one who was to come.” They said these things, testified to the things that followed from them, and then fell silent.
45. One of the scribes cried out from the middle of the people and said, “Your Jesus performed signs and wonders like the magicians, and not like a prophet.” Against him Philip
[?] and said, “With this statement you are accusing Moses too, because he also performed signs and wonders in Egypt in the same manner as Jesus did here.”

He said these things so that the man would understand that the very thing he said about Jesus could also be said about Moses. He said these things, testified to the things that followed from them, and then fell silent.

When one of the Pharisees heard these things, he criticized Philip for saying that Jesus was equal to Moses. Bartholomew spoke against him and explained, “We are not saying that he is equal to Moses.”
But he is greater than Moses, because Moses was a prophet, which Jesus also is; but Moses is not what Jesus Christ is.
Thus, then, Jesus is also what Moses is, but Moses was not what Jesus is. He said these things, testified to the things that followed from them, and then fell silent.
After this, James son of Alphaeus spoke and argued that it was not right to believe Jesus.

[?] that the prophets are prophets, unless Christ himself testifies about them. For it is not right to accept testimony from lesser people as grounds for believing in someone greater and more excellent. Rather, we should recognize the lesser through the testimony of the greater and more excellent.
He said these things, testified to the things that followed from them, and then fell silent.

After this, Lebbaeus strongly rebuked the people because they had not believed in Jesus, who had helped them in everything through his instruction, his healing, and his words of comfort. And besides these things,

they even killed him and hated him—the one who had helped them in everything and had been their benefactor. He said these things, testified to the things that followed from them, and then fell silent.
One of John's disciples came forward and boasted about John, saying that he, and not Jesus, was the Christ. He said, “Jesus himself also said of him that he was greater than the prophets who
