had existed from the beginning. If, then, he is greater than Moses, clearly he is also greater than Jesus, because Jesus arose as one like Moses. It follows that John, who is greater than these, is the Christ.”
Against this man, Simon the Zealot argued that John was greater than those prophets who were born of women,
but not greater than the one who is the Son of Man. For this reason Jesus is also the Christ, whereas John was only a prophet. But in all this, far beyond comparison are
the things of Jesus with those of John, just as the one who is sent and runs ahead is far removed from the one who sends him to run ahead of him,
and the one who serves under the law from the one who established the law. He said these things, and they testified to the things that followed from them, and then he fell silent.
After this, Barabbas, who had become an apostle to the people in place of Judas the betrayer, advised them not to hate Jesus or be hostile to him, because this
is better for someone who does not know that Jesus is the Christ: not to hate him. For [?] has assigned a reward for love, not for hatred.

And because he took a body from among the Jews and became a Jew, God brings no small destruction upon anyone who hates him. He said these things, testified to the things that followed from them, and then fell silent.
After Barabbas's advice, Caiaphas criticized Jesus' teaching, saying that when he came he spoke empty things: he pronounced the poor blessed
and promised earthly gifts, saying that they would inherit a better land and have their fill of food and drink, and other things like these.
Thomas spoke against him and showed that he was unjustly angry with Jesus. He pointed out that even the prophets whom he claimed to believe had said things similar
to these, but had not explained how it was possible that these very things—they had said these things, but had not explained how people could receive these very
things. Jesus, however, had also shown and revealed how they would receive them. He said these things, testified to other things like them, and then fell silent.
After this, Caiaphas looked at me, partly as though advising me and partly as though rebuking me.
He said, “Be quiet! Do not proclaim that Jesus is the Christ, because you are bringing destruction upon yourself. You have gone astray after him, and you are leading others
astray.” He also rebuked me as someone presumptuous, saying, “Although you are an uneducated man and a fisherman by trade, you have found a way to become a teacher!”
When he had said these and similar things, I too spoke to him in words like these: “For my part, the danger to me is small.”
If, as you say, this man is not the Messiah—for you have accepted him as a teacher of the Law—then your own danger is great, not small, if it turns out that he is the Messiah.

But what if he truly is the one? For I have believed in this man who appeared and was revealed, while you suppose that you are preserving your faith for someone else who is unknown. And if, as you said, I am an ordinary man, unlearned and a fisherman,
and I claim to know more than wise elders, I told him that this should make you all the more afraid. For if we had received an education and were refuting you who are wise,
this would have been the work of time and diligence, attributable to nature and not to the power of God.
But since we are people who have not been educated, and we defeat you who are wise by our refutation, this has happened.
Who has any understanding and does not see clearly that this cause of ours does not come from human beings?

Rather, this is the will of God, who can do everything. Now I said these things to him, along with what follows them: We, then, ordinary men and fishermen, testified against the priests concerning God,
and that he alone is in heaven; against the Sadducees concerning the resurrection of the dead; and against the Samaritans concerning Jerusalem in truth,
although we did not enter their city but spoke openly outside; and against the scribes and Pharisees concerning the kingdom of heaven;
and to the disciples of John, so that they would not stumble over him. That is, we declared against them all that Jesus is the Messiah from of old.
Finally, I advised them that, before we went out to the nations to proclaim knowledge of God who is over all,

they should first bring their own people to know God by accepting Jesus. And I told them: For in this way, once you have come to know Jesus, you can receive the Holy Spirit through baptism in the name

of the glorious Trinity, which is the truth, and make your confession, and [?] believe in God alone concerning what he taught. In this way you will receive salvation and eternal life, for it is not possible otherwise,
even if you offer him tens of thousands of burnt offerings. For we know that he is all the more angry because you offer sacrifices
after the appointed time for sacrifices has ended. For this reason the temple itself will also be uprooted, and they will set the abomination of desolation there in the holy place.
Then the good news will be confirmed as a testimony to the nations, for the healing of the divisions that arise, so that your own separation may also become apparent.
For the whole world, generation after generation, was sick through a [?] will, either secretly or openly. Yet the physician had everything needed to carry out
its healing. So we have testified to each one of you concerning what he lacked. It is now your responsibility to examine in it
what will help you, and to act on it. When I said these things, the whole assembly of priests cried out because I had spoken openly about the destruction of the temple.
But when Gamaliel, the leader of the people—who, to help us, was secretly our brother in matters of faith—noticed that they were fiercely grinding their teeth in the great rage
with which they were filled against us, he said: Be still and keep quiet, men of Israel! For we do not know what this trial is that has come upon us.
For this reason, leave these men alone. If this cause comes from human beings, it will come to nothing.
But if it comes from God, why are you sinning to no purpose, when you can accomplish nothing? For the will of God must always overcome every
thing. And now, since today has passed, tomorrow I wish to speak with them here before you, so that I may refute their erroneous teaching.
They, meanwhile, were grinding their teeth and were filled with fury and anger, in the hope that these men would be refuted before everyone the next day.
We willingly fell silent, and he promised them this and dismissed the assembly in peace.
We then went and told James what had been said. While we were speaking with him, we ate a meal, and we all spent the night at his house.
Throughout the night we prayed that, in the discussion to be held the following day, our message of truth would take hold and prevail.
The next day James the bishop also went up to the temple with our entire assembly. There we found a large crowd waiting for us.
We were all in elevated places so that we could be seen by all the people. When a deep silence fell, Gamaliel—the man who, as I said before, had concealed, for the sake of helping us,
that he was one of our brothers—was there. For people hold more firmly to the advice of those who appear to share their views. He therefore secretly kept himself
in this position, particularly so that whenever they planned anything against us, we could learn about those very plans and ward them off,
and through suitable advice we could peacefully persuade even our opponents to change. Nevertheless, he spoke first, skillfully presenting himself as our enemy.
He devised a way, through his own intervention, to persuade the people to listen with a love of truth to what was being said. He looked at James the bishop and began his speech as follows:
“I, Gamaliel, am an old man and have a reputation among the teachers for truth. I am not ashamed to learn from young people and ordinary people anything that is sound and beneficial to my life.
For those who have discerning minds regard nothing as more precious than their own souls.” He showed that neither kings nor friends nor relatives nor fathers nor anything else

is more precious than truth. As though urging and encouraging us, he said, “If you know anything, do not be reluctant to impart it to our people too, because they are your brothers in the matter of reverence for God.
So, brothers, let us entrust ourselves in faith, with a love of listening [?], so that whatever is lacking in either us or you, God himself may supply through whomever he chooses.

But perhaps, because you fear some among us who have acted rashly, you are afraid of their treachery and do not wish to say what would benefit us. I also accept this reason of yours [?], and I swear to you by the
living God that no one will be allowed to lay hands on you. You have these assembled crowds standing nearby as witnesses and mediators, and [?]
has been given to you as a guarantee. Let each of you say without hindrance what he has learned, and we will listen with a love of truth.”
When Gamaliel said these things, Caiaphas was displeased. As I think, he formed some suspicion about him in his mind, and he took it upon himself to question and investigate.

Quietly, as though mocking Gamaliel and James the chief bishop, the high priest himself asked that they conduct a questioning and investigation about the Messiah from Scripture. “So that,” he said, “we may know whether Jesus is indeed the Anointed One or not.”

James said that they should first investigate which source they ought properly to use for the inquiry. After much discussion, he was compelled by the force of necessity and agreed that they should conduct the inquiry from
the Law. Likewise, in his speech James also spoke about the prophets and showed that everything they had said they had taken from the Law, and that in what agreed with it they had spoken the truth.

Then he also spoke about the books of Kings: where, when, and by whom they had been written, and how they should be used. Then they spoke again about the Law, and he explained in his speech how the things contained in it
stood, clarifying and demonstrating them. Finally, he delivered and completed his argument about the Messiah, showing from every source, with countless proofs, that Jesus is the Messiah, in whom all

these things concerning his humble coming were fulfilled. For there are two comings of his: one is the coming in humility, in which he has already come; the second is the coming in glory, in which he will come and reign

over those who have believed in him so as to do everything he commanded. Then he persuaded the people, showing that unless a person is baptized in living, running water in the name of the glorious Trinity, as the true Prophet himself taught.

Nor did he receive forgiveness of sins, nor does he enter the kingdom of God. He showed that all these things exist before [?], belonging to God, the eternal Being, in the hiddenness of his being. And along with
these things he said, “Do not suppose that we speak of two eternal beings, or of one that was divided, or that he became a female vessel for himself, as those wicked people say.”
“Female-male.” That is, he also spoke about the Son: how he is and from whom, and that he is not without a source.

And that the question “When?” is therefore not applied to him, for we leave this matter in its hiddenness. He also said many things about the Paraclete and baptism, and persuaded all the people, together with the high priest,
throughout all seven days, so that they would hurry without delay to come now for baptism. Then a certain man who was an enemy entered the temple with a few men, coming toward

the altar [?], shouting and saying, “What are you doing, men of Israel? How have you been so quickly carried away by miserable men who have gone astray after magicians?” Indeed, he said things of this sort.

He heard the answers to them, and when he was defeated by James the bishop, he began to create a great disturbance, so that the things that were being well spoken would not be examined quietly, understood, and believed.

For this reason he raised a shout against the priests’ folly and weakness, insulting them and saying, “Why are you hesitating? Why do you not seize all those who are with him in his wickedness?” As he said these things, he himself was the first to leap forward and snatch a piece of wood from the altar.
He began to strike with it. Then the rest of the priests who saw him did the same. In the great rout that followed,
some fell upon their companions, and others were struck. Not a few died, and much blood was shed by those who were killed.
That hostile man threw James himself down from the top of the steps. When he fell and lay as though dead, he did not strike him a second time.
When they saw what had happened to James, they approached and snatched him away. For they outnumbered the others, but because of their fear of God they preferred
to endure being killed rather than kill. Although many of them were strong, they appeared weak because of their fear of God. When evening came,
those priests shut the temple, while we came to James’s house and prayed there. Before dawn we went down to Jericho. We numbered about five thousand men.
After three days, one of the brothers came and told us what had happened in the temple itself after we left.
For those priests had been urging him, as a priest, to join them in all their plans, not knowing that he belonged to our faith.

He therefore told us how that hostile man had promised Caiaphas the high priest, in the presence of the priests, that he would destroy all those who believed in Jesus. He had set out for Damascus, carrying
letters from them, so that when he arrived there, the unbelievers would help him and destroy the believers. He said that he wanted to go there first because he thought Peter had gone there.
But after thirty days he passed by us in Jericho. There we buried two brothers at night, in that very place. Every year their graves suddenly turn white,
and they have quenched the anger of many, who learned that they belonged to our faith and had been found worthy of divine remembrance.
After our flight from Jerusalem to Jericho and our prayer there, after the fast there came
a man from there to us, who had been sent by James about six days earlier. He sent him to me with this message: “Do not be distressed that you are traveling alone.
You have many companions who are eager to be with you at all times. So now go about the task to which you have been appointed.

For Zacchaeus, who is in Caesarea of Straton, wrote to me that Simon, a Samaritan man from the village of Gitta, who is a magician by trade, is turning many of our people away and creating divisions. He says of himself, ‘I am the one who stands.’”

And further, he says, “I am the Christ.” He has also said many things about himself, as though in a mystery: “I am a power from that Power which is the Most High, who is higher even than the God who created the world.”
This man performed many signs through sorcery. Some he [?] divided, others he turned away, and others he drew over to himself. And all these things
Zacchaeus wrote about him, including how he performed wonders, having learned this from certain people who had once been his disciples and who previously, as his helpers in their work,
had served. “Many people, then, Peter, are waiting there for your arrival, so that you may debate with him and they may see whose words are true. Go quickly, then, with courage,
since you have God as your helper through Christ. And keep writing to me at every hour about those things that agree
with the message of our teaching, especially during the years of weeks [?].” After saying these things, he returned to his own place.
“I came here to Caesarea in six days. As I was entering, our beloved brother Zacchaeus met me in front of the gate.
He embraced and kissed me and brought me to this dwelling of his here. Immediately he asked me about the brothers, beginning with the honored James.

I told him that [?] James was lame in one leg. When he asked me about the cause, I recounted everything from the beginning, including things he had already heard in part. I told him how those priests had summoned us to a debate before
all the people; how each of us twelve stood on the steps of the temple and testified; and how, on another day, Caiaphas the high priest went up to the temple with James, our bishop.
For seven days he debated and was persuaded. He then wanted to gather all the people so that they might be baptized. But as soon as they began
to come forward, a certain man who was an enemy appeared and did all those things I mentioned earlier, so that I need not repeat the same things again. I also told him how
we fled to Jericho by night, and how that enemy went to Damascus to destroy those who were there, and that James had also sent me here to you,

because you had written to him about Simon, so that, as I said earlier, I might come and put matters here in order as far as I could. When I had told him these things, Zacchaeus in turn told me about Simon.

I do not know how Simon learned that I had arrived. He sent a request that I speak with him tomorrow before the whole assembly. When I agreed, the whole city immediately heard, on the very day I arrived here,
that Peter, the chosen disciple of the one who raised the dead and drove away every pain and disease, would hold a debate tomorrow with Simon of Gitta. And you [?], as I said, Clement,
asked around here, found out where we were staying, and came in to me, led by the excellent Barnabas.
I welcomed you because he had already told me about you, and because I had learned of your zeal in practice. I was very glad at your arrival. I do not know how I was moved in my mind,

but I immediately passed everything on to you. Before everything else came this one great and excellent matter concerning the true prophet: that he alone is a good instrument for teaching the fear of God.
Then I began with the written Law and lovingly explained to you each of its written sections. In my instruction I withheld none of the good things from you, from the first discourse
until today. As for what is to come after tomorrow, beginning with the debate with Simon, you will hear it every day, all the way
to Rome itself, where I expect to go. And when I am there, everything I do and everything I say

you will know, since you will be close by. All the remaining matters will reach their conclusion as it pleases God.” When he had said these things, I gave thanks for his great kindness and that everything
“Whatever I am commanded to do, I am readily prepared to do,” I said. He had me take food, along with those who were with him. He told us to be quiet, and then he fell silent.
When the day on which he was to speak arrived, Peter himself woke us all at the time when the rooster crowed. There were thirteen of us altogether in the house, and he was the foremost among us.
After Peter came Zacchaeus, then Zephaniah, Joseph, Micah, Eleazar, Phinehas, Lazarus, and Elisha; after them came I, Clement, and Nicodemus, and then Nicetas and Aquila.
These last two had formerly been Simon’s disciples, but afterward they were taught by Zacchaeus to become fully established in faith in God through our Lord Jesus Christ.
There was also one woman with us. When we found that the evening lamp was still burning,
we all sat down. When Peter saw that our eyes were fixed on him with complete attentiveness, he greeted us with peace.
Immediately, along with his greeting of peace, he began his instruction and said, “My dear brothers, I marvel at human nature,
at how well suited and ready it is for many things. This particular thing, however, I learned through experience,
and now I have remembered to tell you about it. As soon as midnight has passed, I wake up of my own accord, and after that I cannot go back to sleep. This came about for me
because, out of love for the words I had heard from our Lord, I constantly instructed my mind to wake up, so that, when I awoke,

I might remember and understand them and be able to recall them. As I kept doing this, because I stayed awake joyfully, it became my habit to wake up even when I had nothing to think about. And through habit itself, by

that hidden principle, I have been imperceptibly changed so that this happens to me. Thus another habit combines with and changes the habit that preceded it, truly to the extent that is suitable and proper, and not to an impossible extent.
For it is not possible for us to go entirely without sleep. Otherwise there would not even have been a night suited to the rest that sleep provides.”
When I heard this, I said, “You have spoken well, Peter: one habit is changed by another. For when I too first traveled by sea, at first dizziness and cramps would seize

me. Because of this I would flee, since I could not bear the smell and stench of the sea. Then, after a few days, I became accustomed to it and could easily endure the voyage, as well as the food I ate with the sailor.
Previously I had never tasted any food before seven years [?], but now, through a habit of two [?], hunger comes over me at the very hour when I used to eat with the sailor.
From my earlier experience I also know that even this can be changed by habit. Nevertheless, I believe you that this happened to you in this way,
so that you wake up. But now you wished to speak of this habit because it is useful, so that we too might wish to drive a little of our sleep
away from us, so that instruction might be able to reach us in this way. For after the provision of food, the mind naturally
takes advantage of the quiet of the night and can easily remember the things that are said.” Peter was very glad about this,
because I had understood the helpful purpose of his account, and he praised me. It was clear that he did this to encourage us all in this matter. Then he began to speak as follows:

“It is now time, and it is appropriate for me to ask about the matter before us. I mean Simon, so that I may know what his character is and what he has done. Whoever knows about this should not hesitate
to tell me, for knowing this will help me greatly. For if, concerning food, I have a command that we should first inquire and learn who is worthy, from whom we are going
to receive food, how much more necessary is it for us to know whose words about eternal life we ought to believe? For when we take care
And we are careful about the pearls: we do not throw them to pigs. And we are careful about the pearls: we do not throw them to pigs. How, then, is it not
an act of wickedness to throw words about eternal life to anyone who comes along, exposing them to contempt? Moreover, for this reason I ought to know what sort of man this is.
For if I learn that his conduct is upright in matters that no one disputes, even more so than those who profess reverence for God—I mean,
chastity, justice, compassion, humility, and the qualities that accompany them, which everyone knows are good,
even if they are unwilling to admit it—then, because he is upright in these visible matters, it is right to give him the knowledge he lacks, so
that these evils that defile his conduct may be purged from his mind. But if the opposite of these things, [?] we should reveal the mysteries concerning the knowledge of God
to them. But if perhaps he comes and urges us to say something that it is not right to tell him, because his conduct is not upright, we ought to avoid him wisely. For
it is not fitting to be questioned continually about this, because of certain uneducated hearers, who might suppose that we know nothing
and despise us for this, and so become doubtful and be greatly offended, not knowing our intention.
After Peter had said these things to us, Nicetas asked him for permission to speak. When Peter gave him permission, he said, “Forgive me,
Peter, for I am very afraid that you may be found at a disadvantage in the debate with Simon. For it sometimes happens that, even when someone speaks the truth,

he does not win because of the hearers, who either lack discernment, or have already sided with his opponent, or have no concern for excellence and grant victory as a favor to whomever they please. Besides all this,
Simon himself is a clever and cunning sophist, brought up on twists and elaborate arrangements of arguments.
And what is hardest and worst of all is that he is also highly trained in magic. For this reason I am afraid
that, because he presses his case forcefully from every side, the hearers who do not know him may think he is speaking the truth when he tells lies.
For we ourselves could not have escaped him and believed in Jesus if we had not been familiar with his magic and known that he was a deceiver.”
When Nicetas had said these things, Aquila also asked that he too be given permission
to say something. He began to speak: “Accept me too, and my goodwill toward you, for I too am anxious, like Nicetas. Do not despise me for this.
For a person's concern for his friend comes from love, while despising someone is no less than hatred. I call God as my witness that it is not because you are inferior
in my eyes, or because I consider you weak in debate, that I fear you may be found at a disadvantage against Simon. How could that be, since I have never even been present
when you were conducting a debate? For this reason I do not know your abilities, but I do know his wicked deeds.
I am concerned for your honor, and also for the souls of the hearers,
and above all for the truth. For that magician is capable of anything he wishes, especially since he has no mercy.
For we know everything about him in detail, since from our youth we were his assistants in his household.
And if we had not truly been lovers of God, [?] even now we would still be secretly doing those things of his along with him.”
But the love of God that had become established in us enabled us to become enemies of the evil one and members of the good one's household.

For this reason, I think that our experience was not without providence: that we should first become his friends and learn how he performed these astonishing deeds, and then despise him and distance ourselves
from him. For who would not marvel at these wonders that were taking place and think that he had come from heaven as a god to save humanity? But I confess this about myself:

if I had not been his assistant in these things that were happening, I too would have been swept away. So it is no great wonder that we changed our minds and fled from him, since we knew that he performed them by sorcery, for the man is a sorcerer and magician.
And if you too want to know all about him accurately—whose son he is and where he comes from,
where he is, what he wants, what belongs to him, and what the deeds he performs are like—listen now.
This Simon's father is Antonius, and his mother is Rachel. He is one of the Samaritans, from the village of Gitta. He is a free man and educated himself extensively in Greek learning,
to a very high degree, and became proud and conceited. He wants to be regarded as a power above the Creator. In secret he says of himself, 'I am the Messiah,' and he is called 'the Standing One.'
He uses this name because he says, 'I do not undergo dissolution,' as though his body had been fixed in divinity itself, so that he could
remain forever. This is why he was called 'the Standing One,' as though he could not fall under decay. For when John the Baptist was killed, as you yourself know,
Dositheus assumed the leadership of his sect, together with those leaders, who numbered thirty,
and with a woman called Luna, so that they would be thirty, corresponding to the moon's course. This Simon—I do not know
how—met Dositheus because he loved empty praise. With feigned affection he asked him to appoint him immediately in the place of anyone among those thirty who died.
For no one enters and is appointed before being examined.

Nor is anyone added beyond their number or removed from it. For this reason, all the rest who follow them, because they desire to be considered worthy of that position, display conduct pleasing to their order.
For after the death of one of those thirty, they appoint in the dead man's place whichever of their followers they judge worthy. Dositheus, then, was deceived in many ways,
and when their number fell short, he appointed Simon. A little later, Simon fell in love with the woman called Luna. He told us all about himself: how he was a sorcerer, and how he loved the woman

called Luna and loved praise. Because of the disgrace, he did not want to approach the matter hastily. Instead, he told us, 'With patience and a plan, I can accomplish it,' provided that we too would help him
in what he wanted. As a reward for this service of ours, he promised to grant that we would be regarded as gods and deemed worthy of every honor,
and that everything belonging to him would be ours. He said to us, 'Only grant me this: that I should be your leader.
I can perform many signs through sorcery, so that our glory and honor can endure. For if they want to seize us, I can make myself invisible.

And whenever I want to be seen, I become visible. If I flee, I can pierce a mountain as though it were soft clay and pass through it. If I throw myself from a high mountain, as though someone were carrying me,
I descend gently to the ground. I can free myself and cause those who bound me to be bound. If I am confined in prison, I can open the door.
I can put souls into statues, so that those who see them think they are human beings.
I can make new plants sprout in a dwelling, and bring trees out of the earth with their clump of roots. If I throw myself into fire, I am not burned.
And I change my own form, and I appear to people with two faces. I become a sheep, and I appear as a goat, and I am worshiped.
And I am worthy of honors from everyone, so that they make an image of me and serve and worship me as God. And why do I need to say many things? I can do whatever I wish to do.

For look, I have done many things as demonstrations. Once, he said, when [?], my mother ordered me to go to the reapers. I commanded a sickle that was lying there to go and reap, and so it happened, ten
times over. And I made new plantings of cedars of [?], and with a momentary gesture I made a pole sprout. And I bored through this nearby mountain.
So when he was saying these things about the plantings and the boring through the mountain, we were astonished that he was telling even us lies about himself, since he wanted
to lead us astray. For we knew that they had existed since earlier generations, but he wanted to boast that he had made them.
So, as we heard these things and others more wicked than these, we eagerly acted according to his wishes, spread reports about him to many people, and told many lies about him.
And we did these things before he had performed even one of the things he had promised, so that people would think that he was God. Now, at the beginning, when he was

with those thirty disciples of Dositheus, he used to slander Dositheus to them, saying, “He does not transmit the teaching to you in its purity. He does this not out of envy, but because he does not know.” And when, at one point,

Dositheus became aware of his extensive slander, he wanted to undo this notion planted in the minds of many through Simon’s craft, and to show that he himself was the Standing One. In anger, he came to their meeting place as usual,
and found Simon and struck him. But the staff seemed to pass through Simon as though through smoke. Because of this, Dositheus was astonished and said to him,

“If you are the Standing One, I too will worship you.” And when Simon said, “I am,” Dositheus recognized that he himself was not the Standing One, and fell down and worshiped him. And so, together with those twenty-

nine leaders, he placed himself in a subordinate position, and installed Simon in the position he himself had hoped for, and commanded them to obey him in everything. So when Simon took precedence in the position hoped for
by Dositheus, Dositheus himself, who had taken Simon’s place, fell ill and died. After Dositheus’s death, Simon took Luna for himself and has traveled about until now,

as you see. He leads the crowd astray and says, “I am a power second to the Creator, and I can do a great deal.” And of Luna [?], the woman with him, he says that she descended into the world from the highest heaven.

He says that she is Wisdom, the mother of everything, and that Greeks and barbarians fought over her in the likeness of an image of her true being. For if she truly was, at that time, with that first God,
it is clear that she was with that first one alone. Yet such things, mingled with the stories of the Greeks, he persuasively
relates, and leads many astray. Now I want to tell what I myself saw. For when this Luna of his was in a tower,
and a large crowd had hurried together to see her and stood on every side of the tower, she, from every side of the tower and from all its windows, appeared to the entire
crowd as though she were looking out. And he performed many wonders, and still does, so that people will marvel and think that he is indeed the God of all.
And when Nicetas and I asked him whether he could explain to us how these things could be done [?] through sorcery, and what was the nature of things
like these, Simon promised, as to his dear friends, that he could tell us. And he began to speak as follows: “The soul of an undefiled boy who died by violence,
whom I summoned by secret incantations, I have bound to myself so that it will perform anything, provided only that I command it.” And when I said to him, “Can a soul do things like these?”
He answered me, “This is what I want you to be convinced of: the soul of every human being, once it has cast off this great darkness of the body, can investigate the duality of God.
It also has foreknowledge. For this reason, people summon it and bring it up for necromancy, which they call divination by the dead.”
I answered him again, “Why, then, do the souls of those who have been murdered not turn against those who murdered them?” Simon said, “Remember what I told you:
when the soul leaves the body, it also has foreknowledge.” I said to him, “I remember.” He answered me, “For this reason, as soon as it leaves the body,
immediately, because it knows everything beforehand, it is convinced that there will be a judgment, and that everyone will have to answer and undergo judgment for the evil things they have done here.
For this reason, it no longer wishes to exact vengeance from those who wronged it, because, over the evil things it has itself done here,
it is in mourning. Besides all this, the angels appointed over the souls for this purpose do not allow them to come or do anything.”
I answered him again, “If they are not allowed to come here [?] or do anything they wish, how do they come to the sorcerer who summons them and fulfill his wishes?”
He said to me, “Even when they themselves wish to come, they are not allowed. But when the angels themselves have been adjured by that great and exalted oath,
because they have this means of relief [?], they give us the souls of those we want, under the compulsion we impose on them by our adjurations.
Thus it is not they who are at fault, since they are subjected to compulsion, but we who impose that compulsion on them.”

Then my companion Nicetas, whom you see here, could no longer bear it and hastily answered him. I too was about to do the same, although at first I had wanted to accommodate him in everything. Nicetas said to him, “Are you not afraid,
then, of the day of judgment, when you compel angels, summon souls, and lead people astray, striving to make many people think that you are God?
And how could you also try to persuade us that there will not even be a judgment, as some Jews say, and that souls are not immortal,
as some suppose, when you see them [?] with your own eyes and acknowledge that God will judge human beings, as you said [?]?”
At these words Simon turned pale and answered, “Do not suppose that I am a man of your own kind. For I am not even a sorcerer, nor am I the lover of the moon.
Nor am I the son of Antonius. For before my mother Rachel had intercourse with him, she conceived me while she was a virgin. For I can become great or small, just as I wish.
So I appeared as a human being among human beings. To test you, I first chose friends for myself, so that in those very heavens and in those hidden regions,
after testing you, I might place you. Thus I falsely told those human things about myself to learn fully what love you maintain toward me.”
But I, Aquila, when I heard these things, despised him and was utterly amazed that he felt no shame. I was ashamed on his behalf and feared that something might happen to us because of him.
I nudged Nicetas to join me in yielding to him, and I said to him, “Do not be angry with us, since you are God. We are mortal human beings, but you are imperishable.

Rather, accept our sincere intention. While we still did not know who you were, we could not truly be persuaded to apply to you what concerns God, because we did not know that you were the very one we were seeking.”
We said these things and others like them to him as a pretense. But he thought he had deceived me into being a trembling fool.
He became still more conceited and answered us, “I have compassion on you because of your love for me, who am God.
For when you loved me, you did not know it, and when you sought me, you did not understand. But you do not know that this is what belongs to God: to become small or great, just as he wishes.”

Now I will begin to tell you truthfully how I appeared to human beings. Once, by my own power, I changed air into water, transformed the water into blood, solidified it into flesh, and fashioned a human being, a new young boy.
And I demonstrated a deed greater than that of the one who made the world. For the one who created the world made the human being from earth, but I, from pure air,
accomplished this difficult thing. Then I dissolved him and turned him back into air. I fashioned an image in his likeness and placed it in my inner room as a demonstration and a memorial.
While he was saying these things, we knew that this was the boy who had died a violent death, and whose soul served him in whatever he wanted, as he said.
When Peter heard these things, he wept and said, “I marvel at God's great patience and at the impudence human beings have shown from the beginning.
For what argument can now persuade Simon to acknowledge that God judges, when he employs, as he supposes, the souls of those who committed wickedness and sins for whatever he wants?
In truth, however, they are not souls, but demons that deceive him. He, then, has convinced himself that souls are immortal and are judged for

what they have done here. Moreover, he has seen in practice what we believe on the strength of words. For what does it matter if demons are deceiving him? He nevertheless thinks that he sees the souls themselves.

Yet despite all this, he grows in wickedness. And when will he acknowledge that he has acted and behaved wickedly, or that he will be judged for these things, since he has once and for all made himself God's enemy and boldly commits things that it is not even permissible
to mention? So, my brothers, some people fail to be persuaded by the message of reverence for God, not because of a lack of evidence, but because of the enormity of their sins, which they or

their predecessors [?]. These people are blinded in their understanding by the evil one, and for this reason they cannot even readily come to believe. But since love for the Creator of the world is enough to save and give life to those who love him,
the evil one devised a way to make human beings his enemies. For this reason he also exposed them and brought to light the ingratitude of some of them. For I call as witnesses
heaven and earth: if God had allowed the evil one to make human beings sin as he wished, all human beings would already have perished long ago. And this
God did out of his mercy. For if human beings had persevered in love for him and endured, they would all have been saved and lived,
while being disciplined for minor sins because of his justice. But now many have been exposed as enemies of God. The evil one enters even into the thoughts of some of them
and presents himself to them as though he were greater than the Creator. To some he appears while they are awake, as an illusory vision,
and promises things better than those of the Creator. He has been left free and permitted to do these very things for a certain just reason.”
In response to this, Aquila said, “How, then, are human beings at fault, if the evil one changes himself and takes whatever form he wishes, and promises things better than those of the Creator?”

Peter said, “I think nothing is more just than this. But listen to how this is so, and answer me. Suppose your own son had been brought up with every discipline and care and had grown to manhood by your side,

but then ungratefully abandoned you and gave someone else, because he was rich, the honor he owed you, and for greater gain [?] the father who had cared for him throughout his years. Would you say that he acted justly or unjustly?”
Aquila answered him, “It is clear to everyone that he acted unjustly.”
Peter said, “If, then, you say that this conduct toward a human being is unjust, how much more so toward God, who alone is worthy of honor? Besides showing us kindness
by bringing us from nothing into being, he has also promised us eternal life and delight after we have pleased him here. Is it not far more unjust?
That is why, so that the ungrateful may be exposed, he allowed the evil one to appear in many forms and to promise other things as though they offered great benefits.
But what if there really were another, foreign god besides the God who created us? Would we rightly and properly abandon the one who truly is our maker and our father?
Aquila said, “Far be it! May that never happen!”
Peter said, “How, then, can we say that we are not sinning? For look: with the permission of the one who truly is God, the evil one promises other gods,

either above the one who truly exists or below him, so that those who wish to abandon their creator will be publicly exposed as wrongdoers on the day of judgment and excluded from the eternal kingdom of the one they have wronged. For to those who truly are his friends,
God wishes to give the eternal things that belong to him. But these matters will be discussed carefully and thoroughly another time. I would like to know what Simon eventually did.”
Nicetas answered him, “Finally, when he realized that we thoroughly despised him—for we used to recount his sorcery and his deeds to one another—we abandoned him and approached Zacchaeus.

We told him these things, the same things we have now told you. Good Zacchaeus welcomed us, persuaded us about the things concerning our Lord Jesus Christ, and instructed and strengthened us in the faith.”
While Nicetas was saying these things, Zacchaeus, who had gone out a little earlier, came back in and said, “Now it is time, Peter,
for you to go out and speak. A large crowd has gathered in the courtyard and is waiting for you. Simon stands among them as someone they hold in honor.”
As Peter was about to pray, he told me to withdraw, because I had not yet been baptized to cleanse me from the things I had previously done in ignorance.
He said to the others, “Stand up. Let us pray and ask God, through his Messiah, in his unfailing and limitless mercy, to help me as I go out to bring discernment and life to those people
who were created by him.” After saying these things, he went out into the large open-air courtyard, where great crowds had gathered in separate groups. When he stood there
and saw that, in profound silence, the eyes of all the people were fixed on him, and that Simon the sorcerer stood there like a commander of warriors, he began to speak as follows:
“May peace and harmony be with all of you who are ready to offer your right hands to the truth of God. For those who obey his will, supposing that they are doing him some favor,

are themselves receiving from him something that greatly benefits them, by walking in the way of his righteousness. Therefore, the first and most important thing is to seek his righteousness and his kingdom.
His righteousness concerns deeds and conduct, while his kingdom is like a reward for [?] endurance: for the good, it is the enjoyment of eternal blessings, and for the wicked,
who have not conducted themselves according to his will, it is punishment for their wicked deeds. Here, then, what is fitting and necessary for us is to learn God's will while there is time,

so that we can also carry it out and act upon it, and what we do can bring about a good reward. But if, before actions and deeds, we turn to investigation, seeking and asking, these things cannot be found by us or even seen by us,
and we waste our time like people without understanding. For the time each of us has is short, and when we are judged, it is for our deeds that we are judged,
not for knowledge of hidden things. Therefore, we must not stop seeking what we ought to do to obtain eternal life.
For if we spend this short time of ours occupied with things that cannot be discovered and do not benefit us, we will depart empty of good deeds, having neglected the deeds for which
we will also be judged. Everything has its own time: doing belongs here, while receiving repayment belongs there. So, to avoid wasting our time, let us first seek righteousness,
so that, like good travelers, we may carry provisions with us—namely, good deeds—and go to the kingdom of God as to a city.
For he is manifest and known to those who are upright and sound, because of the world that was created [?], since the evidence for him can be seen throughout his creation.

Since God is manifest and known, let us seek the things of his righteousness and the things of his kingdom, for whose sake we also receive the world. But if our mind tells us to investigate any of those hidden things before doing good deeds, as though our life depended on them, let us reason with ourselves and persuade ourselves.
First, we ought to do good deeds, through which we live there in the Holy Spirit.
And we find rest as pure and good people, and all hidden things, without searching, through the Holy Spirit who is with us, so that we can come to know more
than these things known now. Even if someone searches for them for an unlimited time, he not only fails to know them but goes far astray and brings his soul to destruction.
For he does not wish to enter through the gate of life by the way of righteousness.
For this reason, I advise that we first seek his righteousness, so that, as we walk in it as on a road, we may be able to reach the prophet [?] of truth himself.
Not through swiftness of foot, but through good deeds. Then let us ask him about what we lack concerning the road and the city—the things we want to know—or let us walk with him.
And let us enter the city with him. Then we will see everything with our own eyes. We will stop learning and remain silent, because we will have come to know everything.
Understand, then, that the road is conduct and good deeds, and that those traveling the road are those who do good things. The gate is the prophet.
And the city is the kingdom, in which the eternal Father sits before everyone and is ready to be seen by those who have pure hearts. So let us not grow weary of traveling the road to its completion.
For the [?] of the road is rest. Indeed, the prophet of truth himself has been urging us toward rest from the beginning of the world, and he always runs alongside us. So he is with us every day.

Whenever he needs to reveal himself, he reveals himself. He corrects those who have chosen wrongdoing and, through his truthful words, turns them toward his truth and becomes the source of eternal life for them. My advice, then, is in accordance with what pleases the prophet of truth.
It is this: first we should inquire about righteousness, especially those who profess to know God. So if anyone has something more useful and suitable than this to say, let him say it—
only gently and calmly. Indeed, this is why, at the beginning, I prayed for peace upon you all by way of greeting.
Simon answered these words and said, “We have no need of peace from you.
For agreement and harmony do nothing to help discover the truth. Even robbers, adulterers, and the whole company of evildoers are in harmony and agreement with one another.
And if, for the sake of peace, we too come to agree with every statement there is, we do not help our listeners at all. Rather, we speak opposing views and then part from one another as friends.
For this reason, do not begin by proclaiming peace, but rather war, which is its father. Cure my error as far as you can, without concerning yourself with love, which confirms it
without judgment. For above all I want you to know this: when two people fight one another, peace comes through the defeat of one of them.
For this reason, fight as hard as you can, and do not seek peace without war: this is impossible [?]. But if it is possible, explain how.”
Peter answered and said, “Look, people, and listen with understanding to what I want to show you. Picture the world in your minds and think of it
as a great plain, with [?] two cities belonging to two kings who oppose one another. Let one advocate from each of them come into the middle.

The advocate of the good king would give this advice: that they should all be of one mind and, without killing or the sword, surrender themselves to the one considered superior, so that without war all of them might

be saved and live. But the advocate of the opposing king would say, ‘Not like this, but through war and fighting, so that life and deliverance may belong, not to the one who is worthy, but to the one who is strong, together with those who survive.’
Which would you choose? I think you would choose this: that all of you should be saved in peace, live, and become better people. This, then, is what
I seek—not, as Simon said, that for the sake of peace we should agree with one another about things wrongly said, but that we should listen quietly, with love for the truth.

For some people, when they realize during an inquiry that their error is being exposed, begin causing a disturbance to conceal it, so that their poverty of understanding will not be revealed. That is why I ask that the inquiry be conducted patiently.
For this is right: if anything that is said seems to have been stated incorrectly, we should allow one another to ask further questions—whether [?] it was said in one sense but

heard in another because it was not explained well, or whether it was well stated but understood differently. For this reason, we should wait for one another's thoughts, so that an answer may be given with patient consideration,

and its meaning may become clear to the understanding. So let us not talk over one another, nor cause confusion and interrupt one another. Nor should we hunt for opportunities to catch one another out and stubbornly defend ourselves. Instead, let us take up again and recall the things that were not well stated,
so that, proceeding in every way fairly, we may be able to find what we seek. For we must know that when someone is defeated by a person who knows the truth,
it is not he himself who has been defeated, but the ignorance within him, which is an evil demon. As for anyone who rouses his soul against it and drives it out of himself, the way of life and truth
can help him. For this is the task set before us in our dealings with one another: not to win by wrongful means, but to know the truth for the sake of our lives and to be defeated honorably.
If, then, we inquire with love for the truth and acknowledge [?] what is well said, God himself, who knows everyone's intention, will take what we lack because of the weakness of our thinking

and our inquiry and secretly implant and bestow it in the mind of each one of us. For because he is just, he brings some of us close to discovering what is sought, while for others he makes even what is plain impossible to find.
Since, then, God's way is peace, let us conduct our inquiry quietly. And now, whoever wishes to question me about anything he wishes, I am ready for him. But if no one wishes to inquire with me,
I will begin speaking, and I myself will set out the opposing arguments against my own position and answer them.
Then, when Peter began to deliver an address to everyone, Simon interrupted his speech and said, “Why are you in such a hurry to say what pleases you, so that by trickery

you may prepare them for your arguments in anticipation of what you are about to present? In this way, those who do not know your trickery will think that you are speaking correctly. But this scheme of yours will not succeed
or stand up against me. And now, since you have boldly promised to resolve the question of anyone who questions you, answer me first.”
Peter said to him, “I am ready for you, provided that you intend to speak peaceably.”
Simon replied to this, saying, “Do you not realize, you ignorant man, that you are acting against your own teacher? You seek peace, something foreign to your teacher,
who chose war against human ignorance. But if you are right to seek peace from your listeners, then your teacher acted wrongly when he said, ‘I have not come to bring peace

on earth, but war.’ So if you are acting rightly, he acted wrongly. But if the one who taught you acted rightly, you are acting wrongly, because you have not understood and learned, or because you wish to act against the one who taught you.”
Peter answered these words: “Neither did the one who sent me act wrongly by bringing war, nor am I acting against him

by wishing to bring peace. Rather, you have found fault ignorantly and hastily, before learning the facts. For have you not heard what our teacher said of peacemakers, that they would be called children
of God? Therefore [?], by doing this I have not disobeyed my teacher, who urged people to make peace for the sake of blessedness.”

And Simon said, “When you want to cast out a spirit, do it to yourself! Peter, you have shown that your teacher is very wicked: although he himself did not come to make peace, he advised others to do this.
And how, again, does his other saying agree with this, when he said, ‘It is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher’?”
And Peter said, “Our teacher truly was a prophet, and he was always mindful of himself.

He did not say things contrary to himself, nor did he advise people to do so. For when he said, ‘I have not come to bring peace, but war; and from now on you will see a father divided against his son, and a son against his father, and a husband against his wife,
and a wife against her husband, and a mother against her daughter, and a daughter against her mother, and a brother against his brother, and a mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law,
and a friend against his friends,’ he promised to bring about much peace and instruction. For at the beginning, because he wanted everyone to be saved and live,
he appealed to them and encouraged everyone to endure the trials that fell to their lot. For he pronounced the poor blessed,

because through their poverty they could receive the kingdom of heaven, so that, because of this good hope, they would rejoice in their poverty itself and would not defraud others or become greedy. For oppression is one of the sins that bring destruction. And again, to those

who are hungry and thirsty he promised that they would be satisfied with everlasting good things, so that they would readily endure the hardships of their poverty and would not want to do wrong in anything. In the same way, he also pronounced those who are pure in heart blessed,
saying that through this they would see God, so that everyone who wanted to receive this would not defile his mind with evil desire. Now, while pursuing this purpose,
our teacher urged and taught, at the beginning and peaceably, that even those in distress should remain patient, so that their righteousness could be preserved through patience. But upon those
who were rich and lived in luxury and pride he pronounced woe, so that they would turn to the needy and give to them, lest, because they lacked the things that were necessary and needed,

the needy should sin. The rich were to give them what belonged to them, since they had a commandment to love their neighbors, [?] have compassion on them in their distress. So, as he was saying these things,

he persuaded some of them, while others became his enemies. Then he advised those who had been persuaded by him to make peace with one another, saying, ‘Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God.’

But to those who were not persuaded and chose hostility for themselves, he promised war—that is, rebuke—when he said, ‘From now on you will see a son separated from his father, and a husband from his wife, and a daughter from her mother,

and a brother from his brother, and a father-in-law from his daughter-in-law, and a friend from his friend; and a man’s enemies will be the members of his own household.’ For when this rebuke took place in every household, those who turned back put their conduct right (right), and were saved and lived.
But those who were ashamed and remained as they were became still more hardened, and were shown to be sinners far more than before, and they perished.
He did this at the end of the time allotted for teaching, and he rebuked the scribes and Pharisees because of their evil teaching and their unrighteous deeds.
In truth, it was not all of them, but those who had hidden the teaching handed down to them from Moses, like a key suited to the house of the kingdom. Thus he testified of Moses that he was faithful,
a servant throughout the whole house. So our Lord commanded us also to act in this way. For when he sent us apostles out to preach, he told us, ‘Whatever town or house you enter,
say, “Peace be in this house.” If a son of peace is there, let your peace rest upon them; but if not, let your peace return to you.

And when you leave there, shake the dust off your feet. It will be more bearable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that town or that house.’ But it was not out of kindness
that he told us to shake the dust off our feet against those who would not be persuaded before they had been rebuked.
And so we too act consistently with our teacher. We begin by speaking peaceably, explaining how everyone can be saved and live without discord.”
But when they are not set right by this and do not accept it, then we know that we have been forced by them to contend with them and to confront their wretchedness.
For we do not undertake this lightly. Rather, it brings hostility, conflict, and persecution from unbelievers upon those who believe.

For believers wisely turn peace back upon those who hate it. For this reason, even now, after your error, I could have done this for you; and if I were not a worker for the truth, perhaps I would have made peace with you.

But because such peace on my part toward you could destroy many who are present and do not know your hidden intentions, what I now seek is not peace in the sense of our coming to an agreement with each other, as you suppose, but rather

quiet, rest, and patience, so that, with forbearance and without disturbance, the things being said may be understood by this gathering here, and they may be delivered from division and become worthy to stand before the coming King.
For when they are divided in their thinking, they cannot help falling. For every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste. Now say whatever you wish in reply to these things.”

Simon said, “You act as though you do not know that I do not know you [?]. You set out your teacher’s words and speak as though it had been granted to you that he was a prophet—someone whom I can show

to have said many things that contradict himself. And immediately I will refute him from this very statement you have just made. For you said that your teacher declared, ‘Every kingdom or city or house divided against itself will not stand.’
But elsewhere he said, ‘I am the sword that separates those who are in the same house. From now on you will see a father separated from his son, and a mother from her daughter,
and a brother from his brother, and a mother-in-law from her daughter-in-law, and a friend from his friend. For,’ he says, ‘if there are five in one house,
three will be divided against two; and if there are three, two will be divided against one.’ Therefore, since everything divided must fall,
the one who caused the division is the cause of the downfall. And anyone like that is evil. Say whatever answer you can devise to this.”
Peter said, “Simon, do not criticize things you do not understand so insolently and hastily. First, take a breath concerning that first point on which you criticized me:
that I put forward my teacher’s words at the outset and begin with them. For when our Lord sent us apostles out, he commanded us to teach the nations everything that he had commanded us. Nor
can we simply repeat these things just as we hear them. For he did not command us merely to say them, but to teach about them, explaining how each one truly is.
Nor are we permitted to speak from our own resources. For we are apostles, so that we may take up the things for which we were sent and speak about those alone.

That is, we are to establish and confirm the words of the one who sent us by proofs. Therefore, if I say something that our Lord who sent me did not say, I am a false apostle, because I have allowed myself to say something that did not please him. For anyone

who does such a thing has gone astray, because he thinks himself superior to the one who sent him, and says deficient and inadequate things beyond what pleased the one who sent him, and errs. Or he sets those things out and speaks about them

and is then accepted because he confirms them [?]. Even so, he is not invariably an apostle; rather, he is examined for his agreement with the things believed, and not on the basis that he is an apostle. For it is not

necessarily the case that if someone does something resembling another person’s work, he is that person whom he has managed to resemble. Nevertheless, to convince the listeners, I ought to give my demonstration briefly. This is what I am now undertaking to do.
But I do not please you. And if I try to act in this way, I shall be wishing to compete with the one who sent me—something that cannot be.
For he was a prophet, and he was always consistent with himself. But if he is not a prophet, let us investigate that first.”
Simon said, “I do not need to learn this, but rather how this statement agrees with that one. For if it is shown that this does not agree with that,
you have shown that he is not a prophet.”
Peter said, “But if I first show that he is a prophet, even those things that seem contradictory are not contradictions. For it is not from the agreement
of statements that someone is a prophet, since many people can achieve this. So if agreement itself does not show that someone is a prophet, much less does contradiction.
For there are many things that seem to some people to contradict one another, but in fact agree with one another,
just as there are also a few things that seem to agree with one another but, upon examination, contain a contradiction.
For this reason I say that there is no other way more suitable than this for investigating and examining such matters: first we must know
whether the person who spoke these apparently contradictory things is a prophet. For if he is a prophet, those things that seem contradictory are in agreement,
though they are not understood. Consequently, even I, who am an apostle, am no apostle if I speak on my own authority, since I am not saying what the one who sent me said. But
even if what I say on my own authority is not contrary to it, I have not been entrusted with discretion, for I have received no such command. From now on, therefore, know that we
say nothing on our own authority, but only all the words of the one who sent us and commanded us to teach—that is, to confirm the truth of his words.”
Simon said, “Teach me how this is consistent: if divisions lead to downfall, how is the one who promised to give life and save good, if he himself causes these things?”
Peter said, “Listen to how complete consistency accompanies what seems to you to be a contradiction. Our teacher said that no kingdom, city, or household can stand if it is divided.
He said that this is evil. Yet he promised to do this for good purposes. Listen to how this is deliberate and consistent: everything that is divided cannot stand,

whether it is evil or good. With his true word he divided those who were in error, so that error would fall, just as evil itself wishes to divide the truth by some erroneous statement, so that the truth cannot stand.”
Simon said, “It is not clear whether your teacher was dividing error or truth itself, so that it would fall.”
Peter said, “That is another question. If, then, you agree that everything divided must fall, it now remains for me to show—
if you are willing to inquire peacefully—that our Jesus spoke the truth and divided error so that it would be dissolved and fall.”
Simon said, “Leave aside this talk of peace that you keep repeating. State briefly what you know and teach.”
Peter said, “Why are you afraid to hear about peace repeatedly? Or do you not know that the goal of the righteousness of the law is peace? For disputes arise from sins, and wars follow them.

Thus peace comes from obeying the law, because people do not sin. So too in an investigation, if people question one another out of love for the truth, and in their actual conduct, if they do not sin.”
Simon said, “It seems to me that you cannot state briefly what you know and teach.”

Peter said, “I spoke out of order willingly. I was not compelled by your intervening question, but did so willingly, because I am eager to interject whatever benefits everyone. For this reason I say briefly: there is one God, and he made this world.

Because he is just, he always repays everything and everyone according to their deeds, whenever that may be. Nevertheless, I know that many tens of thousands of arguments are defeated by the demonstration of this.”
Simon said, “I admire the sharpness of your thinking, but I do not accept the unsoundness of your opinion.

For you cleverly anticipated the things said against this assertion of yours, and admitted beforehand that you too know that many tens of thousands of arguments are defeated by the demonstration of this.”
For no one has simply agreed that this claim of yours is true. So, first of all, who has agreed with you on this very point—that there is one God and that the world is his work?
I think that none of the Greeks, whether ordinary people or philosophers, has done so, nor any of the Jews, whether knowledgeable or weak, nor even I, who know their Law.
Peter replied, “Stop telling us about other people’s opinions. You yourself, who are here with me, as I am here with you, tell me what you think.”
Simon said, “I can say what I truly know. But I am reluctant to do this, and I am apprehensive when I consider that, if I say something with which neither you
“nor these uneducated crowds agree, you will act as though you are upset, stop your ears, and run away because you have nothing to say against it. These undiscerning crowds will help you and

“will welcome you as a gentle guide in the things to which they are accustomed. But they will reject me as though I were misleading them with a new and false belief and wanted to disturb and trouble everyone’s mind.”

Peter said, “Why have you accused us beforehand of being undiscerning, unless it is because you have nothing true to say? But if you do, begin speaking without making these preparations beforehand, if you are confident in the words

“you are going to say. If some people do not like what you say, they will change their views; and if they persist in them, they will be compelled by the proofs to be persuaded. Only begin to say what seems good and right (and pleasing) to you.”
Simon said, “I say that there are many gods, but that there is one hidden God who is God of them all.”
Peter asked, “Can you demonstrate the existence of this God whom you say is hidden from the writings that the Jews regard as trustworthy,
“or from other writings unknown to all of us—from Greek writings or from writings of your own? First show that they are prophetic, so that we may believe them cautiously, on the basis of proof.”
Simon said, “I can give you proofs from the Jewish Law alone. For it is clear to everyone that whoever professes reverence for God
“must take pride in this, even though each person has an opinion of his own. For he [?] concerning the entire faith
“of those who profess reverence for God: that this Law belongs to the one who created the world. For this reason,
“whether someone speaks truth or falsehood, unless he constructs from [?] a proof of what he professes, he cannot be accepted. For this reason,
“whether someone speaks truth or falsehood, unless he constructs from it a proof of what he professes, he cannot be accepted. For this reason, I, who am well versed in the knowledge of the Law,
“have rightly said that there are many gods, and that one is hidden, their chief, who is their God. Now, as for there being many gods,
“the Law itself first bears witness for me through the person of the serpent, in what he said to Eve, the first woman: ‘On the day you eat from the tree of knowledge,
“‘you will be like God.’ This means like those who made humanity. For after they ate, God himself bears witness, saying, ‘Look, Adam has become like one of us.’ Thus there are many gods,

“the very ones who made him. For at the beginning God likewise spoke to those with him: ‘Let us make humanity.’ Again, there is his saying, ‘Send him out,’ and also, ‘Come, let us go down and divide their languages.’

“This shows that there are many gods. Again, it is written, ‘You shall not revile the gods, and you shall not curse the leaders of your people.’ Moreover, there is this: ‘The Lord alone led them, and no foreign god was with him.’
“This shows that there are many gods. Indeed, I can show many statements from the Law, explicit and implicit, that there are many,
“and that one of them is the one to whom the Jewish people fell by lot, to be their God [?]. But I was not speaking about this one,
“but about that God of this one, whom even the Jews have not known. For he is not their God, but the God of those who have known him.”
When Peter heard this, he said, “Do not be afraid, Simon. We are neither stopping our ears nor running away, for we have something to demonstrate against your false statement.
First, this: there is only one God, who is the creator of heaven and earth and of all those who have been called gods. He alone is God.
And if I demonstrate that there is no other, new god, but only this one, will you acknowledge that you have gone astray and committed a great offense, greater than any other?”
Simon said, “Why, even if I am unwilling to acknowledge it, those nearby [?] bear witness, since fear has overtaken them too.”
Peter said, “Listen, so that you may first understand that even if those called gods are countless, they are nevertheless subject to the God of the Jews, than whom none is greater,
nor is there anyone like him or equal to him. For it is written that the prophet Moses himself spoke to them as follows: ‘The Lord your God is God of gods and Lord of lords, the great God.’
Thus, although there are many who have been called gods, there is one who is greater than them all: the God of the Jews. He is also the God of those
who have been called gods. For if someone is called a god, that does not mean he really is God. Even Moses was called Pharaoh’s god, and everyone acknowledges that he was a human being.
Judges too were called gods, yet they can plainly be seen to die. The idols of the nations are also called gods,
and we all know that they are nothing. But this has happened to the wicked as a great punishment from above, because they did not recognize the one who truly is God.
Anything whatsoever becomes a god to them, because they were unwilling to receive knowledge of the one who can give everything
and to know him. For this reason they were handed over to those who can do nothing, so that they would not receive anything
they desire when they ask them: from those without souls, because they are nothing at all; and from those who do have souls,
because they cannot give anything or inflict harm, since they are under the authority of that one God. For the word ‘god’ is used in three distinct senses:
one who truly is God, or one who has been sent by the one who truly is God, and exercises authority by the authority of the one who sent him, and uses the name of God, the one
who sent him, exercises authority and uses the name of God, the one who sent him, so that, when someone obeys his name [God’s name] of authority [?],

that obedience may be counted toward the honor of the one who sent him. For this reason, whenever an angel appears to someone, if he is a wise man, he has a true pattern by which to test this knowledge, in the manner followed by Moses

and those who received the truth from Moses. He asks about the name of the angel who appeared, and then presses the one who a little earlier called himself God to acknowledge that he is a lord and not God.
For someone can be lord of what is given to him, on account of the one who allotted it to him, so that he may govern the people given to him.
But after being questioned, he cannot say that he is God. For one who is not truly God is not permitted to testify this about himself.
For the Most High, who alone is God, divided the whole earth into seventy-two portions and appointed rulers over them.
And the greatest of these after God, who is the archangel, was appointed to govern those who flee and take refuge in God, the one who made the division,
to govern them. Thus those people who fear God were themselves called gods of those wicked people [rulers], not by themselves but by God,
since they have authority over their lives, like God, in the same way that Moses was appointed over Pharaoh, and judges over those who are judged.

For this reason it is written, ‘You shall not revile the gods, nor curse the rulers of your people,’ so that the judges of the Jews may be recognized as gods. And the Messiah is the God of the judges.
He who is also the judge of everything. But in truth, neither angels nor human beings,
nor any created thing, can be gods. For they have a constraint imposed upon them, since they came into being: for the angels, that they should suffer; and for human beings,

[for human beings,] that they should die; and for creation, that it should be dissolved. Or rather, truly, the one who wills whatever he does and does whatever he wills—he alone is rightly and properly God.
He not only is alive, but can also grant others life, and, when he has given it, can also take it away whenever he wishes.
For this reason Scripture cries out in this way, speaking in the person of the God of the Jews: “See now, see that I am he, and there is no other
besides me. I put to death and also give life; I wound and also heal, and no one can rescue from my hands.” For there is no other God in whom there is a hidden, inexpressible power
that gives life and puts to death. And again Scripture warns the Jews, because it knew the thoughts that would arise among those who were going to speak of
other gods on earth or in heaven besides the one who truly is God. It says, “The Lord your God is God in heaven above and on earth below,
and there is no other besides him.” How, then, does anyone dare to say that there is another God besides the God of the Jews? I cannot say. And again it says,
“The heavens and the highest heavens, the earth and everything in them, belong to the Lord your God. He chose your ancestors to love them, and you after them.” Thus, then, in every way
Scripture warned that the one who created the world alone is truly God, and also that those others are the offspring of their own imagination. Nevertheless, as an argument,
I also say this to you: even if gods really did exist, they would be subject to the God of the Jews, the one who created everything.
For Scripture says this to the Jews: “The Lord your God is God of gods and Lord of lords.” And Scripture, knowing this one to be just, counsels concerning him

and says, “Fear the Lord your God and serve him alone.” And again, “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one.” Therefore, strengthened in their thoughts by this same understanding, immediately upon being delivered they all cried out together and said,
as though sharing in a drop of the Holy Spirit, “Who is like you among the gods, O Lord?”
And again, “Who is like our God?” Then, insofar as they were able to receive the greatness of his unique sovereignty and lordship—which also, many times, because of the people's constraint,
he makes equal in name [?]—he introduced purity of worship and said, “Do not mention the names of gods.” He also recalled this from the curse upon the serpent,
and said concerning that first speaker of gods, “He was condemned to eat dust,” so that the mouth which first spoke of many gods should be filled with dust.

But if you too are beginning to introduce and sow many gods within the true teaching, under the pretext of another, superior God, you are cleverly seeking to bring about the soul's destruction. But you cannot persuade us to accept your audacity.
For if we go astray and agree with you, when we are judged it will not help us at all

to offer this excuse, saying, “You utterly deceived us.” For neither did it help that first woman, who wrongly believed, to say, “The serpent deceived me.” For she received the punishment of death. Therefore the good [great] Moses

reminded the people of the lordship of one God, warned them, and said, “Take care, and do not stray from the Lord your God.” In the same statement [at the same time], he also reminded them of that woman who went astray and offered an excuse, yet in no way

benefited from it. Moreover, despite all these things, even if someone truly appeared as a prophet of God and gave signs and wonders so that we might believe, but told us to worship other gods besides the God of the Jews,
we would not believe even him. For this is also what God's law taught us.
From the tradition [?], preserve the saying in its purity: “If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises among you and gives you a sign or a wonder.”
And that same person who came and gave you a wonder may come to you and say to you, ‘Let us go and serve other gods, whom you do not know.’ You must not listen
to the words of that prophet or that dreamer of dreams, because he is indeed testing you, to see whether you love the Lord your God. For because of
this, our Lord gave signs and wonders and acknowledged their own God, and was rightly and securely believed by his hearers. But you, even if you truly
