were a prophet and gave these signs and wonders that you promised, yet proclaimed another god or other gods—because clearly, in truth,
a test of the people’s fear of God has arisen—you would certainly not be believed. For in truth there is one God. That is why our Lord Jesus Christ, when he came, advised them to seek
not God himself, because they knew him well, that he exists, but rather his righteousness, which those scribes received from the tradition of Moses and, like a key suited
to the royal house, concealed. Thus they knew God himself. That is why he also advised them not to seek him. And it is impossible that, if they truly did not know God,
he would have neglected to advise them to seek the one who is greater than everything, while reproaching them over those things that are exceedingly insignificant,
especially when compared with God. I mean the blue material of their cloaks and the straps of their shoes,
and their prayer in the streets, and other things like these, which are very insignificant, as I said before, because he had no great matter over which to reproach them.
Simon replied to these things: “I refute you from your own teacher’s words.

For he himself introduced a God who was unknown to your generations, and said so. For Adam knew the one who made him as God, who is the maker of the world. Enoch also knew him, and was taken away by him.

So did Noah, who was commanded by him to make himself an ark. Likewise Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, and the whole people, together with all the nations, acknowledged him as the God who created the world.
This Jesus of yours, who appeared at the end, after your ancestors, said, ‘No one knows the Father except the Son, nor does anyone know the Son except the Father,
and those to whom God wishes to reveal him.’ Thus your Jesus too secretly proclaimed another God, hidden from everyone and unknown.”
Peter said to him, “See how often you contradict yourself, yet you are not ashamed! For if our Jesus knew that hidden God, and Moses,

who appeared earlier, announced Jesus as a prophet who would come in the same form as he himself was, then surely Moses too was not ignorant of him, since he was a prophet, just as Jesus himself knows hidden things.

And what, then, if the Father of all, who is hidden, has had a Son from the beginning, and revealed him in successive generations as he wished? For this reason, none of the ancestors failed to know him.

But how can you attain knowledge of the Father when you deny the Son, whom the whole people honored as the Father and continues to honor until the very end, so that they may all together know that he is the Son?”
Simon replied to these things, “Remember that you also said that God has a Son. Without realizing it, you dishonor

him, for you say that, like those animate and inanimate things, he is subject to suffering. But this is not the time for this argument to expose all your lack of understanding, because I am eager to speak about that limitless light.
Listen to this: perhaps there exists in secret a certain light, a power limitless in its greatness, which neither the Creator knows, nor Moses the lawgiver, nor Jesus the teacher.”

Peter said, “Surely you think that someone is very foolish if, although he believes that there is another above the God who truly exists, he nevertheless says these very things hesitantly, with a ‘perhaps’?”

And before he perfects himself, he perfects someone else through it. This is what he wants to boast about! Is there really anyone more rash and shameless than you, who would explain it to you when you yourself are in doubt?
For if there is another power that neither the creator of the world knew, nor Moses the prophet and lawgiver, nor Jesus the teacher—and how
can that power be so hidden that it is known to no one except one person alone, namely you, such as you are in all these matters?
And how is it that, if he is new, he did not give us another, new sense, so that through that new sense given to us we could come to know him who is new?
But perhaps you say that he cannot give it. How, then, did he give it to you? Perhaps because you wanted it? But we too are capable of wanting it.
But we do not want to be in danger and turmoil. If, then, he revealed it to you,
why not to us too? But if you learned for yourself what the prophets did not know, then at least tell us, like a prophet, what we are thinking.
And not that alone: for if you have a spirit equal to those who resemble you, perhaps you also know these thoughts. But if you cannot tell our thoughts, though we are nearby,
how did you come to know the thoughts of that hidden one? Or even just this much, that he is a being hidden from everyone? But believe me, you would not even
have known what light is if you had not received from him the ability to see, and also this, that he [?] extension, from what you know.

You are sustained by these five kinds of senses that have been shown to you, and even concerning things beyond them, you draw on what you have received through these, you ungrateful man! It is something great
that is really a dream and not the truth. For as long as you cannot demonstrate a new sense beyond the five we have, there is no new God.
Simon said, “Since everything is fulfilled through the five senses, he could not give a new faculty that does not exist.”
Peter said, “You are lying! For there is a sixth sense, which is called foreknowledge. These five senses are receivers of knowledge, but the sixth
reveals knowledge beforehand. But I would like to hear how you know this hidden power, whom even the prophets did not know, when you are not a prophet.”
Then Simon began to say, “This power, which I say exists in secret above the God who created the world,
is known to none of the angels, nor to any of the demons or the Jews, nor to any of the creatures that came into being from the creator.
Even the creator himself does not know him—the one who also established the law. That very law taught me, although it did not itself know what it taught.”
Peter said, “I wonder how you can know more than the law, your teacher! And how can you know more than the law, your teacher,
and how can you offer proofs, when, together with all of us, you do not even know the very one who established the law and created the whole world?
Here you stand, and this little courtyard is enough to contain you!”
When Simon saw Peter laughing along with the whole crowd, he said, “Are you laughing, Peter, when such things are being said?”
Peter answered him, “Do not be angry, Simon. We have done nothing beyond what we promised. We did not stop our ears, nor did we immediately withdraw when we heard it.
But neither were we shaken at all. For this statement of yours is not persuasive enough for us to become alarmed and disturbed in our minds, even because of its resemblance to a true statement.
But present this promise of yours to me, so that we may know how someone seeking God through the law knows what the one who established it knows.”
Simon said, “If you stop laughing as you are doing, I will give you the whole demonstration.”
Peter answered him, “I will even stop laughing, so that I can learn how you knew that the law was established by God—
something that, according to you, even the one who established the law, who is God, does not know.”
Simon said, “Listen, then. Everyone acknowledges, through that indescribable providence, that there is only one, and that God must be good,

greater than all, from whom everything received its standing. Everything that comes after him must necessarily be subject to him as its head. Now, then, I came to know that this God, the creator of the world, according to what the law established by him
says, is deficient in many respects. And this is not [?] perfect; rather, I perceived and understood that another is perfect,
because this one, especially, as the Scriptures say, has shown himself deficient and weak in everything. First, the human being whom he formed did not remain as he wished. And he is not
good, because he laid down a law for that first human being: he was to eat from all the trees in Paradise, but was not to eat from the tree of knowledge; and if he ate, [?].
Why, then, did he forbid him to eat and know what is good or evil, so that he could recognize and flee from evil things and choose good things? But now
he did not even allow him this. When he ate and gained knowledge, he honored him by covering his nakedness, and knew that it was shameful to stand naked before God,

who had made them. Yet he imposed death upon the one who had learned to honor him, and cursed the serpent that had shown him. But if he cursed it as a harmful creature, why did he not restrain it beforehand?
But if he allowed the serpent to enlighten him because he was going to taste something good, he is evil because he did not restrain him from the beginning. For either
he did not know beforehand, and in this case he lacks knowledge; or, if he knew and did not prevent it, he is also weak; or he is not good, since he did not wish to do good.
Thus the one who formed the human being and made the world, as the law says, is weak, as I have demonstrated, and so enables us to know that another is perfect.
For there must be one who is stronger than all, through whom creation itself preserves its order.
From this I know that there must always be one who is better than all and stronger than all. And the one who made the world, whom the Scriptures call God,
is weak, as I have established by comparison. It follows that there must be one who alone is perfect. Both apart from Scripture and from the Scriptures themselves, I have come to know God.

In this way, Peter, I have been able to learn from the law itself what the law does not know. But even if I had lived before the law, or if the law had not wished to speak of the weakness of the one who created the world,
I would have been able to know from the evils that, in the world itself,
occur and are neither corrected nor set right, that the God who created the world is weak, because he does not correct and set right
the things that go wrong. Or, if he is able and has the power but does not wish to correct them, he is evil. But if he is neither able nor willing, then along with
being weak, he is also evil. We must therefore recognize that there is another God who is stronger than all. Say whatever you have to say against these arguments.”
Peter said, “Simon, these are the accusations commonly brought against God

by all those who have dared to read the laws without understanding, and also by those who, before being instructed by the law itself and coming to know it, supposed that they knew its contents accurately.
Yet we, like you, know what is in the Scriptures and explain that God is weak and not good, and all those
The power you put your hope in also falls under this same accusation that you wanted to make against him. Besides, the one you put your hope in is in danger and in a great storm. Perhaps
—and perhaps, then, you also say this about him: he does not correct or remedy these evils that happen here because either he is weak, or, if he is able but unwilling, he is evil.
If he is unable, he is weak. But if he is both unwilling and unable, he is both evil and weak.
Therefore, since he is equally subject to that same accusation, as for the one who created the world, this alone—
that he exists—is evident from his having made this world, and everyone acknowledges it. But the power that you say exists shows nothing.
For how can even this alone—that he exists—be known? How, then, can we abandon God, who made the world, in whose world we live, and whose possessions we enjoy in every way,
and look to someone of whose possessions we not only see nothing at all, but whom we cannot even know, because he does not exist?
But if you say that he is light, brighter than this light here, you have taken the very name from here.
At the same time, you magnify his being with words. And again, whether you call him mind, life, good, or anything else, you take it from here

and say it, and you magnify him only with words. How, then, when you have nothing new even to conceive, can you introduce another new power besides the one who truly is God, when you do not even have a new name to give him?

For this one alone is not called a power; those powers that exist to praise him are also called powers. And does it not please you that we should look to the God who created us, who disciplines us like a father, as he knows best?
But if there is someone else who is good, as you say, he never takes vengeance on us. If he does take vengeance, he is evil.
But this God of ours, of whom I speak, is not evil if he takes vengeance, but just. For he disciplines the human beings who belong to him.
But the one who has been nothing to us—if he takes vengeance on us because we have not fled to him, how is he good, [?] punishing us because we have not abandoned our Father and fled to him
and relied on flimsy ideas? How, then, can you say that someone who is not even just is good?
Simon said, “You are entirely mistaken about this, Peter. For our souls come from that good one on high, but they were brought here as captives.”
Peter said, “Then he is not hidden from everyone, as you said a little while ago. And how did that good one allow this to happen for our punishment, when he is a power superior to all?”
Simon said, “He sent the one who made the world to make it. But the one who made it proclaimed himself and made himself known.”
Peter said, “Then he is not hidden and unknown, as you said a little while ago, since souls also come from there.

And the one who made the world was also sent by him—the one who, as you said, came and, instead of the one who sent him, made himself known and proclaimed himself. But tell me this: did the one who sent him not know the dishonesty of the one being sent?
For if he did not know, he is ignorant. But if he knew and gave him permission, he acted unjustly.
But if he did not give him permission, he is weak. And if he could have done something better than this but did not, he is not good. But if he knew that it would turn out for the good
and did not prevent him, the one who ventured to do good is far superior to the one who could not act before him.”
Simon said, “He helps those who wish to know him and belong to him.”
Peter said, “Not even this is new. For this very thing is also done by this one whom [?] you acknowledge along with me to be God.”
Simon said, “But the Good One helps them only in this respect: that they know him. The one who created the world, however, helps them when they keep his law.”
Peter said, “Then he gives life to the sexually immoral, murderers, and the merciless because of their knowledge of him, but to the chaste, the good, and the merciful, because they have found no sign

at all that he exists and have not known him, he does not give life! This goodness that you promise is very great indeed—not that he gives life to the sexually immoral, but that he does not give life even to the righteous and the chaste!”
Simon said, “For it involves great suffering [?] for human beings to know him
while they are in the body. For this body, which the soul wears, is nothing less than darkness and clay.”
Peter said, “Then the Good One asks for what is difficult, while the one who truly is God demands what is easy. Let him therefore, being good, leave us with our Father who made us.
And when we leave the body and cast off this darkness, we can know him. Then the soul knows its Creator all the more,
that he alone is God. It remains with him and does not wish to belong to another, because it possesses pure knowledge. Nor does it commit the wrong of fleeing and taking refuge in another power,
one who has made himself known to no one else, but only to Simon. And how is he good if he does not want the chaste and the righteous?
And how is he merciful, if he does not know how to help someone unless that person first wrongs his Father? Nor do I know by what senses he
who is so good knows that another God exists. And how is this justice, that when someone wrongs his benefactor, he pleases that god?”
Simon said, “It is not wrongdoing to flee, for the sake of an advantage, to the one who is ready in glory.”
Peter said, “If, as you say, it is not wrongdoing to flee and take refuge with a stranger, then it is much more just to remain with our own Father,
even if he is poor. And if it is not wrongdoing to abandon our own for something better and flee and take refuge with another,
and the God who created the world is not angry about this, then much less will the Good One be angry because we remain with the God who made us. Indeed, I think he will welcome us all the more
because we have remained faithful to the God who made us, reasoning that, even if we belonged to him, we would not have been persuaded to pledge our loyalty to another.

But those who fled and took refuge with him because of a better promise, if they find another who is better than he is, will abandon him too—all the more because they are not called his children and have proved capable of denying their natural Father.”
Simon said, “But what if the souls belong to him and do not know him, and he truly is their Father?”

Peter answered him, “You are introducing a great deal of weakness. For if the souls belonged to that superior one, it would not have been possible for them to be brought down below by the inferior one. Nor, unless they knew

him, would those souls receive punishment from him here when they were separated from the body. Rather, they would be left here too, because they did not know him when they descended into a place that, as you said, was foreign.”
“But it seems to me that you do not know what he is who is both Father and God. Indeed, I could also tell you where those souls came from, and when and how they came into being.
But I cannot tell you now, because you are mistaken about the one who is greater than all.”
Simon said, “A time will come for you when you will regret this: that I told you about that hidden power and you did not recognize it.”

Peter said, “Then give me, as I told you before, a new sense—either as a new god or as someone who has come from that new one—so that through this new sense we may be able to know that new god. For these senses that were created in us, which remain faithful
to the true prophet, have no other means of receiving knowledge of that other one, who is alien to their nature.”
Simon said, “Look, do as I have said, so that you can approach him by an unseen path. Listen to what I mean: have you never been absorbed in thought and stretched your mind toward places

far away, or toward islands? All that time you were there, so that you did not even see the things near you, nor were you aware of yourself or how you were sitting, because of the pleasure of that vision.”
Peter said, “Yes, Simon, this has happened to me at times.”
Simon said, “In the same way, then, stretch your mind toward heaven now, and consider what that place outside the world must be like,
where there is neither heaven nor earth, so that their shadow might in turn produce darkness. For there are no bodies there,
nor is there darkness; it must necessarily be boundless light. Consider what sort of light it is in this way: if this light of the sun fills the whole
world, although the sun is a small body, what do you suppose that light is like, which is unlimited and has no body? So great is it that we must call the light of the sun darkness rather than light.”
When Simon had spoken, Peter answered him and said, “Listen patiently concerning both matters: the illustration about thoughts and that incomprehensible light. I know for certain, Simon,
that I have been absorbed in thought and stretched my mind toward distant islands and places, seeing them in my mind no less clearly than with my eyes. At the beginning, while I was in Capernaum,
when I was fishing, I was sitting on a rock with my hook cast into deep water. I did not notice the fish that had been caught, because my mind was directed
toward Jerusalem, which I loved and to which I often used to go to offer sacrifice. Indeed,
I also lovingly pictured this Caesarea, which many people [?], even though I had never seen it. I imagined about it everything one ought to imagine about a city:
its gates, walls, bathhouses, marketplaces, citadels, and the things associated with them. All this time I thought I was seeing them,
so that I truly forgot myself, just as you said earlier: I did not even see what was near me, nor did I remember where I was sitting.
In short, many times, when my thoughts were especially occupied with distant cities, I did not notice that I had caught a large fish on the hook, although all the while it was pulling me forcefully,
trying to snatch itself away from me by the strength of its pull. But I remained unaware, and many times I was in danger of falling. Then my brother Andrew, who was sitting beside me,
would often prod me hard and rouse me as though I were deeply asleep. He would say, ‘Do you not see, [?], the fish you have caught? Why is your mind wandering?
What has happened to you? Tell me at once!’ But I became a little angry with him, because he had deprived me of the things I loved.
I told him, ‘Nothing bad has happened to me. I was looking at Jerusalem, which I love, and at Caesarea along with it.’
Thus, while I was bodily in Capernaum, in my soul I was wandering through Jerusalem and Caesarea. And Andrew—
I do not know how—spoke a hidden truth to me. He said, ‘Look, Simon, at what you are doing!

For those who are going to become possessed by demons and depart from their natural state of mind begin by indulging in fantasies like this. Then, through the emptiness of imagining things that do not exist, their minds are emptied.
This, then, is the soul’s [?]: when it is caught up in distraction and does not see the things that exist,
but longs for things that do not exist. For those who are insane often think they see apparitions, because their souls are troubled by madness, a multitude of those
[Of these] which we have entered into [?]. Likewise, all those who are sometimes affected by such weakness readily bring things into their minds and see things that exist and are near us.
But things that do not exist they think they see as though they existed and were near. Likewise, many people burning with thirst, when they fall asleep, see springs and rivers as in a mirage.

And although they think they are drinking, they drink nothing. This happens to them because their souls waste away from the dryness of the body. We should therefore consider such mirages to be an affliction of the soul and body.
To understand that this is so, listen: Jerusalem, which you love—even while you are sitting here,
you could see it as it really is, because you had actually seen it before. But now you also say the same about Caesarea,
that you thought you saw it. Yet when I pictured it in my mind, I argued vigorously and boasted, saying that it really was just as I thought
I was seeing it. But when I came here, I despised myself, because in the picture in my mind I had not seen anything resembling it. Rather, what I imagined came from what I knew of gates.
Even the gates I pictured in my mind were actually based on those I had seen before. For no one can imagine anything new unless he takes his starting points
from the forms he has seen before. For if I imagine and think about oxen with five
heads, are not those with five heads derived from the ones I had previously seen, which appeared to me to have one head?
And you too, now—if what you say is true, that by stretching out your mind you think you have seen beyond heaven, as far as the boundless one himself—
it is easy for you to stretch your mind into the hearts of each of those nearby and tell us their ideas and thoughts. But I do not mean those who share your views and are your supporters.
Simon answered these things and said, “Since you say so much as though telling stories, listen: it cannot be that whatever a person thinks of has no real existence. For things that do not exist,
which have no form, cannot even enter a person's mind.”
Peter said, “Then if someone thinks that something exists, or, in the case of a place he has never experienced,
if he imagines that it is light, when it is darkness, how can the very same thing be both light and darkness?”
Simon said, “Leave aside now what I said. Tell me what you think about heaven.”
Peter said, “If I were to wrong the source of light, I would show you
what it is and what the boundless one is like—not through commonplace mirages, but through a sequence and order that necessarily exists in reality. And this would not be
from any other source, but from the Law itself and from nature itself, so that you might know that the Law knows the boundless one exceedingly well.
And if it knows the boundless one, then nothing is hidden from it. The very supposition that there is something God does not know is a falsehood,
[to God.] Since the Law established by him knows everything. But I am not now speaking to you about the boundless one
unless you first agree with me that these finite heavens can be understood—or demonstrate the opposite from the Law itself, as you said.
But if you cannot know these things that are finite, much less do you know the boundless one, nor can you know him.”
Simon answered these things: “It is better, then, to believe simply and plainly that there is a God, and that he is nothing other than the heaven visible over the whole world.”
Peter said, “Not so. Rather, let us say that there truly is one God.”

“As for the heavens, even if they truly exist as the Law says, the highest of them surrounding him, even this visible heaven will be rolled up and pass away at the consummation of everything, so that he who is older than they may appear to those found worthy after the judgment.”
Simon replied to this, “These things may indeed be as you say.
For someone who believes, they can be so. But if someone asks you for proof of them from the Law, you cannot give it to him,
especially concerning knowledge of the limitless light.”
Peter said, “Do not suppose that we hold these things by faith alone,
but also with proof. For this reason I do not wish to present them merely on faith, for that would not be prudent either. It is better to accept something with proof, because

the certainty of what has been given to someone keeps him from losing it. But someone who simply assents to what he is told does not take care over it and perhaps does not remain constantly firm in it. For someone who believes easily does not take care to preserve it.
He also easily ceases to believe and is not steadfast, because he does not know what it is that he believes. Thus, firm faith comes from much disbelief.”
Simon said, “This is a great promise you are making: that you will demonstrate from the Law that it reveals the limitless light that has existed from eternity.”
Then Peter said, “Whenever you wish.” Simon said, “Since today has already passed, tomorrow, when I come forward and argue against you,
show me that the world was made and that souls do not die, and I will become your helper in your preaching.”
After saying this, he went out. More than a third of the crowds with him, numbering about a thousand, went out with him.
The others knelt down and fell before Peter. He prayed over them and drove demons out of some of them.
He healed those among them who were sick and joyfully dismissed the whole crowd, instructing them to come early the next morning.
After the crowds had left, Peter ordered bedding to be spread on the ground in the courtyard, under the open sky, where the discussion had taken place. He reclined with the eleven.
I reclined with some others, dear friends who had also only recently begun to listen, and we ate.
But Peter kindly considered that I might be distressed and said, “It is not out of arrogance, Clement,

that I do not eat with those who have not yet been purified. Rather, I am afraid that I might harm myself without helping them at all. For I was convinced of this: everyone who worships idols—whenever he [?]; I mean those called gods—
is not free from unclean spirits. Because he has become a partner of demons, an indwelling spirit from among them seizes him and drags him along. Thus he is not clean of spirits
that are unclean if he has worshiped idols out of fear or love, or again if he has tasted unclean sacrifices, because he has shared in the table of demons,
or again if he has committed adultery, because of that unlawful union. For these are the demons’ ways of corrupting souls, from which bodily afflictions arise for the sake of fleeing from
sins. For this reason, after purification we baptize those who are worthy, so that the unclean spirits hidden within their souls may come out of them.
What is troubling is that they do not even reveal that they are within, lest, once they appear openly, they should be driven out. For they love being in human bodies,
so that through them they may enjoy the things they love. For when the soul, through an evil inclination, has separated itself from good things, all people who are like
Thus it makes them a dwelling place for demons. One of them is this Simon, who has been seized by this very disease. Because of his past [?], healing cannot take place
for him. For that demon is not in him against his will. If we wished to drive it out of this man, since, so to speak, his soul is inseparable from it,
he would die, and we would be liable to a sentence of death. But let none of you be distressed that he has withdrawn from our table. For each person remains apart for as long as he wishes.

Those who wished to be baptized after a short time remained apart only a little while, whereas those who wished to do so after a long time remained apart a long while. For each person has it in his own power to make the time of his repentance short or long,
concerning his salvation and his life. So it is now up to you to eat with us whenever you wish, not whenever we wish. For we are not permitted to eat with you unless you first

receive baptism. Thus it is you who prevent us from eating with you, not we who prevent you, for we are willing to baptize you immediately.” Having said these things, he pronounced a blessing and ate. After he had eaten his fill, he gave thanks
and offered praise, and [?] went to sleep. We did the same, for evening had come.
Then Peter arose at the time when the rooster crows. As he was about to wake us, he immediately saw that we were all awake, for the lamp was still burning.
He greeted us and saw that we were all sitting down. He began to say, “Do not suppose that it is not difficult to speak about the truth
to crowds made up of people of every kind. For one is not permitted to tell everyone what actually is, because of those who are wicked and evil.
Yet it is not right to lie, because of those who love the truth. What, then, should someone who speaks before crowds do? Should he conceal the truth?
And how would he convince those who are worthy? Or should he speak the truth to those who do not wish to live? He would wrong the one who sent him, who, concerning his words, which are like pearls,
commanded that they should not be given to those who have the character of dogs and pigs. When such people receive them, they wrap them in angry and deceitful words more contemptible than spit,

so that they may enjoy the boast of being praised in the minds of ordinary people. For this reason I have taken many roundabout paths and turns, so that I might hide and conceal from the unworthy the teaching about the divinity that rules over all.”
While Peter was saying these things, Aquila said to him, “You have spoken [?]. For this reason, tell us the things that belong to the truth.”
Peter said, “Now ask whatever you wish.”
Aquila said, “Tell us about the question of sovereignty, or about sovereignties and authority,

and about Simon’s objection that it is not fitting to say that Christ is the Son of God, lest we suppose that he undergoes experiences like those of plants, other things without souls, and animals endowed with souls.”
When Peter saw that we all wished to hear these very things, he entrusted to us the whole teaching about them,

as follows: “The term ‘sovereignty’ is applied to many different things, both things perceived by the senses and things understood by the mind. But because, before experience of things perceived by the senses, and also

to those understood by the mind. But so that we do not think we have approached things understood by the mind before experiencing things perceived by the senses, it is fitting and right that we begin first with visible things.

When we have received reliable proofs from them as a guarantee, we will then proceed to the understanding of things known through the mind. Let us begin with this: the sun was appointed as a ruler to govern the day,
and the moon over what is opposite to it. They were appointed to rule by the very one from whom they also received their existence in the beginning. It was he who, for their sake,

established heaven and earth, having first created them in the beginning. Together with them he also established the animals on land and in the sea, birds, trees, and plants, and afterward the human being.
And the human being received not merely existence on an equal footing, but also life according to the command that God gave him. Thus it is not possible for there to be many sovereignties.”

For there is one first principle, and one that is without beginning. Those that come after these two are spoken of by an extended use of language, even if they are called first principles. But I have already stated the reason
for this progression, which draws and leads upward from perceptible things to intelligible things, so that you may use this path carefully and correctly, and acquire care concerning the transmission
of intelligible things. We say, then, that God is without beginning, as we advance with unfailing diligence and are drawn
toward him—not that he is his own cause, nor that he begot himself. For he is without beginning and is the Being who did not come into being. This does not bring us to know what he is,

but that he did not come into being. But those who called the Being who did not come into being his own father and his own begetter dared to wrong him, having enslaved themselves to feeble ideas and thoughts.

For, like children, they thought and supposed that he who exists before coming into being needed to beget himself. They substituted one who does not exist for one who exists, and said that he came into being through himself,

in the madness into which they had fallen. And those Greeks dared to compare the Being who did not come into being to plants. All these things fall within impiety, and they are also accompanied by a lack of

understanding. For they did not realize that they were saying of the very same one that he exists and does not exist. For insofar as he begot himself, he existed; but insofar as he was begotten by himself, he did not exist.

Therefore he did not exist because he was begotten, and he existed because he begot. But the assurance of reverence for God does not permit us to say both things about him, who is one and the same. Moreover, our inward thoughts themselves

carefully and cautiously drive this blasphemy away from us and allow us to say what befits the Being who did not come into being. What, then, should someone say when questioned by those who have already impiously said, “Did he not exist beforehand, he who was going to become his own father?”
How, then, can he who possesses existence before granting himself existence be said, under any conception, to be his own father and his own begetter?
And what trace of reason is there in saying that he does not exist when he already exists? It is audacity to say that the Being who did not come into being came into being from himself.
But what happens to those who speak this way is—to speak by way of correction—what happens to drunken people who jump over their own shadows as though they were pits.

For this reason, it is fitting that we should first of all investigate those who are not mortal, beginning with the teaching of our Lord, where he teaches us about the servitude of mortals who are subject
to those who do not die: we should endure danger and trial even to death, in hope and expectation of the good things of the kingdom, through his saying, “Do not fear those who kill the body
but cannot kill the soul. Rather, fear him who can destroy both body and soul

in Gehenna.” And indeed, if the soul does not die with the body, nor is it cut apart, nor does it experience any of the things the body experiences, such as inward flow or outward flow, thinness or thickness,
health or sickness, severing or joining together; moreover, even in the generation of human beings, nothing in the flow itself helps the soul.

Rather, in all its movements it remains everywhere unchanged in its own individual existence, and by its distinct mobility it directs the body toward every task. Thus it is the body that undergoes flow and suffering in its own being and individual existence,

as we can observe and learn through actual experience. For after those who are to be born have taken shape, the capacity of the womb, because of the growth of the infant, which pushes and is pushed as though in a struggle through the creative word, [?]; and the one

who has taken shape hastens to come out. This very cause changes the birth pains into deliveries and the fluttering of the form itself [?]. And when suffering or danger occurs, whether affecting the whole or some particular part, as

is generally accepted. For everything that desire for women produces is prepared beforehand and shaped beforehand by nature in all the stages of each person's growth: in one way in a boy, and in a different form in one who has reached youth,
and differently in an adult man. For the boy has within him the capacity for intercourse with them, but he does not also have within his power the impulses of the soul.
He, however, has reached adolescence and is ready for intercourse [?], but does not yet have any use for the things he discharges.
For a grown man possesses, along with his will, the full capacity to use them. Yet it is not from these things alone that we can speak about the soul,

which is immortal, and about the body, which is subject to its direction, but also from those commandments that were given to the inward self, as our Lord himself says: “It was said to those of old, ‘Do not commit adultery.’”

“But I say that you must not become enslaved to desire even through seeing and looking.” He spoke with great divine wisdom. For if the body is naturally bound to the desire for intercourse with women,
that is, forcibly subjected to those things from which it also received its existence and its particular forms, since this belongs primarily to the body, how,

then, could anyone suppose that it was to the body that this was said: “Do not commit adultery; but I say that you must not even become enslaved to desire,” rather than to that which is, in its own being, free from passions like these,

and has the power to lead and direct the body in its actions wherever the command of the supreme authority instructs it? Thus, because we await and hope for the things to come, we do not become angry,
and we overcome wrath. We turn our eyes and thoughts away from women, and through hope for the things to come we make our thoughts soar. As I said, not everything that we are
is a slave subjected to desire for women. Rather, one part of us is a slave by nature, as we have shown, namely the body; but another part of us belongs to the will, which is
the movement of the immortal soul. Since these things are so, we have found, one might say by God's will, a good path toward understanding these intelligible realities.
From now on, let us proceed without stumbling, making use of this conception of the immortal soul. Let us no longer allow bodily passion to enter that intelligible and immortal being, while

we apportion [?] all this honor to each of those intelligible beings, according as their order permits, whether they exist or existed beforehand. First, then, there is the Being who did not come into existence,

about whom the prophets also testified: “I am the first, and I am the last, and besides me there is no other God.” The expression “besides me” indicates that he is without beginning and is the Being who did not come into existence.
Clement and the others were signaling to one another that they wanted to hear what the Being who did not come into existence is.
Peter noticed and said, “It is no small danger to speak about the one who is without beginning,
“or to listen. Yet, because of your delight in and love for what has been said, you are eager to fall into immeasurable danger. You are apparently trying to trap me into suffering the same thing,

“since you suppose that I can attempt to describe the one who is hidden and inexpressible. But I advise you, my brothers and companions, not to inquire what he is, but only to consider hearing that he exists.

“For it is neither fitting nor right to say even this about him at great length. He is, then, the Being who did not come into existence, and he is not honored with an ordinary name. For he also did not come into existence,

“and he is not honored with an ordinary name, for he is also without beginning. This one, who is without beginning and is the Being who did not come into existence, is God. He is not praised on the basis of coming into existence, but only as far as ‘good’ [?].
“He is understood only by himself. For nothing that existed before him, nor anything that came into existence afterward, can see itself in his existence and his being without beginning.

“For this seeking and investigation concerns coming into existence. For this reason, his existence is hidden and cannot be expressed. As for first examining his existence, there is no room for inquiry.
“For his existence is not secondary to his investigating whether he exists. He therefore knows himself and does not go on questioning himself. But these things, even beyond what is right and fitting,

“we have spoken. For the Being who did not come into existence loves to be honored only in stillness and silence. You have therefore learned from us, to the extent of our ability and without danger, that this being is without beginning. He,

“then, is God, who exists without beginning. He begot his firstborn Son before all created things, in a manner fitting for God, without being altered or changed, without being divided or flowing away, and without being diminished in any way.”

For you remember what those bodily sufferings are like—the very ones that we avoid attributing even to the soul, because we fear that its immortality might somehow be destroyed if they were attributed to it.
Therefore, he begot by virtue of his being God, and not by undergoing any division.

For when he willed it, his power was not found deficient in relation to his will, nor did his power go beyond the purpose of his will. Rather, in complete agreement with what he willed, so he also begot.
By virtue of what he is, and not by undergoing suffering. For if those bodies that are subject to the constraint of material density bring shadows into existence,
how much more should we attribute this to that self-existent Power: that the Only Begotten who comes from him accompanies him. For this reason, then, he was truly called an offspring of the will.
For in his own person he is not the Father. But I remember that Simon objected when we said that Christ is the Son of God, and accused us of blasphemy,
saying, “You make God like human beings and plants.” And you were eager with all your souls to learn. But when we all affectionately signaled to him, Peter himself
said, “The way of unbelief is plain, Aquila, and you others. For someone who does not truly know, and is still good only at listening, is afraid to believe beforehand.

But when he is provoked by someone who can drive the cause of his unbelief out of him, he eagerly sets about denying this beginning. And he does not hesitate to conceal his unbelief, which he has imprinted upon his inquiry through his love of wanting to learn.
For the diseases of unbelief are many. But let our discussion of this come later, lest it somehow draw us toward an easily obtained expectation of faith
and bring inquiry before faith. Therefore, everywhere let there first be honor
from us for God, and for the inquiry concerning him. Know, then, that in a manner worthy of God he begot his Only Begotten, his Son, his Firstborn, before all created things.
For he did not come to act upon himself and beget himself; for he would not have remained without suffering and without injury,
if he had acted upon himself. For it is wicked to entertain such ideas about the self-existent One, who is not like these things. For those wicked people are in danger, like the one
whom they devised by will [?], and they greatly blasphemed against him, saying that the self-existent One is female and male. But I remember that I had also reminded you of this, my brothers.
Therefore, God begot by virtue of what he is, as was said before. For this reason he was truly called the Only Begotten. For from the self-existent One comes
his being, and he was truly called Son, for he was begotten from that self-existent One who did not come into being. But their perversity, which leads to harm, let us gently and little

by little expose [?]: those who dare to explain the self-existent One merely by the name of one who came into being, and who boast that the one who came into being—distinguished by the opposite designation—has the personal reality of the self-existent One.
Yet he is spoken of as one who did not come into being. But if he is called something that he is not, while what he is is not his designation—for he is, from
his existence, self-existent in his own person, yet is called one who came into being—he is dishonored by being called what he is not. All the more so, since God is rational of himself,
and he is of himself without beginning. How is this not wicked? Indeed, it is not even possible to say that, while he himself is self-existent,
and he himself is rational, he does not also [?] prefer to join himself to himself, or to fall into the order of duality that he established, honoring begottenness above unbegottenness.
For he is not one [?]. Nor was he giving permission to himself when he said, “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool beneath your feet.” Nor was he divided against himself,
so that one part of him would remain self-existent and another part be drawn into coming into being. To say these things about God is great wickedness.

For it is plain, and all those capable of even a little understanding acknowledge concerning the person of the self-existent One, who did not come into being, that he does not suffer in the begetting that comes from him. But if after the begetting, not even

They have always stood opposed, without agreeing, since they were distinguished in number. For he is not his own father. How much more, then, did the Eternal One desire to remain in the perfection of his being
in his own person, while through generation he was reckoned as two. The mother of this foolishness is ignorance about God, and its companion and sister is lack of learning. But the Holy Spirit,
who is the pledge and guardian of the things given to us by our Lord, whom we received not many days after his ascension, belongs to the Only Begotten.
She is the imprint and exact likeness of his power, just as he too, the only-begotten Son and the Firstborn before everything, is the exact, unchanging image of the likeness
of the power that is unbegotten. He alone is the unchanging image, and by appearing to beings endowed with understanding, he gives a vision of the unbegotten Eternal One, and also
to beings endowed with senses. For he is not himself the unbegotten Eternal One, but he is the entire power of the Eternal One in his being and his divinity, and he reveals him wholly as he is.

To those who do not inquire idly, he was considered an unbegotten being. But those whose inquiry is preceded by the fear of God take care not merely to say that they inquire in this way, but also to conduct themselves accordingly.
There is, then, one unbegotten Eternal One and one true offspring. The Holy Spirit cannot be called the Son, nor the Firstborn.

But she is numbered with the Father and the Son, as the first engraved imprint of the power of the second. For the Son himself is the Father's power, likeness, and solid image of his being, equal in will; as the offspring of his being, he is seen wholly together with him.
He also said many other things about the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and convinced us all.

He gave our hearing an assurance no less than that supplied by the examination of the eye. Thus, as we all listened, we were distressed over people, at how far they had stumbled and turned away from the truth.
At dawn, before the sun rose, Peter went out of the house with a few others.

He returned to us and, as was his custom, prayed and sat down. Then someone came in to us and said that a large crowd of people had arrived and were in the open courtyard, with Simon standing among them.
He was trying to capture their attention beforehand with malicious words. When Peter heard this, he immediately went out and stood in the place where he had spoken with him the day before.
The entire crowd immediately turned and fixed their eyes on him with joy.
When Simon perceived the great favor Peter enjoyed, from the great love that the entire crowd had for him, he was astonished and said, “I am utterly amazed at people's foolishness:
they call me a sorcerer, but they love and cherish Peter! Yet because they are my acquaintances and familiar companions, they ought to love me more. Therefore, from this sign too,
those who have understanding can recognize that Peter is a sorcerer. For although their familiarity with me ought to have made them love me, I do not have their love.

But he has it in abundance, although they had no obligation to love him.” While Simon was saying many such things against Peter, treating him as a sorcerer, Peter greeted the entire crowd and then answered him:
“Simon, a person's own thinking is enough to bring him into contempt. But if you are bewildered that those who were your familiar companions and acquaintances not only do not love you,
but even hate you, you will be ashamed when you hear the reason for this from me. It is because you are a deceiver,
yet you promise the truth. Many lovers of truth became your friends. But because they saw in you the opposite of what you promised,
they not only ceased to love you, but, because they are lovers of truth, as I told you, they hated you as a deceiver. Yet they did not simply abandon you,
because, although you were making promises about greatness, saying that you would show it to them sometime, as long as the one who could truly show it was not near,
they put up with you. But when the hope of greatness came near to them, then they utterly despised you and held you in contempt, while loving greatness itself.”
But while you were doing unlawful things from the beginning and imagining that you were deceiving them, the opposite of what you expected happened to you, because not only

did you not know the truth itself, but you had not even heard it from those who knew it. If you had heard it, you would have known what this means: “There is nothing concealed that will not become known, and nothing hidden that will not be revealed.”
These things are the mysteries of God, and by his will they are revealed to those who are worthy. But if you had listened, whether sooner or later, you would certainly have learned the truth.
Even if you had not believed at once, in the long run, as an unbeliever, you would eventually have been fully convinced and persuaded by experience itself.
When Peter had said these things and what followed them, Simon said, “Do not prevent me from pressing you about your opening statement yesterday.
For you said, ‘I can show that the Law itself points to an unbounded light existing from eternity, although there are only two heavens, which themselves came into being.’

“For this reason, since there is no infinite place in which the one who truly is the hidden Father dwells alone, he passed beyond that throne which remains forever, and this visible one came into being in its likeness. [?]

“And it cannot pass away. Of necessity, the Father of everything is one, for two heavens cannot be found, and it is impossible for two unlimited things to exist. Otherwise, neither of them is infinite, for each is bounded by the other.
“If, then, you not only say that this is not so, but also demonstrate it from the Law itself, leave aside these many words and speak at once.”
Peter said, “If I were required to speak for your sake, since you have come to speak against us continually about this, you would never have heard even a single word from me. But because
the farmer who sows for the sake of his good land must also lose a little seed—for the word, like seed, falls either on rock, or on a well-trodden road, or on uncultivated ground full of thorns.
“Our good Teacher used these very comparisons when he wished to show the differences between people's inclinations, but not [?].”
Simon said, “You seem to me to have become very angry. For this reason I declare that I withdraw from the debate.”

Peter said, “I know that because you realized you were about to be exposed, you wanted to withdraw from the debate under a pretext. Otherwise, what wrong have I done by becoming angry with a man who wants to mislead this entire crowd?

“Besides having nothing to say, he presents himself as humble, yet even gives orders, as though he had authority, that we should conduct the debate as he wishes, rather than as the debate itself properly requires.”
Simon said, “I force myself to be patient with your ignorance so that I may show that you want to mislead these people, whereas I speak the truth.
“Even now I am leaving aside the inquiry about the unlimited one. Answer the question I ask you: If, as you said, God made everything, where does evil come from?”
Peter said, “To ask in this way is not the conduct of someone conducting an inquiry, but of someone learning. So if
you want to learn, admit it. First I will teach you how you can learn, and then, when you know how to listen, I will begin to explain things to you. But if you do not want to learn,
as I have correctly understood, I will first set before us the truth that I proclaim. You, in turn, set before us whatever you think
is true, so that, when the truth claimed by both sides has been openly displayed in the debate itself, it may become known which argument is better and true.”
Simon said, “I feel like laughing at who it is that promises to teach me! Nevertheless, I put up with your ignorance and arrogance, and I admit that I want to learn. Show how you can teach me.”
Peter said, “If you truly want to learn, first learn how ignorantly you asked your question. For you said, ‘If God made everything, where does evil come from?’
“For three questions precede this one [?]: first, whether it exists; next, what it is; and then, why it exists and where it comes from.”

Simon replied, “You ignorant, uneducated man! Who among human beings does not acknowledge that evil exists in the world? That is why I, treating you as someone with intelligence and inward understanding,
asked you where evil comes from. It was not because I wanted to learn from you anything that I know—for you know nothing—but because I wanted to expose you,
because you know nothing. Do not suppose that I spoke so harshly because I was angry with you, but because I pity those standing here whom you want to lead astray.”
Peter said to him, “You are very wicked: after hurling all these insults, you say that you were not angry! Yet smoke cannot be seen unless there is fire first.

Nevertheless, I will speak, so that you do not think I am merely evading the issue [?], as though I could not refute the statement you wrongly made. For you said that everyone acknowledges that evil exists.
But that is a lie. For, in the first place, even if it exists, the whole Jewish people denies it, except only the chair of Moses.”
Simon interrupted him and said, “Then are those who say that evil exists thinking correctly, or not?”

Peter said, “That is not what I have undertaken to demonstrate now, but rather that not all human beings say that evil exists. Next, as a second question, should you not have asked what evil is: whether it is a being and a distinct entity, or an action, or an occurrence?
There are also many other questions, and only after those comes the question of what causes evil, how it exists, and why it exists:
[?] to God, or to an angel, or to human beings, or to the wicked, or to the righteous, or to everyone, or even to no one.
And what, indeed, is useful, or not useful? That is to say, many other questions also follow from this subject that lies before us.”
Simon replied, “Forgive me for going too far with my first question, and consider that I am now asking you first whether evil exists or not.”
Peter said to him, “How are you asking—as a student, as a teacher, or as an investigator? For if you are asking as a student, I must teach you

what you ought to ask before asking about evil, so that, by following the sequence and the proper order, you will come to understand evil for yourself. But if you are asking as a teacher, I have no need to learn, for I have

the one from whom I learned everything. But if you are asking as an investigator, let us both establish in our minds a subject to put before us, and then conduct our discussion. For you ought not to ask as a student
and argue against us as a teacher, so that after I have given my answer, it would be for you to say whether I had stated the matter well or badly.
For you cannot fairly be the judge while occupying the position of an opponent. So if you want to investigate the matter with me in discussion,
let us both establish in our minds a subject to put before us. Then, while we speak against one another as opponents, let this God-loving people standing here be the judge.”
Simon said, “Does it not seem foolish to you that we should choose as our judge a crowd that is ignorant and uneducated?”
Peter said, “It is not always so. For what one person discovers only with difficulty can be grasped by many, whose collective report often even
acts like prophecy. Besides all this, because this crowd standing here loves God, it is united in its agreement concerning the love of truth, just as two people,
when they disagree, do not form one assembly. You can recognize from their silence that this crowd standing here is like one person: how, with all the quiet that is fitting

and proper, as you see, even before learning anything, they offer honor to the truth of God through their quietness and silence. They have not yet learned to give anything more than this of themselves.

That is why I trust in God that he accepts their goodwill toward him and grants victory to the messenger of truth, so that the one who is the herald of truth may also be revealed and made known to them.”
Simon said, “Tell me what you want us to investigate, so that I too may prepare myself accordingly and conduct the inquiry with you.”
Peter answered him: “If you want to do what pleases me, I want to act according to the command of my teacher, who, when he came to our people, the Hebrews,
knew that they acknowledged one God, who made heaven and earth and everything in them. Because they understood this correctly, he did not command them to investigate this, but
advised them to discover his will, because he knew that human beings have the power to discover and do the things for which they are judged.

That is why he told us to inquire, not into where injustice comes from—as you asked a little earlier when you said, ‘Where does evil come from?’ Rather, he advised us first to discover the righteousness of the Good One, saying, ‘Seek first the righteousness of God,
and all these things will be added to you.’ But if they had not known God himself, he would not have advised them to seek his righteousness first.”

Simon said: “Since, then, to the Hebrews, as people who rightly know God, [?] and everyone has it in his own power to do the things for which he is judged—but I do not agree with the things that pleased them—where should I begin?”
Peter said: “I advise that we first investigate whether we have the ability to know the things that are examined through discernment.”
Simon said: “Not always. Rather, about God, on whom the entire created existence of every person also depends.”
Peter said: “Then are you certain that we have the power to know? If so, simply acknowledge that you are certain, and let us begin with God, as you wish.”
Simon said: “This ability is not always within us and in our power.”

Peter said: “Then if this is not in our power, it is pointless to investigate God, if we do not have the power to investigate and discover. That is why I rightly advised that we first investigate whether we have this power.”
Simon said: “We cannot even know whether we have any power.”

Peter realized that Simon, because he had been defeated, had given himself over to quarrelling, intending to turn the whole inquiry into doubt. He answered him: “How, then, do you know that there is nothing a human being has the power to know, when you already know this very thing?”
Simon said: “I do not know whether I know even this. For each person knows, acts, and experiences things according to what has been allotted to him.”
Peter said: “Do you see, our brothers, the utter foolishness and error in which Simon finds himself? Before I came, he was teaching as though human beings had within themselves [?]

[of human beings] and had it in their power both to know and to do what they wanted. But now that he has been brought down by the arguments, he has denied this, saying that human beings do not have the power to know or do anything at all.
Yet he used to teach [what he taught], and now, just recently, he is trying to teach [to teach] those things [these things].
And where, then, is God, who judges concerning truth or conduct those who have nothing in their own power? By this statement everything is ruined and undone. I say

[I say] that even zeal for virtue [?], and the judgments laid upon the heads [perhaps: justly] of the unjust are made unjust, since they did not sin of their own will. And the laws too are spoken of [and also]

which distinguish good actions from evil ones. The virtuous person who perseveres in righteousness is miserable, while the wicked enjoy themselves, rebel, and boast that there is no righteousness or judgment.
And under compulsion, because righteousness exists in the world, [?]. But the unjust person is at ease. Fine and pleasant things always belong
to the wicked, while hateful and harsh things [and evil things] belong to the good. Then God does not exist, nor [and neither] is he just, if goodness is not helped and righteousness is not sought.

Simon, then, has not explained these very things [these things]. He wants to escape the severe refutation and withdraws from the inquiry on the pretext that human beings do not have the power [he says] to investigate and discover. But he
himself, if he really knew this, would not have tried to teach while I was away. But I say that a human being has freedom and has authority over himself.”
Simon said: “What is freedom? Explain what it means to have authority over oneself.”
Peter said, “If it is not within your power to learn, why do you want to listen?”
Simon said, “But do you have nothing to say about this?”
Peter said, “I will speak, not because you have compelled me, but because those present
have asked it of me. Freedom is the soul’s knowledge and discernment, with its capacity to turn toward whatever actions it wishes.”
At this Simon praised Peter and said, “Truly, you have spoken magnificently and beyond comparison. For when you speak well,
I know how to bear witness to what you say. But this is what I ask you, and if you answer me truthfully, I will believe you about the other matters.
What I want to learn is this: if God himself wants something to exist, does it exist, and if he does not want something, does it not exist? Answer me yes or no.”

Peter answered him, “If you do not recognize the fault and foolishness of your question, I forgive you, and I will explain it to you. But if you asked knowingly, you have acted foolishly and wickedly, not rightly.”
Simon said, “I swear by that which is the cause of everything,
which takes vengeance on those who do wrong, whether by nature or by choice, that I plainly have nothing to say: I do not know the foolishness and fault in the question I asked.”
Peter answered him, “Since you have admitted that you do not know, learn that your question demands a single answer about two contrary matters. For these,
in their activity, are divided into two categories: natural necessity and free will. Those things that exist under the necessity of their nature are always that way, while those
that act by their own will are not always so. Thus the sun has received this constraint: to run its course as appointed, whereas a human being acts as he wishes. For those things
that serve in subjection to the necessity imposed at creation cannot do anything other than what they have been appointed to do, and they receive neither honor nor reward.
After they have completed what they were appointed to do, the one who made them preserves them as he wishes. But whoever has it within his power to do whatever he wishes is
subject to honor and reward, and also to punishment. He receives honor if he does what is good. But you said, ‘If God wants something, it exists, and if he does not want something,
it does not exist.’ Thus, when I tell you that whatever he wants exists, and whatever he does not want does not exist, you will say, ‘Then he wants the evils that occur in the world to exist,
because everything he wants exists, and whatever he does not want does not exist.’ And if everything he does not want does not exist, then you have something else to say:
‘Then he is powerless to accomplish what he wants.’ And you will boast as though you had won, although you have said nothing correctly, since you do not know how he wills each of these things.
For he wills that one thing should be unable to do anything other than what has been appointed for it, and therefore it receives neither honor nor punishment.
But he wills that something else should have it within its power to do whatever it wishes, so that, through its own agency, either honor or punishment

may come to it. Since, then, these two categories of choice are distinct, everything God wants exists, and whatever he does not want does not exist: it is not to choose, by the authority of its own will,
whatever it wants for itself, but what has been appointed.”
Simon said, “Could he not have made us all good, so that we could not be anything else?”
Peter said, “This too is connected with the other matter. For if he had made us incapable of changing and bound us to be good, truly—”
They were not good, because they could not do anything else. Thus, what was being done was not a matter of free choice,
but of compulsion, since that was how it was. How, then, can anyone say that someone like that is good, when he is not good by his own choice?
That he is good, when he is not good by his own choice. For this reason, a long period of time was required for the world,
until that number of good souls, which had previously become separated [?] from God, reaches its full total. Then this visible heaven
will be rolled up like a scroll and pass away, and those souls [?] will put on their bodies like light.
But the souls of the wicked, because of their evil deeds, will receive a spirit of fire in their bodies [?].
That these things are so was handed down to us by that prophet who does not lie. If you wish, I will show you that he is a prophet,
and I can give you full assurance through many great proofs. For even among the things that he
said at that time, some are now happening exactly as he described them. Those things that he said would happen afterward are also continually happening.
For the things that have already happened give us confidence in those that are yet to happen.
Now Simon had learned from many people that, if he could firmly establish the argument concerning the prophet and show that the whole inquiry was contained in it,

he asked to hear the argument concerning the prophet. He replied, saying, “Answer me about the things I want to know.” Then he asked this question: “If, as you say, this heaven surrounding the world passes away, why did it come into being in the first place?”
Peter said, “For the sake of the many who are here now, it has become like a fence, so that no unworthy person may see [?] God. For whoever sees him is to live
forever. That is why God is ready to appear only to those who are pure in heart. For this reason, during this time of struggle, he is not seen,
because of this covering of heaven. For those who are victorious, this honor is reserved: God the Father himself will appear to them.”
Simon said, “If the Creator is good, and the world is beautiful, how can the good one destroy this beautiful thing, whenever that may be? And if
he destroys this beautiful thing, how is he good? But if he destroys it because it is ugly, how is he not ugly himself, since he made something ugly in the beginning?”

Peter said, “Since we have promised not to run away from blasphemers, we put up with them, because they will give an account of what they say. Nevertheless, listen: if this heaven that passes away were the only thing,

and had come into being for its own sake, there might be grounds for asking why it passes away. But if it came into being for the sake of something else, it must pass away so that the one for whose sake it came into being may be seen.

Likewise, those shells of [?], which are very beautiful and whose shape is perfectly preserved on every side, must be broken so that the chick for whose sake they came into being may look out and be seen.
So too this heaven surrounding the world passes away, so that the King himself may appear in glory to the good alone.”

Simon said, “The heaven that came into being from God certainly does not pass away. For things that are eternal come from the one who is eternal, and perishable things come from one who is perishable.”
Peter said, “Not necessarily. Perishable things do come from perishable things. But from the one who does not perish, things do not necessarily come into being as perishable or perishable [?],

but as God their maker wills. For things that come into being and continue to exist do not constitute a law opposed to God's power. The law for things that come into being is that they should exist as their maker wills.”

Simon said, “I am bringing you back to that earlier statement you made: that God is not seen now because of the wicked, so that they may not see him and be able to live forever amid good things. For this reason, at another time—”
After he made this visible heaven visible only to the pure and righteous, does it not then seem to you
that this contradicts that declaration of the Law which says that God said, ‘No human being can see me and live’?
Peter answered him: ‘To those who did not receive the Law from the seat of Moses, this true statement of mine seems contradictory, although it is not so. Listen, then, to how it is not.

‘The angels see God, but human beings, as long as they are human beings, cannot see God. At the resurrection of the dead, however, those who become like angels can see him. Thus there is no contradiction.
‘Otherwise, our Teacher himself would not have said, “Blessed are those who are pure in heart, for they will see God.” By saying this, he indicated the world to come, in which they also become like
angels.’ After these words and many others like them that followed, Simon threatened him and said, ‘Only satisfy me on the question of the soul,
whether it is mortal, and I will follow you and submit to your will. But you are to speak about this tomorrow, for today has passed.’
Then, when Peter had finished, Simon left, and very few of his own followers left with him; they were ashamed as well. All the rest of the others sought refuge with Peter.
They knelt on their knees, and those among them who had all kinds of illnesses and pains, and those who had demons, were healed and cleansed through Peter’s prayer.
They departed joyfully, their minds filled with the true teaching concerning God. Those of our household and our friends remained, and they spread a place on the ground
for us. Each of us reclined in his own place, where he knew he had reclined [?] during the day. Thus we ate our food, gave thanks and praise, and went inside and slept.
The next day Peter rose during the night, as was his custom, for the task appointed to him. He found us all ready and began to speak as follows:
‘I ask and implore you, my brothers and companions: if anyone cannot stay awake, he should not force himself out of embarrassment before me. For what someone cannot do immediately,
he can accomplish over a long time. For since we come from different habits, it is over different periods
and long stretches of time that we can change and adapt. For habit is a second nature. For bear witness for me that, since we come from different habits, it is over different periods
and long stretches of time that we can change and adapt. For habit is a second nature. God is my witness that I am not troubled

if someone does not stay awake, but rather if someone sleeps all night and does not make up during the day for what he missed at night. For it is fitting and right that he should constantly attend to the teaching,
so that the mind may contain only the remembrance of God. For where the remembrance of him is, evil cannot creep in.’
When Peter said these things, we all earnestly and eagerly assured him, saying, ‘We had our fill of sleep a good while ago and woke up, but we were embarrassed to wake you,
because it is not fitting for disciples to give orders to their benefactor, although we were strongly compelled to take the liberty. For our heart and mind leap within us from joy in these words,
driving sleep away and banishing it. Because of our love for the teaching, they urged us to give this precedence and honor, and compelled us to wake you.’
Peter said, ‘Since, then, you have acknowledged that it is out of love for these words that you keep vigil and remain awake,

I now wish not only to recall the discussion about the things spoken of yesterday and lovingly hand it on to you in full, with all the proper order, but also to recall the discussions that take place each day,
in whatever inquiry falls to us, every night, when we have more opportunity to speak among ourselves, remembering them in their order and supplying whatever is lacking in them.’
Having said this, he began to show us the order in which the inquiry into the matters of the previous day ought to have proceeded, but had not, because of his opponent’s empty boasting.
And I admired the opponent’s arrogance—or his ignorance. For this reason I acknowledge that you spoke profoundly and completely dismantled and refuted the opponent’s arguments.
But as for my arguments, you did not state all of them, nor did you state them clearly. So complete for us the discussion of our arguments, as they deserve, in their proper order.
But since it was now dawn, he went outside and, as on the previous day, turned and prayed. Then he came and stood in the place where he had stood the previous day.

He saw that a large crowd had gathered, and that Simon was standing in the middle of the crowd, as he had yesterday, in his customary manner. He greeted them and said, “I think it is right for us to feel sorrow
and mourn over certain people who approach us and ask to learn from us, but when we begin to teach them,
secretly want to be our teachers. For they ask questions as though they were ignorant,

but argue against us as though they were knowledgeable. Yet perhaps one of you will consider this and say, ‘Someone who asks a question asks in order to learn. But when he hears and realizes that the answer is incorrect,
he replies.’ Many people think this amounts to contradicting the speaker, but in truth it is one question following another.
But I say that learning has a first stage, a second, and a third—a third [?]—

and a third [?], and countless others. These can be discovered if they are investigated. But if they are pursued out of order, they seem impossible to discover. For this reason, one must first observe the order of the initial stages.

Whatever someone is seeking, he must first seek and find what properly comes first. In this way he takes the beginning of the road. Having traveled easily through the first stage, he also runs through the second.
From the second, in turn, he finds the third still more easily. The farther he travels, the more the good road is revealed to him and opens up, until he reaches that city of truth

which he wished to reach. But someone who is ignorant and foolish, who does not know the paths of inquiry, is like a complete stranger by nature [?]. He will not bear to resemble someone who belongs to the city. Outside the gate of [?],
he is shut out and remains outside. And so, in the darkness of night, without any order, along paths to destruction,

he travels where they lead. Therefore, since these matters are discovered when they are investigated in their proper order, but the foolish and ignorant person does not know the proper order of inquiry, it is fitting and right that he should either submit to someone knowledgeable—
being himself untrained—or first learn the rules of inquiry and its proper order. Only then should he engage in questions and answers about these matters.”
Simon answered him, “Then truth does not belong to everyone, but only to those who know its knowledge [?] and the proper order of inquiry. This is unfair: although there is one God,
not everyone is equally able to discover and know what pleases him.”
Peter said, “They all came from him equally, and they are equally capable of discovering the truth. For not even one of those
who are considered knowledgeable became knowledgeable in a single day. Rather, a person is born knowing nothing at all, and afterward, as a second step, takes up inquiry.
For the human mind is equipped for every kind of knowledge. Who does not know that those who have learned these things did not know them before?”
Simon said, “What you say is true.”
Peter said, “If, then, in worldly trades people first learn and then teach, it is all the more necessary for those who promise to provide for souls
to learn first and then teach. They should not promise knowledge to others while they themselves are ignorant.”
Simon said, “But in worldly trades, everyone who has learned is certain that he knows. Here, however, the listener does not always understand what is his own [?].”
Peter said, “Someone who listens in an orderly way, as is fitting and appropriate, knows the truth. But because he does not want to submit to the authority of its rules of conduct,
