which follow from the truth, he does not admit that he has been persuaded. Likewise, many people, after learning trades, abandon them as unsuitable for themselves and turn to doing something else. To relieve their feelings about this
foolishness of abandoning what they learned, they contrive to speak disparagingly and insultingly about the trade they abandoned.”
Simon said, “Everyone who heard ought to have believed that what he heard was true.”
Peter said, “Indeed, those who listen in an orderly way to things that accord with the truth,

since they cannot speak against them, truly recognize them. If they wish to live by them, they also hasten to acknowledge them. But the fact that others hear and are unwilling to devote themselves to doing good shows that it lies within their own power
to do what they wish. If, however, all those who heard were either deceived
or unpersuaded, then being persuaded would have been a matter of nature, since everyone’s course would always have been the same. For just as it is impossible to persuade someone to become short
or tall, because nature does not allow it, so too, in truth, if everyone were changed by the message,
or remained unchanged, it would have been nature that determined that everyone should always be changed by the message, or that no one should ever be changed.”
Simon answered him, “Then teach us what someone who loves the truth ought to learn first.”
Peter said, “Before anything else, we ought to investigate what a person can succeed in discovering through inquiry. For it is very necessary, since God is going to judge everyone for their actions,
that a person should be willing to act in this way and should also readily know what is good or evil. For this reason I say
that no one can discover what anything is like unless he first applies himself to the things for which he will be judged. As for things beyond these,
the prophet alone knows them. This takes priority. For why do people need, or why are they required, to learn how the world came into being? For those,
however, who wish to live in fear of the one who made them, it is fitting to learn this. Yet I do not think that people can become God’s fellow craftsmen,
so that they should puzzle over and occupy themselves with how he made it. For they will not be judged for failing to learn how the world came into being,

but concerning knowledge of the one who made it: that they should know him to be just, and concerning the way of righteousness that they can learn. For this reason, even if someone knows that he alone is good, this
knowledge is not enough for his salvation and life. For although everyone now enjoys his gift, those who have only come to know that he is good, and for whom this knowledge alone has sufficed, die

without having done anything more than those who did not know him. But those who have also known his justice and done the things that follow from this knowledge of theirs will also enjoy forever the good things that are to come.
For this reason he used to say first of all to those Hebrews who knew him, ‘Seek his righteousness first,’ since they knew that he was good but did not know his justice.
Because of this they did not understand [?], as though they had a God who was only good, and they did not know that he was also just. He is good in this world
of the present, so that everyone may be able to live. But he is just in the judgment to come, so that salvation and everlasting life may belong only to those who are worthy.”
Simon said, “How can the very same one be both good and just?”
And Peter said, “Without justice, the good one is necessarily unjust. For it belongs to a good person to give sunshine and rain equally to everyone, both the just and the unjust.
Thus, insofar as he gives, he is good; but insofar as he gives equally to the wicked and the good, he is unjust—unless he now gives sunshine and rain for the sake of the wheat seed,
for nourishment, while thorns also grow along with it until the harvest, when justice overtakes kindness: the thorns are taken outside, and the wheat is gathered inside. So too,
now, when the just and the unjust enjoy his gifts equally, he is good because of his generosity. But on the day of judgment, when the just enter his kingdom
and the unjust go outside, his justice is revealed. Otherwise, if the wicked remained forever on equal terms with the good, this would necessarily have to be regarded as not only
no kindness at all, but even injustice, or a lack of discrimination and judgment, since the good have a share with him equal to that of the wicked.”
And Simon said, “I want assurance about just one thing: whether the soul is immortal. For I cannot take the burden of righteousness upon myself unless
I am first assured of this. For if it is not immortal, none of these foundations of reverence for God can stand.”
And Peter said, “First let us investigate whether God is just. If that is established, I will establish everything concerning reverence for him and his teaching.”
And Simon said, “I think you pride yourself on knowing the proper order of an argument, yet now you have given an answer out of order. For when I asked
to learn how the soul is immortal, so that I might accept these promises of yours, you said, ‘First let us investigate whether he is just.’”
And Peter said, “This is far more appropriate, beyond comparison.”
And Simon said, “I want to learn.”
And Peter said, “Listen, then. Some people blasphemed against him and committed injustice, enjoyed themselves, and died a natural death in their beds.
They were granted an honorable burial by their own people. But other people praised him and acted justly, endured hunger in poverty, and died as martyrs for righteousness, and were not even
granted burial. Where, then, is God’s justice if the soul is not immortal, so that what each person lacks [?] may be made up to it? I say
that for the one who enjoyed himself wickedly, [?] there; but for the one who endured all these afflictions because of his righteousness, there is enjoyment there of everlasting good things.”

And Simon said, “This very thing leads us not to believe: many good people suffered affliction and departed from the world miserably, while many wicked people enjoyed themselves wickedly and died peacefully at a very old age.”
And Peter said, “This very thing that leads you not to believe convinces us that there will be judgment at some time. For once our God is known to be just, there must be another world
in which everyone receives the consequences of what they have done by their own free choice and power, and God’s justice [?] is revealed.
But if each person now received according to what they did, we would be liars when we say that there will be judgment at some time,

if everyone now received what they deserved. Therefore, the fact that each person does not now invariably receive according to their deeds convinces all of us who know that God is just that there will be judgment.”
And Simon said, “Why, then, am I not convinced?”
And Peter said, “Because you have not listened to the true prophet, who says, ‘Seek his righteousness first, and all these things will be added to you.’”
And Simon said, “Leave me alone, for I do not want to investigate his justice first, before I know whether the soul is immortal.”
Peter said, “Only allow me this: not to do anything beyond what the true Prophet advised us to do when he was with us.”
Simon said, “You plainly show that you cannot demonstrate that the soul is immortal. For this reason,
you wish to do so, knowing that if it is shown to be mortal, all those promises of the fear of God are dissolved and nullified. This is why your mind is set against me.
But I do not commend your progress, for you persuade many wicked human souls to overcome pleasure and desire through hope and expectation of those good things to come,
with the result that they neither enjoy the things here nor obtain the things there, because at the very moment they die, their soul dies too.”
When Peter heard these things, he quietly ground his teeth, wiped his face, sighed, and said, “You are an evil reptile,
and the gall of the deceiving serpent is in you. For at the beginning you professed, like a wise man, that you wished to learn, but like the serpent you tried to make people believe in many gods.
When you were refuted on this point, you asserted and said that there is no God at all, and that it was necessary and right either that there should be someone greater than this God
of truth who created and made the world, since this one is evil, or that there should be many like him, or that there should be no God at all.
Then, when you could not demonstrate these things either, you said that the soul is mortal,
so that no one would live righteously in the hope of goodness. For no one can live in luxury and pleasure unless he wrongs others.
But let us set this aside, so that at another time I may give the appropriate answer concerning these matters. You are determined to bring all this turmoil into this miserable world,
yet you say that you yourself are virtuous, while you say that I am wicked,

because I do not allow people, for the sake of [?] virtue, to take up the tares of discord, fight one another, plunder, and destroy for their own pleasure and desire, as though this were the advantage
of every person: to enjoy himself and live in luxury, since there is no other hope. But what pleasure do those who struggle and fight one another have? For those who do evil to their neighbors must
themselves suffer the same or similar things from them, either inwardly or outwardly. But I know that you are a leader and guide in war, not peace, and in injustice and wickedness,
not righteousness and law. For injustice is the mother of plunder and sins, while law is the father of peace. Even now, it was not because I could not demonstrate

that the soul is immortal that I was moved to anger. I wish to demonstrate the very thing you requested. For I will explain this too, but not as though you had compelled me. I also know how to explain it [?]. And I am not persuading you alone,
but reminding you, while giving full instruction to those who do not know, whenever it is appropriate.”
Simon said, “But if you are angry, I cannot even learn. You do not even want me to listen.”
Peter said, “If you are looking for an excuse because you want to run away, you are free to run away even without an excuse. For everyone has heard
these words of yours, which make nothing known. You have said and demonstrated nothing, but have merely made assertions. And when you heard what was said, you spoke against it.
Anyone can do this: after all the demonstrations, say, ‘You have said nothing.’ But to show that I can convince you with one statement that the soul is immortal,
I will ask you something everyone knows. Tell me, and with one statement I will convince you that the soul is immortal.”
Simon had found this excuse—that Peter was angry—and was preparing to run away, but he stayed because of the greatness of the promise.
And he persisted, saying, “Answer the question I asked you—the thing you said everyone knows—so that I may hear, in a single statement, as you promised, how the soul is immortal.”
Peter said, “I will speak to you as someone who knows and understands beyond everyone else. Only answer me this: which can more effectively convince someone who does not believe—sight or hearing?”
Simon answered, “Sight is more effective.”
Peter said, “Why, then, do you ask me to convince you about the soul through words, when you are convinced through an actual deed?”
Simon said, “I do not understand what you are saying.”
Peter said, “If you know me [?], go to your house and enter your inner room.

There you will see an image set up for you, bearing the likeness of a boy who died a violent death, wrapped in purple garments. Ask him, and he will teach you simply by appearing; and if you wish, he will also speak with you.
But why do you need to hear from him whether the soul is immortal, when it is present and visible?
For how can something that does not exist be seen? But if you do not know which image I mean, let us go to your house immediately with ten men.”

When Simon heard this from him, he took it to heart and became absorbed in thought, and his face turned pale. As I suppose, he was afraid that, if he denied it, this matter would be investigated [?] through him, or that Peter would become angry about it
and openly state it and expose it, and that he himself would be still more severely rebuked and exposed before everyone. He answered,
“I ask you, Peter, to overcome the evil in me with your goodness and accept my repentance. You can have me as a helper in your preaching.
For now I have learned through actual experience that you are indeed a prophet of the true God, since you alone know these hidden things about people.”
Peter said, “You see, brothers, that Simon has now repented. In a little while you will see him persisting in his wickedness again.
For he thinks I am a prophet because I revealed these evil things he has done in secret, and he has promised to repent.
But I will not lie about myself in this matter, which I am not permitted to do, regardless of whether this wicked man lives or does not live.

For heaven and earth are my witnesses that it was not through prophecy that I told him these things, which I mentioned somewhat obscurely before the crowds, as was appropriate. Rather, it was from certain people who used to be his helpers
and who now share my faith that I learned them and spoke of them. That is why I learned and told these things; I did not speak through foreknowledge, as you have heard.”

When Simon heard these things, he began to insult him and cause a disturbance, saying, “You abusive man, full of deceit! Learn how you have won by chance, not by truth. For I did not speak as someone who needed knowledge

and say that I had repented. Rather, I wanted you to think that I had repented and was your disciple, so that you would set out and tell all these hidden things you promise, and I could expose you in the end.
But because you are crafty and realized that I said I had repented as a [?], you agreed with me as though you had not recognized the trick,
so that you could first show before these crowds that I am ignorant. You realized that after this exposure
I would be driven by anger to admit that I had not truly wanted to repent, and you spoke of my wickedness in advance,
so that victory would always be yours, whether I persisted in the repentance I had professed or did not persist.
And in this too you are clever, because you knew beforehand, while I was defeated as though in a storm, because I had not recognized your deceit beforehand.”
But you have learned about me. You therefore resorted to trickery and won by chance, not in truth. But I know why
you did not know that I am the one who stands. In my kindness I spoke with you and received you. But now I will show you my divinity [?], so that you will fall down and worship me.
I am the first power, and I had no beginning to my existence, for I have always existed. I entered Rachel’s womb and was born as a human being so that I could appear to human beings.
I flew and mingled with fire and air, and I gave souls to statues. I turned stones into bread, flew from mountain to mountain, was carried by the hands of angels, and came down to earth.
I did not do these things only once in the past; I can also do them now, so that through deeds I may convince everyone that I myself am that Jesus of yours who stands forever.

And I can raise up those who believe in me. But your words are empty and cannot demonstrate anything in practice, in truth, just as the one who sent you, who was a magician, could not even save himself from the cross.
When Simon said these things, Peter answered him in reply [?]:

Do not attribute these things of yours to others. For by the things you have done, you have admitted that you are a magician, and you have been openly exposed. But our teacher, who is the Son of God and the Son of Man, is good.

Yes, Jesus alone is truly the Son of God. This was said when it was appropriate, and it is said again. But unless you admit that you are a magician, I will go to your house with many others. Then it will be known and revealed that he is a magician.
When Peter said these things, Simon began to blaspheme, so that there would be an uproar and his exposure would not be noticed.
But Peter, because of his insults [?], restrained himself [?], so that he would not be thought to have been defeated.

When Peter therefore approached again [?] and persisted in wanting to expose him, the crowd became angry with Simon. They pushed him out through the courtyard gate, and only one person followed him as he went out.
Then, when there was silence, Peter began to say, “My brothers, you must patiently [?] bear with evil people, knowing this: even God himself, who could

cut them off beforehand and destroy them [?], bears with them until that day which he has appointed, when everyone will be judged. Should we not, therefore, also bear with what God himself bears with? And why
should we not also bear insults with humility and purity of soul, when even the one who is honored above all is insulted? Although he can avenge himself, he does not wish to do so now, so
that his patience may also become known and all the wicked may be exposed. For if the evil one had not found Simon, he could have found someone else. For stumbling blocks must come into the world.

But woe to those through whom they come! For this reason we ought to grieve and be distressed over Simon, because he has become a chosen instrument of the evil one. He would not have led him astray and set him up as a teacher

unless he had gained power over him. For what does it matter even if he has not believed in our Jesus, especially since he has convinced himself that souls do not die? For what does it matter even if demons are caught through him?
Yet he thinks that he has the soul of a boy who died a violent death to serve him [?], though it is really a demon.
For this reason I said what I said about him in accordance with what he has in mind. But he has also heard from the Jews that there will be a judgment.

For the evil one appears to those who, while in the true faith, do wrong and sin without repenting, as to traitors, through their sins [?], and is caught through those in whom there is no longer any room for repentance.
Therefore, you who repent and turn back, kneel before God.”
When Peter said these things, the whole crowd knelt down. Peter raised his eyes to heaven and prayed with weeping and tears that God himself, in his mercy and kindness,
would receive those who had drawn near to him. After praying, he said, “Gather early tomorrow,” and dismissed the crowd. Then, as was our custom, we ate a meal and went to sleep.

Then Peter himself rose at the hour of the night appointed for him, saw that we were all awake, and greeted us. Nicetas was the first to say to him, “If you permit me, my lord Peter, I have something to say.”
Peter said, “I give permission not only to you but to all of you, and not only now but at any time, so that everyone may disclose the part of his soul that pains him,

and healing may be provided for him. For troubles that are kept silent, because they remain unknown to us, linger and persist in the soul and produce in it a suffering that is difficult to heal. Therefore I cannot
offer those who remain silent a word that is useful and appropriate for them, unless those who are suffering disclose the part that pains them. But when they do not disclose it, God alone
can provide suitable healing. As for us, we can reach someone who remains silent and conceals things in his mind only after a long time.
For as we proceed in order from the beginning, we must reach everyone through all the demonstrations. For it is impossible, when we encounter all
the objections raised against us and their solutions, that we should not at some point also address the particular matter that someone needs.
Yet this can involve a very long delay. With the orderly arrangement as its aid, as I said, it can accomplish everything that is needed. But now, too, say whatever you wish.”
Nicetas said, “We acknowledge, Peter, that you are generous. But what I wish to learn is this: why can Simon, who acts in opposition to God, do such things?
For he did not lie about any of the things that he openly admitted he had done.”
Peter began to speak as follows: “There is one God, and he wishes to provide good friends for his firstborn Son. But because he knows that they cannot be good unless they are given
understanding and a free will that governs itself, so that by their own will they may be whatever they wish—for otherwise those who are not like this are not [?] good,
unless they are what they are by their own will, since they cannot be anything else—for this reason he entrusted them with this authority, to be whatever they wish.
Moreover, he knew beforehand that, because they have freedom through their self-governing will, some of them would choose to do good things and others evil things, and thus
the whole multitude of humanity would fall into two distinct groups. For each of the two groups there would be a king whom they themselves chose,

and he allowed each to have a place. The first of them to reign delighted in corruption, while the other, who reigns over the good, delighted in good things. He commanded [?] to shine upon the righteous and save them.

Thus decrees were laid down beforehand for both of these by a law that cannot be transgressed. Since there are many people with us, I wish to recall something useful concerning these matters—not for your sake, Clement,
for I previously gave you [?] an account of predestination, but for the sake of those gathered here with us, so that Nicetas too
may learn the explanation of the matter he asked about: for what reason Simon, who is reckoned an adversary, can, in opposition to me, a herald [?] of the truth,
perform such wonders. First, then, God has decreed this: that a person is evil who
despises what benefits him, which he receives when he asks for it. For how can someone who is so good and loves humanity fail to love himself?
And whose enemy is someone who has been unable to be his own friend? Therefore, so that those who choose evil may be clearly seen,

as well as those who wish to live in goodness, God himself concealed this great benefit, namely, possession of the kingdom of heaven. But how was he to hide the treasure and put it where it would not be found, so that no one could find it by his own power?

And the report about it has reached the hearing of everyone in every generation under distinct names, so that those who did not seek what would help them may be shown to be wicked in their contempt for their own benefit, and may be deprived of what they did not wish to acquire.

But those who, out of love for truth, sought what would [?] them and were shown to be good will find it—not by their own power, but by the will of the one who hid it, so that to the righteous who seek it
he may grant that they find it. Therefore, if someone loves it more than anything else, he can receive it; but if not, he does not even know it.
For even if he is wiser than everyone else—when I say that he must love it more than anything else, I mean more than wealth, comfort, desire, parents, relatives, and friends, resolutely stripping off
habit, preconception, contempt, and things like these. Therefore, if someone seeks this wisely, he can find it.
But if someone is rich and gives first place and honor to wealth here, and loves praise, he has what he valued first. Yet he does not know whether even this will last.
And if he chooses desire, he takes pleasure in it as much as he can, not as much as he wishes. But if he loves comfort—
for what is there that gives lasting comfort? And if someone honors anything else before God, he is a fool. For if it is parents, they die;
if it is relatives, they do not last; and if it is friends, what friend is there who does not fear God? And if he clings to a preconception, it is not the truth.
But if he scorns receiving what would help him, he is wholly wicked, so that in his wickedness he far surpasses the very head of wickedness. For that one has conformed to the role permitted him

and does not use God's goodness rightly; but this person has despised his own help, so that he will not be saved and live. Therefore, because of people like these—I mean those who despise it—they have been removed from the world.
As a test for all those who are now [?], ten pairs, like that demonstration in Egypt. For once, when the people were living there as foreigners, Moses appeared and asked [?]
the king of the Egyptians to let the Hebrew people leave Egypt, so that they could return and come to the land of their ancestors.
He promised ten times, and likewise broke his promise ten times. Because of this, every time he broke his promise, he suffered a plague along with all the Egyptians.
And whenever he repented, he was delivered again. He himself was the cause of their suffering these terrible things ten times, together with the Egyptians who shared his outlook.
For when Moses [?], at God's command, demanded the people, the king from whom they were being demanded told Moses to give him a miracle as a sign,
of some kind. At God's command, he threw the staff he was holding onto the ground, and it truly became a snake. But while the king was immediately being persuaded under compulsion,
that wicked faction, who were magicians by their own free choice and will, thought they could do something resembling what had happened through faith in God.

And they turned the king and the Egyptians away, so that they would not believe willingly, as they ought. Because of the resemblance, they thought that Moses had not been sent by God to demand the people,

and that he could do this since the magicians too, as they supposed, could do similar things. Yet the very name “magicians” was enough to make it known that what happened through them occurred by mental suggestion, just as the tradition itself is known
concerning how far those magicians were able, as has been said, to perform similar things. But the final plague was the death of their firstborn.
When Moses sacrificed a lamb and redeemed the people with blood, they eventually offered them gifts along with their pleading, and asked them all to leave. So it is also
now in our own time: I see these things happening among us. For just as at that time, when Moses was persuading the king with signs and wonders,
and for the Egyptians to believe in God. But those magicians, by drawing attention to the similar things they were doing, were hindering the unjust from being saved.
So now, too, when I have gone out to persuade people from the nations through signs to believe in the true God, this same Simon the magician
stands against me and does things that seem similar to mine, just as his teachers also stood against Moses,
the servant, so that those among the nations who judge matters unjustly may be exposed, while those who judge justly may be saved and live.
While Peter was saying these things, Nicetas said, “I ask you, since something has come to my mind, to allow me to say what I wish.”
Peter was pleased with the disciples’ eagerness and told him to speak.
Nicetas said, “What wrong, then, did those Egyptians do at that time by not believing Moses, since the magicians also did similar things, even if only in appearance?
Indeed, if I had been there at that time, would I not, because the magicians did similar things, also have thought that Moses was a magician?

Or I would have thought that those magicians, too, acted by God’s will, reasoning that magicians could not do things resembling those of someone sent by God, even for a short time. And again, as for the things happening now:
what wrong do those who believe Simon because of such wonders do? Or are they not wonders—

his flying in the air, mingling with fire, making statues walk, and showing stone dogs barking like living creatures? For they do not know how to distinguish fraudulent wonders from those that truly happen.
And besides these things, he appears to have turned stones into bread and performed other great deeds. But if someone who believes because of
wonders does wrong, how could anyone not say [?] that those who believed in our Lord because of the signs and wonders he performed also did wrong?”
Peter said, “I welcome your eagerness, because you have not concealed the thing in your soul that was troubling your faith. For because of
this it can also receive healing. Do you remember that I said that the worst person of all is someone who scorns learning what would benefit him?”
Nicetas said, “I remember.”
Peter said, “And also this: how God himself has hidden his truth so that he may grant those who seek out of love for the truth to find it.”
Nicetas said, “I have not forgotten that either.”

Peter said, “What, then, do you think? Did God bury his truth in the earth and put a mountain over it, so that people would have to dig a great deal and labor to find it? No, it is not like that. Rather, just as the earth and mountains are covered by the covering
of heaven, so too are his purposes, which he [?] should be hidden, so that they may be found by those who are worthy. As I said before, in all
those pairs, the first to come is evil, while the second is good, so that whoever approaches matters justly, whether he is simple
or wise, will always encounter the truth. For if [?], when the first comes, the simple person believes his words and signs,
then afterward, when the true one comes, he makes the first unworthy of belief. Thus the simple person, who chose to believe everyone, believes the second, who is good, and changes. And how

he learns that he ought not to believe everyone, you will understand from what follows and from the order of what is being said. But if he is not persuaded by the second, he is found to be unjust [?], because he has unjustly
committed injustice: namely, believing the first but not believing the second. For let him say why he believed the first and why he did not believe the second.”
But he cannot say this, for a simple person is guileless and has not approached these matters through investigation, but without discernment and at random,
has thrown himself into them at random, as though this were acceptable, as those who worship idols suppose—those who, through evil habit, love the things that harm
them and do not wish, through knowledge, to distance these evils from themselves. They perish, imagining that they are harming us.
If, then, we are to concede something impossible to those who despise their own benefit because they persist in evil, then also to those
who are simple in the fear of God—that is, guileless—it must be granted that they truly encounter the truth. These things have been said about simple people.
But if someone who is wise also approaches these matters unjustly, his wisdom does nothing to help him attain virtue. For it is right that, toward the
first one who came, he should either disbelieve or believe, and that he should act in the same way toward the second. I mean that if he knows the truth and did not believe the first,
he should not believe the second either. For, being healthy, he has no need of a physician to heal him. But if someone believes the first, he should also believe the second.
For when he is wounded by the first one's deception, he needs the second one to heal him. So now you have heard why the evil one
came first, and the good one second. As for signs and wonders, together with the things that result from them,
[?] distinguish these wonders. For the evil one performs wonders that have no benefit, while the good one performs those that are helpful. For it is of no benefit
to display statues that walk, stone dogs that bark, or mountains that leap—these and similar things that they say Simon once performed.
But all the things our Lord performed are helpful: he made the blind see, the deaf hear, and the lame and crippled become straight.
He also drove out demons, healed the sick, and raised the dead, just like all these things that you also see me doing—
things that bring help and mercy to human beings. The evil one also performs them, but only once, at the end, when he mixes in good signs,
that is, when he drives out demons and makes diseases flee. Because of this, since he has crossed his own boundaries, divided against himself, and fought against those
who belong to him, he is stripped of the authority that was left to him. For he has encroached on the boundaries belonging to the Majesty, to enter the righteous, who have learned

that a good [?] produces good fruit, and the evil one bad fruit. Those who are to learn beforehand should learn that in the ninth pair the evil one comes with the things belonging to the good one, and in the
tenth pair he performs beneficial wonders, so that, if possible, he might deceive even the elect, and they would all perish. There are, then, ten pairs, beginning with Adam:
Cain and Abel; the second is the one in Noah's days; the third, Pharaoh and Abraham; the fourth, the Philistines and Isaac; the fifth, Esau and Jacob;

the sixth, John and the lawgiver; the seventh, the tempter and the Son of Man; the eighth, Simon [?] and me, Peter; the ninth, the sowing of weeds and the gospel sent out for conversion, when the sanctuary is uprooted

and they set up an abomination to bring about its desolation; and the tenth, the one opposed to Christ and Christ himself. The one opposed to Christ comes and performs helpful miracles, through which those are deceived
who did not first believe the one who, in the ninth pair, gave advance warning and proclaimed eternal life, if they remain righteous and are not deceived by the evil one's messiahship.
Then the whole situation takes a different course, as I will explain fully another time in a lengthy account concerning the pairs.
When Peter had said these things, Aquila said to him, “Indeed, constant instruction is needed, so that a person may always apply himself to each of these things.”
Peter answered him, “Who, then, undertakes the effort of constant learning,
except someone who loves his soul and wishes to save it? He inquires about everything, seeking where he can constantly hear the word. He alone is wise
in the judgment of the true prophet: the person who wishes above all to live and save his soul. For who would undertake to cast everything aside and preserve his soul for its help and benefit,
except someone who is wise? He knows how great the difference is between temporary things and eternal things,
between these little things and things without limit, and between human beings and God, who can do everything. And who expects to receive eternal good things except a good person?
And who is good except someone who loves God? And who loves God except someone who is always acquainted with his wisdom?
And how can anyone become acquainted with it unless he constantly listens to it, marvels at it, and honors it, lovingly longing for the things that belong to it? He considers it a great loss
whenever he is compelled to speak about anything else, even for an instant. For a soul filled with the love of God cannot look at or contemplate anything else

except what pleases him. For those who are unwilling first to see in their minds the things that please him, and then to speak accordingly, are like people who have remained in deep darkness and cannot see the heavenly light.
Even before they begin investigating great matters, they grow weary. For they have roused themselves amid the evils of error,
and when they hear about God, as though through speech in which they find no rest [?], they are enlightened by the law and distressed by it.”
While Peter was saying these things, dawn broke. One of Simon’s disciples came, crying out and lamenting, and said, “I beg you, Peter, receive me, a wicked man who was nearly
carried away by Simon the magician. For I clung to him as though to the heavenly God, marveling at him because of the wonders he performed.
But when you spoke with him, he was exposed and shown to be an evil man. No one followed him, and I alone went out with him.
For I had not yet fully recognized that wicked man for what he was. He saw that I was following him and said to me, ‘You are blessed.’
He took me to his house, and in the middle of the night he began saying to me, ‘I will make you greater than all other people,
if you are willing to remain with me to the end.’ When I promised him that I would always remain with him,
he demanded an oath from me that I would remain faithful to him. Then he tied up a bundle of unclean and secret things and made me carry it. He instructed me to carry it, and when we came to the sea,
his boat was there. He went aboard alone and took that bundle. A little later he came out without
the bundle he had taken in with him. It is clear that he threw it into the depths of the sea. He asked me to travel with him immediately, saying, ‘When I go to Rome,
I can succeed in all this, so that people will think I am God and I will be honored by everyone. Then I will make you rich in silver.
And if you wish to return here, I will send you back with a great deal.’ But when I heard these things from him and saw that there was nothing of God’s promise in them,
and realized that he was a magician and a deceiver, I said to him, ‘I beg you, let me stay, because my legs hurt, and for this reason I cannot leave Caesarea.
Besides, I also have a wife and young children, and I cannot leave them.’
But when he heard these things, he insulted and reviled me. He went out alone toward [?] and said, “You will regret this when you hear what happens to me in Rome.”
After saying these things, he departed, apparently for Rome, while I came here immediately,
so that you might receive me, for I regret the things with which I was formerly occupied.
When the man who had come in to us said these things, Peter told him to wait in a place in the courtyard. While he was waiting, Peter came.
He entered and saw that the crowd was larger than on any previous day. He stood in the same place [?] as yesterday and pointed out to them the man who had come in to him.
He began to speak as follows: “My brothers, this man whom I am pointing out to you came to me earlier and told me about Simon’s sorcery:
how he threw his magical equipment into the depths of the sea, not because he had repented, but because he was afraid of being exposed and found out.
He made a request of this man, as the man says, and also promised him gifts of this world.
But when, as the man says, he would not agree to his request, Simon reviled and insulted him and departed. As he says, Simon intends to make his journey to Rome.”
When Peter had said these things, that same man who had come in to us openly recounted all these secret and evil things about Simon and his deeds to the crowds nearby.
When the people were distressed over Simon’s sorcery and his evil deeds, Peter said to them, “Do not be distressed over what has passed.
Instead, beware of what is to come. For the things that have passed have reached their end, but the things to come have a struggle

to bring upon those who fall into them. For stumbling blocks are never removed from the world as long as the adversary is permitted to act shamelessly according to his will, so that those who are discerning
and love instruction may escape and be saved, while those among us who lack discernment and have no regard for themselves may fall into the hands of deceivers and be trapped. For
therefore, since, as you too have heard, Simon has gone out to be the first to gain the obedience of the Gentiles who have been called to salvation and life, I too must go out after him
and correct and turn back the Gentiles whom he is corrupting. But it is right that I should take greater care of you yourselves, since you are now within the wall of life.
For if someone who has already been gained is lost, the loss is great. But if someone who has not yet been gained is won over, that is a gain.

And if not, the loss consists only in his not having been gained. Therefore, so that you yourselves may be more firmly established in the truth, and those Gentiles who have been called to life may not be too far overtaken by evil,
I want to appoint Zacchaeus as your shepherd. I myself will remain with you for three months from today, and then go out to the Gentiles, so that I may reach them too,
lest, after being too far overtaken by Simon’s sorcery, they find it difficult to be healed.”
When he said these things, the whole assembly wept, because they heard that he was going to leave.
Peter himself was choked with grief over them and also wept. He raised his eyes to heaven and said, “We ask you, God of heaven and earth,
who established everything in them: comfort and encourage those who take refuge in you and are distressed. For it is because of their love for you that they love me,
because I am their teacher of your truth. Therefore, guard and save them with your merciful right hand, for neither Zacchaeus nor any other human being is able
to be their guardian.” After saying these things and what followed them, he laid his hand on Zacchaeus.
And he prayed over him that he might fulfill the office of bishop without reproach. Then he selected twelve elders and appointed four deacons.
And he said to them, “I have appointed Zacchaeus as your bishop because, along with his fear of God, he also possesses great learning. Since he is the image of Christ,
honor him by obeying him for the sake of your salvation and life. Be assured also of this: the honor and dishonor shown to him reach Christ, and from Christ they
ascend to God. Therefore, listen to his teachings continually and diligently; receive advice and admonition from the elders, and guidance and encouragement from the deacons.
Support the widows, help the orphans, have compassion on the poor, and teach the young to be chaste. To put it briefly, stand by one another and help one another in everything, so that, as
you worship God, the Creator of heaven and earth, believe in Christ, and love one another, you may demonstrate your love in practice.”

After saying these things and others like them, he made this announcement to them: “Since I intend to remain with you for three months, whoever among you is at rest [?] and wishes to be baptized should be baptized, so that the evil deeds he previously committed

may be canceled, and through the good deeds he does from now on he may become an heir to everlasting blessings. But he should approach Zacchaeus, tell him his name, hear from him the mysteries of the coming kingdom, and fast continually.
He should examine himself, and then, when the three months are completed and Passover draws near, he should be baptized. Let everyone among you who wishes be baptized
in flowing water, while the glorious name of the Trinity is pronounced over him, and let him learn what is fitting and right.

First, however, he is anointed with oil consecrated by holy prayer, so that, once you have been sanctified, you may be able to receive holiness.” He said many things to them about baptism, dismissed the crowds, and entered his lodging, as was his custom.
And when we twelve were nearby—I mean Zacchaeus, Zephaniah, Joseph, Micah, Eleazar, Phinehas, Lazarus, Elisha,
myself, Clement, Nicodemus, Nicetas, and Aquila—he spoke as follows: “Let us consider what is right, my brothers. We now have a concern:
how the nations can receive help. For while you were present, you heard what Simon planned and intended, and he has already departed from his place.
It would therefore have been right for us to go after him and expose him wherever he could and wished to act. But because it is wrong

for me to abandon those from his place who have sought refuge with us, and to give priority to the salvation of those who are still far from us in every respect, I decided to remain with those here for three
months, to strengthen them and make them watchful over themselves. Yet I will not entirely abandon those far away, lest those who are first instructed in evil teaching should, after a long time,
find it difficult to turn away from it. For this reason, I wish to do the following, if it also seems good to you. It is right that, in place of Zacchaeus, who has been appointed bishop here,
I should add Benjamin son of Sheba to the number of the twelve; and in place of Clement, whom I have decided should always remain with me,
and who is from the nations and greatly thirsts for the word, Ananias son of Saphra; and in place of Nicetas and Aquila,
who have also only recently become disciples of the word of Christ, Reuben, Zacchaeus’s brother, and Zechariah the builder.” Thus he brought four in place of four
into their number, so that we—myself, Clement, Nicetas, and Aquila—might always remain with him. And he said to those twelve, “I want you
to set out the day after tomorrow among the nations, following Simon, so that you may send word to me and inform me of what he is doing. You will also gain experience of each person’s disposition.
Tell them beforehand about my coming, which is certain to take place. And, to avoid speaking to you at length, prepare them in advance so that they may long for my coming.”

After saying these and similar things, he added, “Concerning these matters, my brothers, let each of you say what seems good to him, lest this proposal, which has pleased me greatly, should in fact be wrong.”
They all praised him as though with one soul, and asked him not to act on their advice,
but simply to command whatever seemed good to him. They said, “At this moment it is fitting and right for us to carry out whatever you command us.”
When they had said this, he sent for Benjamin, Hananiah, Reuben, and Zechariah. When they arrived, he spoke with them too in the same appropriate manner.
Then, one day later, those same men came and said, “Do not think ill of us, my lord Peter.

For we are deeply distressed that we will be deprived of your teaching for three months. Nevertheless, for the sake of helping, we willingly carry out what you have commanded, always seeing your face in our minds.

And now, as you commanded, we are leaving joyfully and peacefully.” He prayed over them and accompanied them on their way. Those sent ahead of him were, in place of Zacchaeus, Benjamin son of Shaba, Zephaniah, Joseph,

Micah, Eliezer, Phinehas, Lazarus, Elisha, and Nicodemus; and in place of Hananiah, and in place of Nicetas and Aquila, Reuben and Zechariah. When they had gone, Peter went in and stood in the place where he usually spoke.

He saw that the crowd was very large and was looking at him and weeping, because the day before he had told them that he would have to leave them because of the urgent matter concerning Simon. He too looked at them,

and it was clear that he was distressed just as they were. For the tears he shed and all his trembling made it plain to them that he too was inwardly sorrowful and distressed, just as they were. Nevertheless, he wiped his face with his hand

and said, “Take courage and be strong, my brothers, for you have compassionate souls. Let us therefore comfort and encourage ourselves with sound thinking, and entrust everything to God, whose will alone we have chosen to honor above all else.
For if, because of my love for you, I were to oppose his will and wish to remain with you, could he not send me by death on a journey along a distant road?
Therefore let us willingly endure this small thing, as righteous people who fear him, since we have resolved and chosen to obey God's own will in everything.
You too profess that you will obey in everything with upright faith. And I know that you love me for no other reason
than your love for him. Therefore, as friends of God, yield to his will and follow it.

Along with these things, consider justice itself: how unjust it would have been if, when you were being led astray by Simon, I had not come to you because I was being held back by the earlier brothers there,

even though you had Zacchaeus, an excellent and good man, who was also skilled in speaking. In the same way, it would also be wicked if I did not go out to those Gentiles who have been thoroughly corrupted and against whom Simon is fighting, because I am being held back by you.

Let us fear and take care lest, through misguided love, we do the will of the evil one. Nevertheless, I will remain with you for three months. During that time, come frequently and eagerly, and listen to the word of life.
When the three months are over, let all those who can rightly accompany me do so. By ‘rightly’ I mean without distressing anyone whom they ought not to distress,
whether a wife who shares his outlook, or anyone else with whom they must remain for some other reason.” He spoke with them every day during those three months.
When Passover drew near, he [?] more than ten thousand there.
During those days he received a letter from those he had sent ahead of him, reporting Simon's evil deeds. The letter described how Simon, from the day he left Caesarea,
was misleading the crowd in every city, insulting and abusing Peter. He stayed a long time in Tripolis.

His whole preparation was directed toward this: that when Peter appeared, no one would even give him a hearing, regarding him as a sorcerer, a godless man, an abusive man, a scoundrel, and an ignoramus,
who promised things that could not happen. He said that the dead rise, which, Simon claimed, was impossible.

That it should be [?]. And he reportedly tries to kill those who rebuke him secretly, through certain men who assist him. “For this reason,” he said, “I defeated him and exposed him, and I was afraid of his treachery and fled, lest he kill me by his sorcery or secretly hand me over to be killed.”
Then Peter himself, when Passover came, before the last day, read the letter to the assembly and spoke with them about obeying Zacchaeus in everything, the man whom he had appointed bishop

for them. Then he entrusted the elders, together with the deacons, to them—to the people themselves. He spoke with them as was fitting and proper, gave them instructions, and told them, “I will wait in Tripolis.”
Now those words spoken there openly before everyone, because of certain people who were unworthy,
were not spoken in full. But privately, among us, as his dear friends, he completed them, and he instructed me to write them in volumes and send them to you.
The first of these volumes contains a discussion of the truth of the prophet and matters concerning the Law, and how he fulfills the seat of Moses.
The second concerns sovereignty and whether it is one or not, and that he does not err concerning the Law of the Hebrews, which is not bounded in any direction.
The third concerns God and the things that were [?] by him.
The fourth explains that, although many have been called gods, there is one who is truly God, as the divine Scriptures testify.
The fifth explains that there are only two heavens. One of them is the visible heaven, which he also made; the other is never seen.

The sixth concerns the good one and the evil one: concerning the good one, that everything is turned over to him by the Father’s will; and concerning the evil one, why, how, and from where he exists, and that he assists goodness through his evil will;
and which signs belong to the good one, which belong to the evil one, and what the distinction is between the second and the pairs.
The seventh concerns the things to which the Twelve testified before the people in the Temple itself.
The eighth concerns the Teacher’s words, and that he is a prophet and does not speak contradictions, although he was thought to do so. He went through these words together with their explanations.
The ninth explains that, having been appointed by God, he alone is righteous in everything, and that he can establish harmony and peace through mercy.
The tenth contains a discussion of birth, including human birth, and birth from water, which is baptism; and, concerning a human being, who it is that distinguishes his seed,
and what the account of his soul is, and how he is free and has authority over himself; and that one who is not [?] to become good is not truly good.
But, as I said before, when he left there, he gave me permission to send you these volumes about the words spoken there. He went ahead with a few people who had departed from Caesarea of Straton.
When we left Caesarea of Straton to go to Tripolis in Phoenicia, we were on the road on the first day. Because we were near the city we had left, a large crowd
of those who had received the teaching came out and accompanied us. On the second day [?], we reached Ptolemais, and we stayed there ten days.
We spoke with some people, and to a few others who were very eager for instruction and wanted to detain us, we promised that we would speak with them in Tripolis.
We made this promise [variant: we agreed] and departed [variant: he departed] from there. We did the same for the people of Tyre, and likewise for the people of Sidon and Beirut,
who also very much wanted to detain us. He told them, “We will wait in Tripolis.” The book of Clement’s first discourse is finished.
[The account of Clement, who accompanied Simon Peter, is finished.]
